title: Ironbound
content: Ironbound The Ironbound are living suits of armor made of black iron, created by the Priests of Pollux in Nerekhall to be beyond the corruption of mortal beings and immune to magic both malign and beneficial, out of fear of ever again falling to the lure of the Ynfernael. These constructs exceeded the expectations of the artificers who made them and soon replaced most of Nerekhall's militia; today they are a common sight on the city's streets, safeguarding the citizenry against flagrant acts of evil magic, and those who claim to have witnessed one malfunction or fail are harshly punished for spreading malicious rumors. Armed with long spears and heavy shields and covered in armor plates bearing special runic wards granting further immunity to destructive magic, the Ironbound are Terrinoth's strongest response to its magic-wielding enemies, though they lack initiative and drive and can often be defeated through cunning and ingenuity — a fact useful to travelers who run afoul of Nerekhall's many laws against uncivil behavior or its antimagic ordinances. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 148 Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 153

title: Irram
content: Irram Perched on the edge of the Desert of Eternity, Irram is the oldest of Al-Kalim's cities aside from the capital Al-Madena, one of the four vizier city-states. Its master, the Sun Priestess Sharish, is both leader of her people and custodian of the Grand Temple of A'tar. Irram is a center of religion and worship, and pilgrims travel from across the Caliphate to pray in its many shrines. In the middle of its sprawling tangle of ancient sandstone buildings stands the tomb of the first Caliph; once each Caliph's reign is over, their body is brought here baked in clay, so it might be entombed within their likeness forever. Irram is often in conflict with the Collegiate Arcane, and its own conclave of wizards has little power within the city walls, for Sharish believes that the fruits of Djinn magic are intrinsically tainted, and she would see the Caliphate's reliance upon them ended — a stance that also brings her into opposition with other viziers who see only the wealth ancient Djinn artifacts can bring. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245

title: Isheim
content: Isheim Isheim is a frozen wilderness perched on the edge of the world, across the roiling northern seas from Terrinoth, where cold skies heavy with snow and sleet press down upon the land and a keening wind howls forth from ice-clad peaks. Overview Isheim is the lost land of the Salishwyrd, ancient Elves who ruled this continent before years of hunger and darkness turned their paradise into a frozen nightmare. Beneath the snow and ice, the glories of their northern empire still hide, hunted by heroes and fought over by scheming ice wyrms and savage Hearthlords. Heroes traveling to this remote land might find themselves caught up in the Weik lords' trade wars, delve into the secret depths of the volcanic city of Vrede, or join an expedition of ice-blood hunters as they seek out frozen beasts. The paths of the most daring could even take them far beyond the coastal cities and settlements, past the lands of the Onoit and the lairs of the ice wyrms, to discover the ruins of the Elven empire and perhaps even The Green Vale, last city of the Salishwyrd. The land is divided between The Raider's Coast of the Weik, the middle wilderness roamed by the Onoit, and the far north known as The White Death. Sources Isheim (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 232

title: Jade Glen
content: Jade Glen The Jade Glen is a range of hills in Eastern Terrinoth, offering the region's people a peaceful respite from the bleak landscape of the nearby Borderlands. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Jararr
content: Jararr Jararr is the great panther god of the Wild Hunt, vicious brother of Hamzah the Pridelord. Hunters of Zanaga offer this ferocious figure of blood and death prayers before the kill and raise gore-streaked obsidian statues in his honor. Whereas Hamzah stands for civilization and tribe, Jararr is a loner; among the Singhara, the worship of Jararr is practiced by outcasts who choose to dye their manes black in deference to their brutal master. Adventurers seek out Jararr that they might hunt at the great panther's side, for if they can keep pace with the giant beast and bring down his quarry, a measure of the kill can be theirs. Equally, evil Singhara potionmasters have been known to place Jararr's prey mark upon their enemies. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 254

title: Jatok
content: Jatok Jatok, the Water Temple, is a former lizardman temple now a nest of naga power in Zanaga, a sunken tomb into which all of Zanaga's rivers eventually flow. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Jendra's Harbor
content: Jendra's Harbor Jendra's Harbor is the most prosperous city of the barony of Telor, seated on the southern side of Kingless Bay where the river of Korina's Tears meets the sea. The port is one of the few reliable landings for ships arriving from across the sea, hosting travelers from Lorimor and as far as Al-Kalim, and serves as a departure point for ships bound for the Torue Albes or, occasionally, Zanaga. Though Baron Echard officially rules Telor, Countess Sela's stewardship of the harbor has granted her greater influence throughout Terrinoth and beyond. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Jenti the Just
content: Jenti the Just Jenti the Just was a sightless sorcerer of the Lorimor Imperial Court who, aided by a Vision Rune, overcame unhealable injuries to become a famed figure at court. [not stated in source: no further biographical detail is given] Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 121

title: Jer'Kul Urak
content: Jer'Kul Urak The Jer'Kul, or "Lower-Dwellers," live most of their lives within The Kul Valleys, the wide valleys formed when earthquakes split The Broken Plains apart across hundreds of leagues. Unlike most of the other Orc tribes, this tribe relies on agriculture and animal husbandry to survive. Its members grow crops on small plots of valley land, which they tend and harvest as they roam across the Kul with herds of small elk, jarn deer, and other wildlife that long ago fell into the valleys and evolved to exist here. Most other Orc tribes look down on the Jer'Kul (literally), but the valley-dwellers make intricate metalworks of silver that many view as blessed by the spirits of the underworld. It is possible their beliefs could be true, but not as they imagine — there are vents in some of the valleys where some hear dark whispers and can make out terrible visages floating in the choking smoke that emerges from the ground. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 200

title: Jerem Camford
content: Jerem Camford Baron Jerem Camford led a force ambushed by undead cavalry at the Battle of Ramscrossing while negotiating a swollen river during the Second Darkness. When Camford ordered a retreat, Ardus Ix'Erebus's Deathborn forces harried his troops so brutally that they were in no state to defend their lands upon regrouping; the Deathborn Legion soon fell upon the Barony of Camford in force, utterly ravaging it and slaughtering the baron and his heirs. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 41

title: Jerlon Penacor
content: Jerlon Penacor King Jerlon Penacor came to the throne of Talindon in 286 showing every sign of proving worthy of the crown, his capable queen Riya celebrated at court for her intelligence and charm, and their infant sons Farrengol and Farrendon showing every sign of becoming fine princes of the Penacor line. History Love tore the realm apart, however. Queen Riya and the king's greatest friend and highest councilor, Rusticar Lorimor, had fallen deeply for each other despite their respective vows to husband and throne; when the king learned of this, his priests and advisors begged him to show no clemency, but Jerlon still loved his queen and grew melancholic rather than wrathful. He annulled his marriage and forever banished Riya and Rusticar from the kingdom — a large group of the king's subjects joined them in exile, a happenstance that led some to wonder if there was more to the betrayal than mere love, and that Jerlon had trouble commanding the loyalty of his subjects. Rusticar and Riya went on to found the Lorimor Empire on the shores of the western ocean. In Talindon, Jerlon lamented his lost love and refused to countenance taking another queen; behind his back, his courtiers began to call him the King of Grief. His remaining son Farrengol, lacking any parental hand with his mother exiled and his father lost to melancholy, fell in with coarser members of the household guard and was eventually condemned to death by his own father for the crimes of the outlaw band he had formed — Farrengol would later return from death as the undead lord Farrenghast. The King of Grief returned to his castle after the execution and eked out a few more miserable years, dying a lonely and largely unmourned monarch; his surviving son Farrendon shared none of his father's frailties and displayed more of the robust spirit associated with the Penacor line. Sources Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), pp. 32–33

title: Jorgul
content: Jorgul Jorgul, the Spear of the Desert, is general of the grand army of the Caliph and often challenges Hiresh's claim to being the most influential of the Caliph's advisors. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Jornall Mountains
content: Jornall Mountains The Jornall Mountains are where the Malcari, the eleventh Elven tribe, settled after venturing forth from The Aymhelin, believing Emorial had pursued the Ynfernael's servants there after abandoning the Elves. Centuries later, Dwarves fleeing the destruction of The Karok Doum also settled in the Jornall Mountains, forming the Jornall Clan; during the Third Darkness, the Dragonlord Gehennor launched an overly confident subterranean campaign against the Jornall Clan but was repulsed at tremendous cost, caught by surprise by the arrival of Orc reinforcements. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 27 The Early History of the Dwarves (Tales of Darkness), p. 31 The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 47

title: Joulnar Dwarves
content: Joulnar Dwarves The Joulnar Dwarves are a Dwarven people with whom the barony of Kell trades, alongside the nearby Dunwarr Dwarves and the barony of Dhernas. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Jutta
content: Jutta Elder Jutta, alongside her sister Spiritspeaker Anka, leads the wise council governing Mok'Thul Urak, the Grey Moon Tribe — supernaturally ancient sisters who have seen several normal Orc lifetimes come and go, and are almost certainly sustained by the phantasms they commune with. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Jyrrii
content: Jyrrii Jyrrii is an A'tari Djinn who granted Urnas the Unmarked the wish that no blade might ever cut his flesh again, in exchange for the slaughter of a thousand mortals — Urnas's petrified form still stands in the ruins of Jyrrii's city. Sources The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Kajir
content: Kajir Kajir, the City of Dark Dreams, was one of the great cities of the Djinni before the coming of A'tar, ruled by the Djinn Darmarr. The city traded in nightmares, its obsidian mines filled with the screams of sleeping captives, which fueled the depraved thirsts of its master. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Kalishar Nomads
content: Kalishar Nomads The Kalishar Nomads are a collection of dozens of clans who raise their banners in defiance of the Caliph, haunting the ruins of the Beggar's Maze though even they do not wander too deep into the city's ruined heart. Sources The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Karok Zon
content: Karok Zon Karok Zon is one of the ruined Dwarven cities of The Karok Doum, its fallen walls and crumbling towers shattered and seared by dragon fire. Sources The Karok Doum (The Molten Heath), p. 194

title: Katrin
content: Katrin Baroness Katrin of the Sephone family rules Allerfeldt from Goldhall, a castle representing several hundred years of her family's legacy. In recent times Goldhall has taken on a more administrative than military role, its vast complexes, immense library, and facilities for hosting dignitaries making it a frequent site for diplomatic actions, treaties, and declarations of war. Within her barony, the Sephone line has historically allowed the Catfolk community of Hyrrinx in the Eventide Forest to govern itself independently and remain untaxed, a status quo Katrin has thus far maintained. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 142 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Kaylor Morbis
content: Kaylor Morbis Kaylor Morbis is a lake in The Ru around which sits the greatest Uthuk settlement, a circle of war camps. Long ago, at the lake's edge, the plains elders met to settle their disputes and trade both goods and promises; now it is the bloodsisters who hold court there, settling disputes via ritual combat, gathering their forces, and planning invasions of other lands. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211

title: Kayree Sandspear
content: Kayree Sandspear Kayree Sandspear, Maiden of the Wastes, commands an army in Siryasa in the name of the Caliph, and it is from her fighting schools and training lodges that many of Al-Kalim's greatest warriors emerge. Once a year, Sandspear herself steps into the Arena of Blades at Siryasa's summit and dares any to challenge her for the right to govern the city; many have tried, but all have met their end upon her paired viper blades. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245

title: Keiren O'Brallen
content: Keiren O'Brallen Keiren O'Brallen, a Gnome rogue, met the Elf Lathina Veintralla in Archaut and joined her voyage aboard the Wavedancer to the lands of Zanaga and the Sunderlands. Keiren returned from the five-year voyage with little more than a small gold humanoid statue and a newfound paranoia towards "curses" and "monkey hunters"; he vanished into the crowded streets of Dawnsmoor soon after and was never heard from again. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 53

title: Keldarim
content: Keldarim The Feredel sorcerer Keldarim was among the companions Glaciel Snowstar gathered on his quest to seek the dragons' aid against Malcorne and the corrupted Daewyl, helping bring about his downfall at The Battle of Enfreil. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: Kell
content: Kell Kell, the Shield of Daqan, lies along the Dunwarr mountain range that shields Terrinoth from the foreboding Charg'r Wastes, its southern end abutting the Borderlands that separate Terrinoth from the Ru. Due to its border position, Kell maintains one of the largest and most heavily trained armies of all the baronies, fed by a fertile river valley and based out of numerous ancient keeps; in the depths of several keeps, magnificent rune golems await the day they are woken and called to war once more, though most outside Kell take its protection for granted and rarely consider the Ru a source of threat. Kell's soldiers watch the Ru's desolation and the fords of the Lothan River at Hernfar Isle from ancient, crumbling watchtowers whose builders are long forgotten. Behind these timeworn fortresses, Kell's citizens prosper: valley farms keep the barony fed with enough surplus to trade with the nearby Dunwarr and Joulnar Dwarves and the barony of Dhernas, and a rich trade in timber and iron flows into Baron Fredric's vaults, seldom resting long before he puts it toward the betterment of his people. It is said that Roland of Kell slew High Lord Margath at the culmination of the Dragon Wars, and many see that nobility in his descendant. Baroness Elyana of Kell, in the last years of the 1500s, restored the Council of Thirteen after a generation of famine and baronial neglect. Not far from Castle Kellar stands Orrush Khatak, generally called the Gate of the Furnace — a great arch of blood red rock large enough for four hundred soldiers to march under shoulder to shoulder, its origin as natural formation, luck charm, or ritual site now lost to memory, and one where the wind is said to carry anguished cries few will admit to being more than a trick of the breeze. Beyond it runs the wide river Lothan, and Hernfar Isle, the furthest eastern outpost of the Daqan Lords, sits where the river is widest; recruits joke that insubordination in the Kell militia earns assignment to the garrison at Hernfar Keep. The isle seems unremarkable but for its proximity to the Ru Steppes, and soldiers posted there report shadows that seem to lengthen or flicker, luminescent eyes staring from across the water, and on nights when the moon is heavy and red, a cacophony of howls and screams that few can confidently call merely animal. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 51 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 138–141

title: Kellos's Breath
content: Kellos's Breath Kellos's Breath is a sweeping plain in Western Terrinoth that gives the region a flat aspect, relatively safe from the depredations of the undead to the north and the stranger dangers to the east. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Kellos
content: Kellos Kellos, the Blazing Light of Life and Justice, also called the Red-Handed God, is the god of Life, Flame, and Justice, a fiery deity whose presence is anathema to anything tainted by the foul magic of undeath or other dark sorceries. Table of Contents Origins The Church of Kellos Sources Origins Two differing accounts of Kellos's origin survive. The Grand Hierophants of Kellos hold that, soon after the Second Darkness, a vile necromancer near Vynelvale sought to create an undead empire for himself; a band of heroes assembled to defeat him but were struck down, and the last survivor, moments from a sorcerous death, called out for aid and swore eternal service to any who would come. His eyes clouded, his body wreathed in flame, and he smote the necromancer and banished his undead army forever — this survivor became the first Hierophant of Kellos and, upon his death, the church's first saint. Historians and religious legend alike instead place his rise during the height of Waiqar's Scourge, when the Deathborn Legion laid waste to Terrinoth and the Death Cults spread fear and disorder through the nation's cities like an evil plague. By this account, a stranger arrived by boat at the refugee camp of Dawnsmoor, introducing himself as Kellos and working miracles of healing among the settlers there. He took up his mace and swore to see an end to the vile undead, and with his holy fire burned the flesh and bone of Waiqar's foul creations; he called many brave adventurers to his side, and when they fell in defense of the realm, he saved them from death with his powers of healing, bidding them rise again from the flame. Kellos the Hero was soon lauded as Kellos the Bright and Kellos the Savior, one of the brightest lights of humankind amid the darkness that had washed over the land — within weeks he was the central figure of a burgeoning cult, surrounded by priests who could perform minor versions of his own miracles, and many claimed he had himself recovered from death after being struck down by an assassin's blade. Kellos freed the baronial forces from the need to guard Terrinoth's cities by concentrating on locating and executing the ringleaders of the death cults, and sent envoys to beseech the Latari Elves and Dunwarr Dwarves for aid against Waiqar; with their combined might, the Deathborn Legion was finally forced to retreat to the Cursed Barony in 521. At the final battle, when Waiqar's armies were driven back to the Mistlands, Kellos disappeared — perhaps slain in combat, making a final sacrifice for the people and lands he loved, or perhaps emerging unscathed to settle in some far-off hamlet and enjoy peace long denied him. His followers believe he ascended to godhood that day, so that he might forever empower those who would fight death with the light and life of fire; his disciples returned to Vynelvale, now a Free City, and lit the Eternal Fire in his name. As they built a cathedral to their founder, Kellos's followers taught that heat and life were inextricably intertwined, and that magic which utilized heat and fire could also be used to heal — soon many citizens of Vynelvale and the surrounding lands had been blessed with Kellos's healing gifts, and tales of these wondrous miracles spread across Terrinoth, with the most pious and powerful priests even said to bring the dead back to life through resurrection. It is said, too, that he still travels the world to this day, seeking new foes to defeat, and those in Vynelvale patiently await his eventual return to Terrinoth. Though there is much debate whether Kellos was merely a hero or truly a god — some Greyhaven scholars hold that the magics of his priests are not divinely sourced at all, but mislabeled applications of the Turning or accidental invocations of the Empyrean — none deny that his priests are worthy allies in the fight to keep Terrinoth safe from the terrors that lurk in the dark. The Church of Kellos Those who join the Church of Kellos are called Acolytes, low-ranking clergy who tend his flames and flocks in shrines across Terrinoth. Those Acolytes who have the ability to perform divine feats in Kellos's name are initiated through the rite of the Fire's Embrace and become Priests or Knights of Kellos, bringing healing to towns and villages or traveling the roads to smite evil wherever it arises. The most powerful of Kellos's followers are his High Priests, who preside over the cathedral at Vynelvale; High Priests called Justicars lead contingents of the priesthood into battle in the most dire times, among them Lady Anastel during the War of Ten Brothers. In battle, Kellos's priests most often use the power of flame, the symbol of their deity, to smite evil — conjuring mystical flame around hand or weapon, or casting gouts of living flame to consume their foes; their brilliant red robes are a welcome sight across Terrinoth, promising wrath for the wicked and mercy for the meek. Kellos's faith is centered on Vynelvale, site of the Grand Cathedral of Kellos and the Eternal Fire. Some temples of Kellos teach that the undead are the agents of his twin brother Nordros, and that Nordros's power will only be broken, and winter forever banished, once Kellos returns. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), pp. 122–123 The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 41–42 The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149 Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 153

title: Kennsir Dwarf
content: Kennsir Dwarf Kennsir Dwarves take the tunnel warfare common to the Dunwarr Mountains to horrifying levels of strategic brutality, living for battle in the claustrophobic, fortified tunnels beneath the peaks. They employ the unconventional, unpredictable strategies of guerrilla warriors — tunneling deep behind invaders' flanks, collapsing mine shafts, or choking their foes in noxious gasses supplied by the Alchemists' League — and there are none better at tunnel fighting in all the world. Sources Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 192

title: King Aanir
content: King Aanir King Aanir of the Latari organized a massive sally from the silver palace of Caelcira during the Third Darkness, leading a spearhead of Leonx Riders under cover of darkness into the heart of the encamped forces of the Dragonlord Baalesh. The charge did not prove the decisive action Aanir had hoped, and before his cavalry could regroup, he was pinned to the ground by Baalesh and devoured. His son Prince Faolan survived him as protector of the northern borders, and his brother Aenoeth would later take up his dead brother's crown to lead the Latari's recovery in the Age of Courage. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 47 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 51

title: Kingless Bay
content: Kingless Bay Kingless Bay is where the river of Korina's Tears meets the sea in the barony of Telor, home to the port city of Jendra's Harbor on its southern side. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Kingless Coast
content: Kingless Coast The Kingless Coast lies close to Eventide Forest and stretches into the barony of Telor, home of the port city Jendra's Harbor on Kingless Bay. Beyond the busy harbor, many of the coast's smaller ports and villages lie abandoned and half-ruined, victims of fierce storms or ravening merriods and other horrid creatures of the deep. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Kobold
content: Kobold Kobolds are a race of beastmen twisted by magic centuries ago by a sorcerer desperately in need of minions, who made them smaller so they could work in tight spaces, slashed their intelligence so they would never revolt against him, made them genderless so they wouldn't be distracted by mating instincts, and gave them the ability to reproduce asexually so they would always have large enough numbers for their tasks — an exceptionally powerful magician whose intellect was matched only by his lack of foresight. The kobolds reproduced at an astonishing rate and soon overwhelmed the wizard, his stronghold, and the surrounding lands. Being small and about as bright as a particularly dim dog, they tend to fall prey to anything higher up the food chain, yet remain a blight on every corner of Mennara; occasionally a kobold figures out how to construct simple traps, make rudimentary weapons, or lead a group of fellows in some semblance of tactics, at which point a pack can go from nuisance to menace, raiding isolated villages or farms for fresh meat, shiny baubles, and small domesticated animals. Packs of kobolds infest the Dunwarr Mountains, where the Dwarves view them as the rest of the world does — annoying, predatory vermin — and their extermination is one of the more onerous duties shared by the Rangers' Guild and Warriors' Guild, usually falling to their newest members. Sources Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 192

title: Korina's Tears
content: Korina's Tears Korina's Tears is a river that extends across the barony of Carthridge, and further south meets the sea at Kingless Bay near Jendra's Harbor in the barony of Telor. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Kul the Serpent
content: Kul the Serpent Kul the Serpent, also known as the Viper, was the greatest archer of the Uthuk Y'llan and one of Llovar's most feared lieutenants, commanding a contingent of the Host of Thorns during the First Darkness. History At the Battle of the Locusts, Kul led the third wave of Llovar's assault, concentrating covering fire on his vanguard as they broke through to Timmorran's position. As scything bone blades slashed at the wizard, King Triamlavar leapt before the charging Uthuk; while Triamlavar was distracted, Kul punched an envenomed arrow through the Elf king's belly. Enraged, Halgir Son of Grom challenged Kul to face his axe, only to have his own skull pierced by a bodkin for his bravery; Ashan the Elder then stepped up, and Kul sent a barrage of shafts that perforated the Sunderman's lungs. These sacrifices were not in vain, though, for Kul's efforts exhausted him, and Timmorran survived the onslaught long enough to strike down Llovar himself. Kul's ultimate fate, like that of Llovar's other lieutenants, is not known. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 37

title: Kurnos
content: Kurnos Kurnos, Lord of the Hunt, taught the primitive people who lived in the lands that would become Terrinoth during The Years of Hunger to take only what they need from the land and honor the animals whose deaths brought them life, in exchange for the bounty of the forest. History Some claim Kurnos was an Elf who, upon exile to Mennara, grew enchanted with the trackless forests and abandoned his fellow Latari; such was his love of the wild that when he encountered one of the mortal races, he taught them to live as one with nature. Given the endless nature of the Elves, he may wander the world still, though such musings hold little interest for his followers, to whom he is simply their patron, and every hunt an act of worship. Worship These days, the farms and cities of Terrinoth rely on farming for sustenance, and often only rangers, nomads, and isolated villages remember Kurnos. Shrines to him are scattered throughout the countryside, and his devotees claim that everything beneath the canopy is his sacred domain; when a hunter wants to honor Kurnos, they often hide a portion of their kill as cleverly as they can, and the Lord of the Hunt always tracks down these offerings, the more challenging the hunt, the greater the reward he may grant in return. The druids of Kurnos also work miracles of healing and can control the behavior of wild beasts, finding shelter even in the most hostile environments as they roam the wilds tending to the needs of the land and ensuring harmony between peoples, plant, and beast. The most devout of his followers sometimes gather to celebrate the full moons at Hunter's Circle by Kurnan Lake, where they howl at the moon beside their animal companions. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 124

title: Kyndrithul
content: Kyndrithul Kyndrithul is a powerful vampire, current leader of House Dalibor and lord of Castle Dalibor, serving Waiqar not out of desire for power but because he has been forced to. At heart an experimenter and genius, Kyndrithul has spent centuries mastering the various magical disciplines needed to create the perfect Reanimated servant, exulting in figuring out new ways to mold living flesh with necromancy — his boldest recent experiments infuse living flesh with the dust of Waiqar's own Deathborn Legion, a crime punishable with a fate beyond death. He offers Waiqar aided passage through his lands and staging points for raids into Terrinoth, playing the part of a humble servant while reaping the rewards of his secret work, even as Waiqar's Deathborn generals regard him with disgust and suspicion. As one of the Lords of Bilehall, he has had hundreds of years to set traps, arrange countermeasures, and prepare against almost any enemy. Sources Castle Dalibor (The Mistlands), pp. 161–162 Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), p. 165

title: L'jan
content: L'jan The L'jan were a tribe of the Ru plains many times larger than Llovar's own Loth K'har, forced to bend the knee to Llovar's growing confederation in the years before the First Darkness, becoming part of the Uthuk Y'llan. Sources The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), p. 34

title: Labyrinth of Deurg
content: Labyrinth of Deurg The Labyrinth of Deurg is a sealed and forbidden network of mines in the Dunwarr Mountains, named for Master Miner Deurg, whose team from the Miners' Guild discovered it many centuries ago while following an unusual seam of black, obsidian-like ore toward the mountain's surface. Overview The Smiths' Guild determined that the ore, once smelted, produced a shining metal of unparalleled strength and resilience, and Deurg redoubled his miners' efforts to excavate it. Before long the miners began to lose their bearings underground — a phenomenon entirely new to Dwarves — digging for days without seeming to move, or finding the richest deposits exactly where they expected the seam to end. Eventually they broke into unexpected caves and chambers lined with razor-sharp outcroppings of the black stone and threaded with strands of the strange metal. History Then the whispering started. The miners had been hearing it for weeks before realizing it was more than excitement in their own heads: a voice urging them to "dig," promising that the most valuable lodes lay just ahead. Reports of the whispers were the last word to leave the mines. When search parties from Thelgrim found the tunnel entrances caved in, the Dwarves dug through, but found no trace of the missing miners inside. The reigning Deeplord ruled that all ingots of the strange metal be returned to the mine, which was then sealed forever behind runes of warding and binding, and all exploration of what Dwarves now call the Labyrinth of Deurg was forbidden on pain of death. The prohibition has held for hundreds of years, though occasionally a band of foolhardy adventurers is seduced by tales of the mythical ore; all who have found a new entrance into the Labyrinth have vanished within its depths forever. Persistent rumors also claim that a young blacksmith once spirited away a portion of the metal before it could be returned, forged it into a deadly blade, and went adventuring, only to be lost in the Woods of Woe. The tale of the Labyrinth's discovery is also linked in Dwarven memory to the Pact of Stonesense, which holds that the Dwarves' singular affinity with the Dimora began when the first Dwarves, fleeing deeper into the mountains to escape the dragons, encountered the Dimora in the Dunwarr's very roots. Sources Labyrinth of Deurg (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 189–190

title: Labyrinth of Ruin
content: Labyrinth of Ruin The Labyrinth of Ruin is a dungeon from which bold adventurers once recovered the Serpent Dagger. Scholars imagine the dagger's true origin lay elsewhere, in Al-Kalim or even the Ru, rather than in the Labyrinth itself. [not stated in source: no further detail on the Labyrinth's location or nature is given] Sources Magic Items, p. 109

title: Lady Anastel
content: Lady Anastel Lady Anastel of Kellos's Order was anointed Justicar to combat the threat of Geist the Usurper during the War of Ten Brothers, retrieving the Shield of Coals from its resting place beneath the Eternal Flame and marching alongside a force of zealous priests and knights. Geist's magics warned him of her approach, and he ambushed the forces of Kellos as soon as they crossed the border; most who did not fall were corrupted and turned by the foul bite of the ferrox, barely one in four living to return to Vynelvale. Anastel was not among them, and Geist pried the Shield of Coals from her dead hands. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 52

title: Lady Ysbet
content: Lady Ysbet The Terrinoth noble Lady Ysbet led an army to Yrthwright's Forge during the Third Darkness and orchestrated a brilliant series of tunnel fights that ended in her slaying the Dragonlord Avox, who had enslaved the city's Dwarves and forced them to dig deep into the mountains. The freed slaves hailed her as a savior and asked her to become governor of the settlement, now envisioned as a new Free City — after the depredations of the dragons, the inhabitants brooked no association with the name of the Yrthwrights. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 47

title: Lagart
content: Lagart Lagart, largest of the Weik cities on The Raider's Coast, is home to the High Hall and the seat of Hearthlord Ulfred Varl — a high-walled city of frozen, winding streets, its halls built from the hulls of ancient ships. Lagart is also home to the great ship hoists above the Steaming River; in the summer months when the river thaws, the hoists can lift ships from the sea below and allow them passage into Isheim's interior. Perhaps most importantly, Lagart is the meeting place of the Reaver Council, the alliance of the twelve Weik Hearthlords. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), p. 233

title: Lagrul the Red
content: Lagrul the Red Lagrul the Red was the Weik captain who first spied the snowcapped coast of Isheim and proclaimed it the last port, turning his fleet of nomadic seafarers toward its cliffs when the Weik's twelve pirate fleets had grown too numerous for their island hideaways and open-ocean flotilla towns. The Hearthlords trace their title of jarl back to Lagrul and the first captains who followed him ashore. Sources Lords of the Hearth (Isheim), p. 234

title: Lake Falstar
content: Lake Falstar Lake Falstar is an otherwise small and unremarkable lake in the remote parts of Carthridge, notable for the single island at its center that is home to the Temple of Four Storms. On some nights, amid howling winds and blinding rain, flashes of lightning reveal mysterious figures assembled on the small island across the water. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 145

title: Lake of Silence
content: Lake of Silence The Lake of Silence is a haunt within The White Death so cold that the air steals one's very breath — a visitor can't even scream as ice shades tear them asunder. Sources Realm of the White Death (Isheim), p. 236

title: Last Haven
content: Last Haven Last Haven is a bandit city built upon the ancient foundations of a Dwarven mining fortress in The Borderlands, a refuge for those cast out by their own peoples — criminals escaping the justice of the Citadel, disgraced knights, wizards seeking to conduct their experiments far from prying eyes, and countless other miscreants. No records of why the fortress was abandoned exist, but huge claw marks and deep gouges in the thick rock of the lower levels lead many to believe that the miners woke something terrible in the depths: something ancient and hungry. Now a mire of crude stone buildings and twisting streets, Last Haven has become a retreat for the disenfranchised and the despised. Travelers seeking to push deeper into the Ru often pass through Last Haven to stock up on supplies and information, although wise travelers keep one hand on their purse and the other on the hilt of their weapon as they do so. There is no law in Last Haven, and each city block or large building is almost a realm unto itself. In the heart of the city, a former guild upright named Diggor maintains the pretense of legitimate commerce, buying and selling what plundered wealth the Borderlands have to offer, while the Orc Xor's fighting pits offer a chance to win or lose coin, as well as perhaps some teeth. Possibly the most interesting part of Last Haven, however, is the Silent Chantry. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 211–212

title: Latari
content: Latari The Latari are the Elves of The Aymhelin, a nation ruled from Lithelin whose civilization has been carefully harmonized with the ancient forest around it over millennia. Table of Contents Overview Description Sources Overview The Latari follow the Path of the Stars, venerating Latariana, and trace their society back to their descent to Mennara at The Ailatar. Elven society is organized around castes and tribes: the ruling houses of the Eolam court, the lower-blood Verdelam, and tribes such as the Daewyl and Loth Caara, whose historical corruption still colors High Court politics. All Latari, wherever they live, fiercely guard the forests from outside intrusion, lest contaminations disrupt the Elves' eternal quest to return to the Empyrean. Description Beyond Lithelin, Latari society spreads across the whole of the Aymhelin: the frontier warriors of Blackthorn Grove, the foresters and hunters of The Bloodwood, the seafarers and spiritspeakers of the Selenic Coast, the moonstone miners and Swordsmasters of The Darnati Highlands, the guardians of The Deepwood, and the farmers of The Thalian Glades each represent a distinct facet of Elven life, bound together by shared reverence for nature and vigilance against the many unnatural threats that test the borders of their ancient homeland. Sources The Aymhelin (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 174 Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), pp. 174–176 Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), p. 178

title: Latariana
content: Latariana Lady Latariana, called Mother to the Elves and Lady Protectress of Air, was the wife of Emorial whose covetous desire for greater power set in motion the Elves' rebellion against The First and their exile to Mennara. Table of Contents History The Tears of Latariana Worship Sources History The First undertook the creation of Lord Emorial and Lady Latariana together, prominent among the more familiar beings born from the Empyrean spheres: he the Lord Protector of Light, she the Lady Protectress of Air. It is not entirely clear whether the two were themselves the literal progenitors of the Elven people or merely the first of them to be created and gain particular recognition, but certainly they were lovers, wedded in the fashion of their folk, and soon the Elves numbered in legions. As the Verto Magica turned and time passed, Latariana slowly began to covet more than her existence in the Empyrean, longing for a Crown of Dreams and Life — greater power than the Elves possessed in that plane. Scholars ponder over why she became avaricious; consensus suggests a shadowy spirit from the Ynfernael tempted her in secret murmurs, though others suggest the First, lacking personality, were simply too cold a presence for Elves to form any deep relationship with. Whatever her motives, she cajoled her husband with ceaseless requests to win her dominion over the primary spheres, or perhaps all the spheres, of the Empyrean. Emorial eventually agreed, traveling to the farthest edge of creation to demand the First relinquish control; they did not so much as deign to respond, leaving him humiliated and wrathful. He returned to the Elves and marshaled them in mutiny, marching his host with Latariana at his side through The Gate of Years — the Elves believed they would pass into the halls of the First, but instead found themselves crossing into the Aenlong, and after countless days lost among its hazards, they came at last to the glade that would become The Aymhelin, where they met its architect, the Yrthwright Mennara. The great dragon passed the judgments of the First down upon the rebellious Elves: they were exiled from the Empyrean, Light and Air no longer theirs to command, the Lays of the First no longer freely nourishing their hearts, and — the cruelest judgment of all — they were now imprisoned upon the very mortal plane that had been both their destination and their damnation, this world that some dare name after the Yrthwright of this tale. The Tears of Latariana The Elves begged Mennara for mercy, but it would not heed them; instead it turned to Latariana and offered her a terrible choice. A window to the Empyrean could be left open for the Elves to return through one day, but the cost was high: Latariana would have to enter the Void, taking with her the Ynfernael temptation that had led to her greed. With a heavy heart, she agreed, whispering her last tender words to Emorial before climbing onto the Yrthwright's back; the majestic creature spread its wings and flew her up into the darkening skies. The Elves watched as she was borne from the world into the Void, and as she grew too distant to see, a bright light shone in her place — the first star. More stars appeared thereafter, reminders of Latariana's sacrifice, still watched by her followers today from The Ailatar, the clearing where the Elves first descended to Mennara. Emorial could not look away; staring at his hands, wet with Latariana's tears, he watched them transform before his eyes into eleven stunning pearlescent jewels, mere echoes of his lost love's beauty — tokens of hope, like the stars, that the Elves might one day earn forgiveness. Wracked with shame, anger, and grief he could not accept for himself, Emorial called forth eleven Elven nobles and divided his host into eleven tribes, sharing between them the Tears of Latariana as marks of office, directing the nobles to lead their people into the future of this new world until a path back to the Empyrean was made clear. He then took up his sword and, with cold fury in his heart, left his people — the Elves say he journeyed to the Ynfernael plane to seek vengeance on the corrupting shadow that had murmured temptations to his bride. Two centuries after their arrival, the eleven tribes scattered to far-flung territories and developed distinct cultures, though they kept links of trade and friendship; only the Latari Elves remained in the forested clearing of the Aymhelin. Among the eleventh tribe, the Malcari, the bearer of a Tear named Malcorne, Lord of the Daewyl Tribe, would in time corrupt his own Tear into the Shadow Tear and plunge the Elves into the Shadow War (also called The War of the Shadow Tear) — the Shadow Tear went missing during that war and, if it remains unbroken, a powerful artifact combining both Empyrean and Ynfernael magic still waits somewhere for someone to find it. Even the surviving Tears of Latariana, guarded within Caelcira to this day, were not immune to the corruption of the Ynfernael, and an old adage among the Eolam court holds that Latariana's tears actually fall again due to the innumerable intrigues, plots, and jealousies that plague the court. In their original form, the Tears were crystallized Empyrean energy, and are believed to be artifacts that anticipated the form and function of the Stars of Timmorran in many ways — great batteries of energy that could conceivably power hugely potent spells. Being only eleven in number, they are even rarer than the few unbound Stars that remain in the world; each is kept carefully guarded by the leader of its tribe as both a potent magical artifact and a revered badge of office, and while an Elven lord might on occasion allow a Tear to be used in some great working for the benefit of all Mennara, none would ever trust its use to someone from outside the tribes. Worship Latariana is the guiding light of the Latari Elves, visible among the other glimmering lights in the night sky from The Ailatar. Her followers venerate her through the Path to the Stars. The Highborn Elves — those only slightly removed from the most ancient bloodlines who dwelled in the Empyrean — hold the strongest natural connection to Latariana's Door, and many devote their lives to deepening that connection and ascending Latariana's Stair in hope of earning redemption for all Elvenkind. The Daughters of the Empyrean and the Darnati warriors are most often drawn from this caste. Sources The Elves (Tales of Darkness), pp. 26–27 The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 27 Spiritspeaking (Call to Adventure), pp. 126–127 Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), pp. 174–175 Whispers of the Ynfernael (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 218

title: Lathina Veintralla
content: Lathina Veintralla Lathina Veintralla, a Free Cities Elf, met the Gnome rogue Keiren O'Brallen in Archaut and traveled with him to Dallak in the Torue Albes, where the unlikely duo commissioned the sturdy vessel Wavedancer and set sail west into the sunset in search of long-forgotten lands. History As the weeks dragged on to months and months to years, the folk of Dallak assumed the ship lost — they were shocked when five years later the Wavedancer returned to port, less one of its masts and half its crew. Lathina brought back marvelous tales of the lands of Zanaga and the Sunderlands, along with a hold of animal and plant specimens, gems, exotic spices, and even the skull of a "great aquatic wyrm" they had barely slain, lest anyone think her stories fabrications. She granted Greyhaven the great gift of maps from her travels, maps still used today. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 53

title: Lava Elemental
content: Lava Elemental Lava elementals live in a few hot lairs within The Heart of The Molten Heath, though most elementals reside in the distant lands of Al-Kalim. The volcanoes of the Heart are an ideal environment for these magical creatures, though it is uncertain whether the elementals are the cause of the deadly heat or the volcanoes attracted their attention. This matters little to those unfortunate adventurers who might encounter them, though — lava elementals jealously guard their lairs and are always seeking to expand any area where rock is still stubbornly solid, which is usually a place where mortals are to be found. Sources Life on the Heath (The Molten Heath), p. 196

title: Lazra the Huntress
content: Lazra the Huntress Lazra the Huntress, an Orc chieftain, married Baroness Georgiana Delacroux of Frest in 1827 when she abdicated her position for love — a scandal that plunged the barony into a succession crisis its various claimants fought over for years, until Harriet Laurel's rebellion won the barony instead. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 53

title: Ledish Schall
content: Ledish Schall Ledish Schall is the ancestral seat of the Etharyon champion Dareine, standing at the center of Methras within The Bloodwood. Sources The Bloodwood (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Legendum Magicara
content: Legendum Magicara The Legendum Magicara is a collection of theses authored by Timmorran Lokander that corroborates much Elven legend regarding the myths of creation, treated by scholars such as Alanya of Greyhaven as the most authoritative guide available on matters otherwise known only through Elven mysticism. The great wizard drew a line at the end of the War of the Shadow Tear in his own account, before which all ought to be treated as Elven mysticism and legend, pertaining to no more than metaphorical accounts of real events. Even Timmorran, with all his insight, had to take the word of the Elves on matters preceding that war, and — as later events would show — Timmorran was not always the finest judge of character. Sources The Myths of Creation (Tales of Darkness), p. 24 The Troubled Rise of the Younger Races (Tales of Darkness), p. 30

title: Leonx Rider
content: Leonx Rider Leonx Riders exemplify the primal, wild nature of the Verdelam Elves more than any others, charging into battle atop the ferocious Leonx, large sentient felines native to The Aymhelin, piercing through enemy lines with the force of a storm. Many Elves see the nomadic Leonx Riders as little more than feral barbarians who have lost their connection to the teachings of Latariana and the Path of the Stars. Far from unthinking savages, the Free Hunters, as they were called in ancient days, saw their wild nature as a way to better attune themselves with the wild lands around them. In time they learned to temper their tremendous skill for hunting and combat with a deeper wisdom gained from their animal family: the mightiest killed only to survive, and the pack went to war only in defense of their own. Over time, songs were sung in Caelcira of lost Latari children rescued from the wild by strange, feral Elves, or even whole villages saved by Elven nomads who could speak the tongues of animals. Nevertheless, some of the most prominent leaders of the Latari noble houses wished to exile these "barbarians" from their sacred forest, and still shunned by the rest of Latari society, the Leonx Riders now keep mostly to themselves and their pack, only making contact with outsiders to offer aid. Sources Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), pp. 179–180

title: Leonx
content: Leonx The Leonx are large, sentient felines native to The Aymhelin and one of Mennara's most fearsome predators, bonded for life to their Leonx Rider in a partnership akin to family. In battle, the Leonx and rider coordinate their movements as one, fusing Elven skill with the deadly instincts of the beast. Sources Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), p. 180

title: Lesser Rune
content: Lesser Rune Some runes are capable of legendary feats of magic. Some are, well, not, and of little interest to anyone but a Runemaster, who is capable of bending their capabilities beyond their design. Though lacking the fame of other runebound shards, these items are still priceless and the subject of many a quest — each one is capable of a small beneficial effect that varies from shard to shard, such as casting light as a torch, conjuring a small illusionary creature, throwing one's voice, or starting small fires as a tinderbox. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 119

title: Levirax
content: Levirax Levirax was one of the six dragonlords — alongside Margath, Baalesh, Zir the Black, Avox, and Gehennor — who each led a band of lesser drakes against a different part of the world during the Third Darkness, motivated by greed for the Stars of Timmorran. Levirax's ultimate fate, like those of Baalesh and Gehennor, is not recorded in any scrolls to be found. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 45, 48

title: Library of Adrashi
content: Library of Adrashi The Library of Adrashi is one of the glorious places in Al-Madena where A'tar's radiance can be seen, its vaults holding great knowledge. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Lightning Strike Rune
content: Lightning Strike Rune A lightning strike rune is used to call down a bolt of lightning. It is a powerful weapon; most foes struck with a bolt of lightning are either killed outright or stunned senseless. Certain creatures, constructs, and undead beings, though, are resistant to this magic to some degree, as they would be to natural lightning. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 119

title: Lithelin
content: Lithelin Lithelin is the heart of the Elven empire, a gleaming city of white towers rising proudly in the heart of the ancient forest of The Aymhelin, ruled from its High Court by King Aenoeth. Table of Contents Overview Description Sources Overview The palace and the oldest rings of Lithelin are isolated from the opulent, verdant bowl of vigorous forest green that surrounds the city, but its outer districts have grown into, through, and among the forest in a graceful merging of Elven architecture and natural beauty. At its center stands Caelcira, the political and spiritual heart of the Aymhelin, and nearby lies the Ailatar, the Plain of Stars where the Elves descended to Mennara. At the head of the High Court sits King Aenoeth, an Elf with a centuries-long reputation as a fair and benevolent ruler; at his side is his trusted advisor and consort Maegan Cyndewin, viewed with suspicion by much of the court despite her own valor in defending the city. Description In the center of Lithelin is Caelcira, or "First Gate," which has watched over the city for over four thousand years, standing proud against the assaults of Dragonlord Baalesh and his fiery brood; it is said Caelcira is built on the founding stone of the world itself and will never fall to evil, unless all of Mennara shall fall first. Here the Tear of the Latari tribe and those of the lost nations are guarded carefully, lest they fall into the hands of evil. Although the Tears are officially named for Latariana, an old adage among the Eolam court holds that her tears actually fall again due to the innumerable intrigues, plots, and jealousies that plague the court. Not all politicking in the High Court is guileful, however. Maegan Cyndewin, though she fought valiantly and was wounded repeatedly while defending the Elven nation, is still deeply distrusted by many in the Court and conspired against whenever possible — a rueful hatred fueled in part by the legacy of her father, a member of the Daewyl tribe that allied with demons in its covetous pursuit of Latariana's Tears, and by the legacy of her mother, a Loth Caara tribeswoman who lived to see Llovar corrupt her people. Her parentage serves as a perpetual blight to her honor despite how instrumental she was in defending Caelcira, and many fear she has been corrupted by the same power that seduced her parents' tribes and is working to bring about the same downfall of the Latari. Between the palace and the walls lie swaths of verdant lands interspersed with pure, spring-fed ponds, wild-growing wheat, and panon-fruit trees delicately transplanted from the surrounding forests. Originally created as groves for the Forest Guardians who lend aid in defense of Caelcira, these vales have become the spiritual hub of Lithelin, home to a dizzying array of shrines, prayer gardens, and temples dedicated to the Path of the Stars, maintained by High Priestess Ancela, and to sanctums for the Wealdworkers and Dreamweavers. Beyond these vales, in towering spires, reside the powerful storm sorceresses. Hidden far behind the borders of the green lands, obscured from the view of any travelers who may venture to or from the palace, are the jarring, uncharacteristically dilapidated homes of the Verdelam, Elves of lower blood desperate to prove themselves worthy of social ascension. Each morning they journey to the keep and surrounding temples to perform the mundane tasks and menial labor that keep the kingdom functioning smoothly, allowing them — at a pace that would mortify any of the world's shortlived races — to slowly earn the respect and prestige necessary to rise to meaningful posts within Elven society. Those who fail to ascend but are unwilling or unable to return to their former lives usually embrace the life of an adventurer or join the ranks of the Latari army; while noble blood is required to become an officer, Captain Ilendar accepts into the rank and file all who can meet the physical requirements of soldiering. Sources Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), pp. 174–176

title: Lizardmen
content: Lizardmen The lizardmen are a fallen race of Zanaga, broken by the wheel of history and little recovered after their grand empire vanished centuries ago. Taller and thinner than the Mahkim, and more similar in appearance to a scaled Human, they dwell in the ruins of their once-magnificent cities. Description In the sacred moon city of Xitotl, the upper levels house Humans and Mahkim, while the lizardmen live in the shadows below. The living ziggurat of Teno'tek, whose location changes from season to season, remains a center for the lizardmen, although they have long forgotten how to open its great sun gates and venture inside. Often found alongside Mahkim, lizardmen wear trappings of ancient, broken technologies and wield strange tools with purposes that are a mystery even to their owners. The lizard god, Moakileki, is an ancient figure of legend believed to have caused the downfall of the great lizardman empire. Some say the last act of the lizardmen's potent spellcasters, the Crystal Seers, was to cage Moakileki, giving up their lives in the last days of their empire to entomb the god somewhere beneath the jungles of Zanaga. Along with the Mahkim, the surviving lizardmen were instrumental in averting the total victory of Tarakhe, the Plague God, who grew from the decline and ruin of their empire. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), pp. 256–257

title: Llander
content: Llander Llander was the elder brother of Llovar, a member of the Loth K'har who showed quality as a raider and forager despite his tender years, and who remained a close confidant of his brother's rule even after voicing misgivings about his growing corruption. History On the Night of Summons, Llander's wife Rala gave birth to a son, Timmorran, whom nightseers hailed as a man of great import to come. Fearful of his brother's increasing depravity, Llander fled with his family to the wastes to start life anew, making for the distant coastal empire of Lorimor. Llovar regarded his brother's abandonment as a dreadful betrayal and called for Ynfernael forces to curse the runaways; whether the curse was effective is not known, but Rala died of a lingering sickness on the road, and Llander mysteriously vanished shortly before Timmorran, by then a boy of five, reached the gates of Lorimor. Sources The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), pp. 33–34 The Rise of Timmorran (Tales of Darkness), p. 35

title: Llovar
content: Llovar Llovar Rutonu Lokander, born in 412, was a prodigiously gifted nightseer of the Loth K'har who fell into irrevocable corruption in the T'mara T'rusheen and forged his people into the Uthuk Y'llan, plunging Mennara into the First Darkness. Table of Contents Early Life Llovar Ascendant The First Darkness Death and Legacy Sources Early Life Llovar's family was noted among the Loth K'har for producing many renowned nightseers and chiefs, from tribespeople able to survive even in the far-eastern wastes where deep volcanic vents usher poisonous fumes from the world's depths; some scholars suspect one of the Daewyl rents between Mennara and the Ynfernael can be found within those eastern wastes, and that Llovar was sensitive to the Ynfernael's influence from infancy. His elder brother Llander showed quality as a raider and forager despite his tender years, but much was expected of young Llovar, and he defied those expectations further still: he quickly became recognized for his prodigious dreamwalking abilities, earning the title of nightseer by his eleventh birthday. He grew increasingly reckless, though, and during a lengthy sojourn in the T'mara T'rusheen, Llovar is said to have met with an aspect of the Ynfernael and fallen into irrevocable corruption. Within the harsh but otherwise peaceful society of the Loth K'har, his prowess and wayward genius was celebrated despite the clear signs of malign influence; the chieftains of his tribe hailed him as a holy figure, then made him their peer, then their leader. Those who opposed his increasing power were shunned or executed, though Llander remained a close confidant despite having voiced misgivings about his brother's rule. Llovar Ascendant Llovar sprung his carefully laid scheme during the Night of Summons, leading his tribe's greatest warriors into the T'mara T'rusheen with promises of great rewards and forbidden bindings; they emerged physically transformed by Ynfernael influence, their wiry muscles grown supernaturally powerful and their very bones pushing through their skin to form great spikes and blades. With these warriors at his side, Llovar formed a confederation of tribes, conquering those who refused to ally willingly — even the chiefs of the Scal and L'jan tribes, many times larger than the Loth K'har, bent the knee. His campaign bloomed into full civil war between the tribes of the plains, and the Loth K'har and their allies took on a new title, the Uthuk Y'llan, "locust swarm" in the language of the plains people, as they conquered more and more of The Ru. By 478, Llovar had finished his consolidation of the northern plains, and the Uthuk Y'llan armies marched to despoil the southern lands, bringing about the First Darkness. He could not have brought war to Talindon alone, however: the Orcs of The Broken Plains were the first to pledge allegiance to the Locust Lord under their bellicose Chief Lukosh, later joined by Warlord Hellspanth and his band of dragons from the far north. Llovar reserved final say on matters of strategy and led the Uthuk atop his beloved steed Dire, a carnivorous beast he had personally summoned from the Ynfernael. The First Darkness Throughout 478, Llovar's armies burned the eastern groves of The Aymhelin and plundered Talindon, bettering the forces of King Falladir Penacor in open battle. The following year, Llovar sent his Orc allies raiding while he marched his Uthuk north to besiege Thelgrim, considering the Dwarven capital a particular prize for its command of surrounding supply routes; lacking the equipment to storm it, his forces instead encircled the fortress to starve out its defenders. An alliance of Humans and Elves under Falladir and King Triamlavar relieved the siege, and by 483 Timmorran's campaign, aided by Falladir and Triamlavar, began to turn the tide — at the Battle of the Burning Hills, Timmorran struck down Chief Lukosh, breaking the Orcs' loyalty to Llovar's cause, and by 486 Llovar could no longer call upon a single Orcish regiment. Llovar's own lost legion under the general Waiqar Sumarion, sent by Timmorran directly toward Llovar's Black Citadel in the Charg'r Wastes, vanished from all record for the rest of the war, its path becoming known as the Road of Skulls. In the distant Ru Darklands, Llovar gathered his reserves, now able to rely only on Warlord Hellspanth's dragons after the loss of his Orc allies; still, the army grown so great it was called the Host of Thorns, split into contingents led by trusted lieutenants — the bone-witch Q'aro Fenn, Melinesh the Cruel and Terrible, Nashaia King's Bane, and Kul the Serpent, the greatest archer of the Uthuk. In 487 the Host of Thorns invaded Talindon, and at The Ashen Field it fell upon an army led by Falladir and his sons, slaying all three Penacors and their soldiers; only a small band of survivors led by the young Baron Daqan escaped, warning Timmorran of Llovar's renewed force. Timmorran made his stand in the foothills of the Razor Crags, reinforced unexpectedly by Dwarven troops from Thelgrim under Halgir Son of Grom. At the Battle of the Locusts, Kul's assault nearly broke Timmorran's position, wounding Triamlavar, killing Halgir, and killing Ashan the Elder, but Timmorran had conserved his own magical energies for the final clash — he boiled away Llovar's summoned Ynfernael monstrosities with blazing arcane light, withstood the Locust Lord's ensorcelled blade behind a shield of pure force, and at last pierced his uncle's rotten heart with a lance of arcane power. Dire fell alongside his master, his body dissolving as its energies returned to the Ynfernael, and the Host of Thorns turned and fled; the First Darkness had passed. Death and Legacy In the ensuing chaos, the body of the Locust Lord was lost amid looting and disorganized pursuit, and the fate of his lieutenants was never confirmed. Some say Q'aro Fenn rescued Llovar's corpse from the crags and took it to a secret place far beyond the Ru, a resting place said to be found only by following the trail of her bitter tears; when Llovar was slain, his lieutenants slaughtered every last Uthuk who knew of the Black Citadel's location, before sacrificing themselves in one last act of loyalty to their master, so that the Black Citadel disappeared from history, its wealth and secrets hidden by sorcery somewhere deep in the Darklands. Timmorran later journeyed with an army into the Charg'r Wastes to rescue Waiqar Sumarion, discovering the Black Citadel and vanquishing the horrors that dwelt therein along with the forlorn general, and — inadvertently — releasing the ancient Elf Zarihell as well. The Flayed Kindred, descended from Llovar's inner circle, hold many of the keys believed to open the Black Citadel's gates, and many of their witches and warlocks believe that if it can be found, Llovar himself might be returned to the world. The nightseer Quin'tar Shymaex seeks to transform all Uthuk into true demons, a goal that eluded even Llovar himself. The corrupted Elven tribe of the Daewyl also drew on the same Ynfernael power, in their covetous pursuit of Latariana's Tears, while Maegan Cyndewin's mother of the Loth Caara lived to see Llovar corrupt her own people in turn. Sources The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), pp. 33–34 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35–37 The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 38 Whispers of the Ynfernael (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 218–219 A Tear in the Veil (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 212 Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 213–214 The Charg'r Wastes (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 210–211

title: Locust Swarm
content: Locust Swarm The Locust Swarm, or Locust Horde, is the name given to the transformed host of the Uthuk Y'llan, the once-peaceful Loth K'har turned into a hungry horde of locusts when Llovar fell prey to the Ynfernael. The Gore Claws are the self-proclaimed inheritors of the Locust Swarm, and it was long before the rise of the Locust Horde that a tribe of Dwarves built the empire now known as The Hollow Kingdom in The Ru. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211 The Ru and the Darkness (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 210 Whispers of the Ynfernael (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 218

title: Lok Urak
content: Lok Urak Legend says that the Lok Urak, the "Bow Tribe" that inhabits the eastern edges of The Broken Plains along The Lok Cliffs, were the first Orcs to craft bows of bone, horn, and sinew. Regardless of the truth, the Lok Urak are amazing hunters whose precision with their powerful U'Rek bows not only provides them with a near limitless supply of elk along the mountain edges, but also makes them an exceptionally dangerous tribe to war with. Like most Orcs in the Plains, they are nomadic, though they do stay longer in one spot than others as their land is often more bountiful and forgiving than many other places. Under the watchful eye of Chieftain Mogro the Swift, these Orcs begin training with their bows from the day they can first hold an U'Rek, and there is not a day of a Lok Urak's life that they are spared from weapons training. Assisting Mogro is the council leader Scurr the Huntress, the Orc most directly responsible for keeping the tribe fed. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 200–201

title: Looking Glass Spire
content: Looking Glass Spire The Looking Glass Spire is a college of the Collegiate Arcane which guards the gates of Siryasa, named for a relic looking glass early spellcasters crafted to trap a measure of Djinn power. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 244

title: Lord of Bilehall
content: Lord of Bilehall The Lords of Bilehall are the vampiric nobility of Bilehall who, when they discarded their humanity to join Waiqar, tied their fates to his; they became immensely more powerful as the corrupting mists covered their lands and they rose in undeath. Today they are an arrogant line, besotted from centuries of indulging in their every desire, exulting in the pleasures of immortality — each has become a ruler in their own right, and even the lowest vampire of the line can claim a crypt-fortress as their own. The ages have made the Lords of Bilehall both shrewd and knowledgeable; some, such as Kyndrithul and Vorun'thul, have dedicated themselves to necromancy, even gaining enough power to raise lesser Reanimates, while others have become masters of warfare and lead raids on the baronies to the south or even into Dunwarr and other realms. It is rare to encounter such creatures without powerful minions to defend them, but such is their hubris that they fear little except Waiqar himself and may step forth alone to toy with those who dare venture into their domains — to survive such an occurrence is even rarer, for Lords such as Kyndrithul and Vorun'thul have had hundreds of years to set traps, arrange countermeasures, and prepare themselves for almost any enemy. Sources Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), pp. 165–166

title: Lorim's Gate Mountains
content: Lorim's Gate Mountains The Lorim's Gate Mountains lie west of the barony of Trast, bordering the empire of Lorimor along with the badlands of the Traitor's Wastes; together with lingering memories of Lorimor's founders, they prevent much overland trade between the two lands. In the foothills of Lorim's Gate on the Trast side, ancient menhirs rise from a rough circle of earthen mounds, where twice a year adherents of forbidden beliefs are said to gather to commune with unknowable entities under dark and twisted priests. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 137–138

title: Lorim
content: Lorim Lorim is the capital of the Lorimor Empire, one of the most scenic cities to be found anywhere, a setting of vibrant markets and spectacular public works whose architects and stonemasons have crafted breathtaking coliseums and enormous legendary statues and monuments, many dedicated to its dual founders Rusticar Lorimor and Riya Penacor. Lorimor grew around this city, establishing powerful armies and the greatest navy in the world. Lorim is recognized as a power in Mennara, but its time as the dominant nation has long since vanished, and the city has become filled with conspiracies and plots — as the empire has weakened, its chancellors, princes, merchant lords, spymasters, and other principals have grown ever more desperate to hold onto whatever power remains. Visitors from abroad often make for excellent cats' paws in their intrigues; travelers here may be able to gain royal audiences and perhaps agree to take on quests against raiding monsters or troublesome bandits, and even local authorities may call on outsiders to deal with matters they would rather not become public. Still, the city can offer much to travelers and traders: the long continuity of the Lorimor Empire means there are troves of scholarship here, opportunities to learn about anything from architecture and shipbuilding to the latest exotic discoveries from other realms, and centuries of trade ensure that goods of almost any nature can be bought here. Sources Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 220–221

title: Lorimor Marine
content: Lorimor Marine Lorimor is known for its fleets, but while its ships are among the finest on the seas, it is the quality of the crews that really make them shine — as not all seafaring ventures are peaceful ones, the crews always include a contingent of marines ready to both repel boarders and lead assaults against enemy vessels. Each marine is a skilled fighter, even on uncertain decks awash with saltwater and blood. The sight of them high in the riggings, ready to cross with a boarding rope in one hand and shortsword in the other, has made many an enemy captain quickly offer surrender. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 227

title: Lorimor and the Torue Albes
content: Lorimor and the Torue Albes To the west of Terrinoth lies a huge peninsula and associated islands that project into the vast deep waters that stretch on seemingly forever, settled long ago in a tale of tragedy and betrayal. These lands have since become a bastion of civilization and exploration. The Empire of Lorimor, which occupies the peninsula, hosts what many claim to be the greatest Human nation in Mennara's history. None would confuse The Torue Albes with the heights of civilization, but the many pirates, ruffians, and eccentrics that make the islands their home port have made the archipelago the start of many adventures into the unknown, both out to sea and in the still-uncharted wilds inland. Sources Lorimor and the Torue Albes (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 220

title: Lorimor
content: Lorimor Lorimor is a gleaming spear upon which humanity has flourished, a temperate land that juts out into the sea, founded when Rusticar Lorimor and Riya Penacor were banished from Terrinoth for betraying their king — who was his closest friend and her husband. Table of Contents History The Inlands The Coastlands Sources History Many historians cite Lorimor's founding as one of the critical moments in the early history of the Penacor Kings, a singular event that defined the course of Terrinoth for millennia, though to focus on this alone would be to ignore the greater history of Lorimor as a proud, noble nation in its own right, a land of romantics, poets, builders, philosophers, sailors, and soldiers. Lorimor was founded near the beginning of the Age of Steel, late in the third century of the Human calendar. The exiles' travels led them to a huge, unexplored peninsula extending to the north, running between the Teallin Sea and the Kingless Coast to the east, and dark blue waters on the west that seemed to go on forever. As they entered the region, there appeared to be no hope for settlement — the lands were pleasant enough, but edible game was scarce and their imported crops struggled in the rockier soil, and the lands seemed utterly indefensible should the king decide his judgment had been too lenient, or should the inscrutable Elves of the Aymhelin wish to extend their domain. After many months, the exiles and their followers finally reached a more suitable location, forested and thick with sustenance; this became their new home, and in time the city of Lorim became the capital of the new Lorimor Empire. From here, scouts explored outward to found new cities, such as Orris along the coast, and went on to establish new colonies in the islands to the north that became The Torue Albes. The Inlands The interior of Lorimor was the first to be occupied, and its peoples still dominate the nation via the political power of the capital and the surrounding cities to which it has close ties. Huge areas of the peninsula are unexplored and wild to this day, however, and small settlements exist in these areas in relative isolation, where those seeking shelter from prying eyes can undertake rituals and experiments that would lead to banishment or worse in civilized regions. Notable landmarks of the Inlands include Mounts Arrik and Orrik and The Lost Keeps. The Coastlands Though the inlands dominate Lorimor politically, the coastal cities dominate it monetarily. Trade is their watchword, and mercantile ships travel across the known world and beyond from Lorimor's many harbors, extending to Terrinoth and the fabled markets of Tamalir, as the empire and the land of its origin reconciled when they fought together against the darkness. Lorim struggles to maintain control over the coasts, but there are always factions more concerned with gold than with supporting the capital. The principal coastal cities are Orris and Redwater. Sources Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 220–223

title: Lost Knight
content: Lost Knight One of the mysteries of the Lorimor peninsula are the lost knights sometimes seen in the hinterlands and rougher inland areas. Descriptions range from proud wanderers in gleaming plate armor to wizened ancients with rusted swords and long, grey beards, but they all seem to share weary expressions that speak of far too many years, if not centuries, of endless and hopeless existence. These mysterious knights rarely, if ever, speak of their pasts or origins, leading some to wonder if they are members of Rusticar Lorimor's bonded knights who followed him and Riya Penacor into exile. Records indicate not all of the company made it to what would become the city of Lorim, as some gave up on the trek and their new lord. Tavern tales in the Albes speculate these figures may still be questing across Lorimor in search of rights to wrong, hoping one day to be allowed to achieve a final rest. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 227

title: Loth Caara
content: Loth Caara The Loth Caara, Elven for "dream walkers," are a Latari tribe who named themselves after the nightseer shamans of the Loth K'har, whose prophetic talents so impressed them — the Loth K'har in turn took their own name from this term. Llovar corrupted the Loth Caara in his day, and Maegan Cyndewin's mother was a Loth Caara tribeswoman who lived to see this corruption, a legacy that fuels much of the High Court's distrust of her daughter. Sources The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), p. 33 Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 175

title: Loth K'har
content: Loth K'har The Loth K'har were the peaceful, nomadic plains-dwellers of The Ru before Llovar fell prey to the demons and transformed them into the Uthuk Y'llan, the hungry horde of locusts, on the Night of Summons. History During good times, the Loth K'har roved the plains, searching for fresh grazing grounds for their animals and trading with the many settlements that ringed the wastes; in leaner times, they would turn into vicious raiders, falling on those same settlements for loot.
