Their shamans learned of a realm known as the T'mara T'rusheen, and from it gleaned prophetic advice; the most skillful among these shamans formed a caste known as the nightseers, said to have been close to members of a distant Elven tribe so impressed by their talents that they called them the Loth Caara, Elven for "dream walkers" — from this term the Loth K'har derive their own name. Llovar himself, born in 412, was among the most gifted of these nightseers, earning the title by his eleventh birthday before his corruption in the T'mara T'rusheen set the tribe's transformation in motion. As the Ynfernael's power corrupted and transformed their flesh, it twisted the magics of the Loth K'har as well: the nightseers of their ancient dreamwalking tradition, who once used their abilities to travel to and commune with benevolent spirits, now used them to travel to and commune with demons from beyond, and their ancient ability to link minds into harmonious discussion grew darker until it became their method to command and dominate the Locust armies. Those who spoke out against the corruption of their ancient ways were destroyed, leaving only rage and hate in their place. Sources The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), pp. 33–34 Whispers of the Ynfernael (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 218

title: Lothan River
content: Lothan River The Lothan is a long, wide river running beyond Orrush Khatak in Eastern Terrinoth, at its widest point forming Hernfar Isle, the furthest eastern outpost of the Daqan Lords. Soldiers of Kell keep watch over its fords from ancient watchtowers, and the low foothills of the badlands beyond, together with the river, are all that separate them from the Darklands. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Lumii Tamar
content: Lumii Tamar Lumii Tamar was the foremost of the acolytes who studied at the Tower of Meringyr, entrusted by Timmorran on the Night of Betrayal with the shattered fragments of the Orb of the Sky and sworn to distribute them throughout the world to those wise enough to use them. History Through a quite unprecedented act of high magic, Lumii slipped past the terrible forces laying waste to the Wizard's Vale, escaping with all but a single fragment of the Orb. He made his way to Archaut, arriving during the Council of 516 as a shrouded stranger claiming to be a survivor of the slaughter; bearing nothing more offensive than a velvet pouch, he was permitted to address the Council and gave his account of Waiqar's betrayal. In the wake of this revelation and the death of Baron Irehythe, Lumii suggested that the fragments he carried — which he named the Stars of Timmorran — be kept secret and safe, and the Council granted him the authority to create and head an order of wizards tasked with protecting the Stars and advising on matters regarding them. Lumii, and the Stars, pass from history at this moment. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 40–41

title: Lutetia Dallia
content: Lutetia Dallia Lutetia Dallia was a famed mercenary captain who conducted a brilliant campaign on behalf of Grand Duke Consino to win him the throne of The Torue Albes in the wake of the islands' revolt against Lorimor, only for Consino to try to sell her out for the favor of House Harthorn. History Lutetia survived several assassination attempts organized by Consino and captured and interrogated one of her intended killers, showing him no mercy until he revealed who had paid him. She then led a force of elite mercenaries to storm the Grand Duke's castle and threw him into his own deepest oubliette, taking the position of ruler of the Torue Albes for herself and naming its capital city — Dallak — for her line. In time she gave birth to many sons and daughters, and wishing to keep control of the islands in the family, established a strong system of royal rule that persists there to this day; the rulers of the Torue Albes, especially its queens, remain fierce in their independence and known for ruthless governance. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), p. 50

title: Lyssa Svensdottir
content: Lyssa Svensdottir Skirmisher Captain Lyssa Svensdottir commands the southern barracks of the Warriors' Guild in Thelgrim, overseeing all Dunwarr military action outside the mountains. She is the sister of Guard Captain Einalf Svensson, who commands the city's northern barracks and the defenses of the Dunwarr Deeps. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Mace of Kellos
content: Mace of Kellos Priests of Kellos once ordered the forging of a flanged mace, performing a series of warlike rituals upon it and imbuing it with the spirit of their god's wrathful aspect. When the Mace of Kellos is hefted in anger, the head of the weapon bursts into flames that scorch the foe. Sources Magic Items, p. 109

title: Maegan Cyndewin
content: Maegan Cyndewin Maegan Cyndewin is the trusted advisor and long-time consort of King Aenoeth of Lithelin, though many in the High Court still deeply distrust her and conspire against her whenever they can. Theirs is a rueful hatred fueled in part by the legacy of her father, a member of the Daewyl tribe, which allied with demons in its covetous pursuit of Latariana's Tears, and by the legacy of her mother, a Loth Caara tribeswoman who lived to see Llovar corrupt her people. Her parentage serves as a perpetual blight to her honor despite how instrumental she was in defending Caelcira, having fought valiantly and been wounded repeatedly in the Elven nation's defense; many fear she has been corrupted by the same power that seduced her parents' tribes and is working to bring about the same downfall of the Latari. In the early years of the 1600s, it was at Maegan's urging that King Aenoeth judged the time right for the Latari to take renewed interest in the outside world, dispatching scouts into Terrinoth and beyond over the vehement objections of Prince Faolan. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 51 Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 175

title: Mag Ugluk Urak
content: Mag Ugluk Urak The Mag Ugluk Urak, loosely the "Great Beast Tribe," remain the most nomadic of the modern Orcs of The Ugluk Badlands; conflicts with other Orc tribes are simultaneously inevitable and unpredictable, and it is a life almost completely lacking in comfort or security. For most people, even for most Orcs, the challenges of that ever-moving existence would simply be too much — but not for the Mag Ugluk Urak, because they have the Gurak Tol. Young Orcs are sent to steal the eggs of these huge, six-legged lizards from the clutches of watchful brood mothers and raise them on their own; having raised them since hatching, the tribe's Beast Riders (see Orc Outrider) form an emotional connection with their mounts that gives the pair unrivaled skills and adaptability compared with mundane cavalry, and they are unquestionably among the most feared mounted warriors in the world. Leading the Great Beast Tribe, and coordinating their efforts both for and against the surrounding Orc tribes, is the legendary rider Skorn. At Skorn's right hand stands Gorhta Tamer Uglar, the leader of the tribal council and Master of Obedience who oversees all the various forms of beast training. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Magrit Kalrif
content: Magrit Kalrif Baroness Magrit Kalrif rules Dhernas from Dhernar Keep, in the shadow of the Broken Crags overlooking the River of Sleep — a militantly minded ruler whose spearmen and knights are respected across Terrinoth for their discipline and fine arms and armor. Her forces march under a banner bearing a sword and open gauntlet, symbolizing justice and mercy. Kalrif's soldiers have already begun deploying in response to rumors of threats from the Ru, which she eagerly anticipates joining on the field. Along with Baron Gilliam Xarles of Cailn, she has quietly begun seeking information that might turn the people of Frest against Baroness Harriet, wary of the risks of open war. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138 Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Mahkim
content: Mahkim The Mahkim are a four-armed reptilian race, and the inheritors of the lizardman empire of Zanaga. Once they were the martial scions of the lizardmen, and the legacy of those glorious days remains in their advanced tactics, unique weapons, and jungle combat skills. Description While those lizardmen who remain are primitive descendants who remember little of their ancestors' glory, the Mahkim have lost little of their culture. Many tribes of Mahkim dwell upon ancient roads or in the shadow of an old lizardman temple, protecting these structures from the agents and war parties of the Nagas, who are eager to steal their secrets. Adventurers may find themselves allies or enemies of the Mahkim, depending on whether they come seeking their guidance or to plunder their eggs — clutches of these milky-green orbs fetch a high price in the ports of Terrinoth and Al-Kalim, where their healing properties are well known. Mahkim are the masters of the inland waterways and guides without peer, which can come in handy when trying to avoid naga hunters in the depths of the old lizardman empire; explorers sometimes recruit Mahkim warriors or hunters, the race's young having a reputation for striking out on their own to make their fortune. The largest Mahkim village, and the spiritual center of their people, rides on the back of the huge crocodile Ravin. When challenged or wronged, Mahkim warriors paint the god's likeness on their hides and cry out his name as they charge into battle; these same devotees then devour their fallen enemies, each gulp of meat another prayer to their god. Mahkim warriors (also spelled "Makhim" in some sources) are as fierce as any in Zanaga, employing weapons that only a four-armed fighter could wield, like the dagger-like dolochs they wear as gauntlets, alongside leather slings twisted and swung to send a missile flying with tremendous momentum. They are seldom encountered alone, usually traveling in great war parties, some scouting ahead, others staying to the shadows, until the jungle comes alive with a cacophony of hissing war cries. Along with the few surviving lizardmen, the Mahkim were instrumental in averting the total victory of Tarakhe, the Plague God, and continue to fight against the remnants of his threat. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), pp. 256–257 Life in the Jungle (Zanaga), p. 258

title: Malcari
content: Malcari The Malcari were the eleventh of the Elven tribes among whom Emorial divided the Tears of Latariana, venturing forth from the boughs of The Aymhelin to settle in the Jornall Mountains, where Emorial was believed to have pursued the Ynfernael's servants. Under their chieftain Malcorne, the Malcari were nearly extinguished when their corruption into the Daewyl triggered The War of the Shadow Tear and their subsequent destruction at The Battle of Enfreil. At least one surviving group, now calling themselves the Deep Elves, seeks to atone for the Malcari's sins by destroying demons. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), pp. 27–29

title: Malcorne, the Corrupted One
content: Malcorne, the Corrupted One Malcorne was the proud bearer of a Tear of Latariana and chieftain of the Malcari, the eleventh Elven tribe, whose corruption plunged the Elves into The War of the Shadow Tear — a stain the Deep Elves have dedicated their endless crusade against the Ynfernael to redeeming. Table of Contents History The Shadow Tear Downfall Sources History The Malcari ventured forth from the boughs of The Aymhelin and roamed far from the other tribes, settling at last in the Jornall Mountains, where Emorial was believed to have pursued the Ynfernael's servants after abandoning the Elves. Among the other tribes, Malcorne's folk had a mixed reputation — hailed as heroes for carrying Emorial's legacy into the present, but also regarded as aloof and criticized for taking action without consulting the other tribes, having begun to study and use the demons' very power against them in their efforts to fight the Ynfernael. During one patrol, Malcorne was leading a band of demon hunters deep into the caverns when their battles caused a cave-in that separated him from the others; he was thought to have perished alongside the treacherous demons, and his tribe wept for their lost leader. When he returned to the Malcari city, having somehow miraculously survived his encounter with a demon, Malcorne was a changed chieftain, given to brooding moods and regarding his fellows with suspicious glances. In time, he gathered a small coterie of his most trusted allies and explained that in his wanderings he had found Emorial himself, who revealed to him that the Tears of Latariana were a gift in disguise, powerful enough to open a door to the Aenlong and allow the Elves to return to their rightful home — and that the promise the Yrthwright Mennara had given Latariana was a lie, meant only to keep the Elves subservient and obsequious toward the First for the rest of eternity. In his dying breath, this Emorial charged Malcorne with revealing the truth to the other tribes and leading them in rebellion against their former masters. The Latari Elves maintain to this day that it was not Emorial whom Malcorne encountered in the cave, but a cunning demon wearing his face. The Shadow Tear Knowing the Elves would need strong allies to cast down the First, Malcorne used his Tear to pull down the shields between the Firma Dracem and the Aenlong, finding there a horde of demons who had crossed over from where the Ynfernael overlapped with the Aenlong. In that moment, the Tear of Latariana that Malcorne possessed grew dull and shadowy, losing the light it once held, becoming the Shadow Tear. Once he had corrupted his birthright, Malcorne used it to open up rents in the fabric of reality, though the process was arduous; he reached out to the other tribes, explaining Mennara's supposed lie and that their Tears were needed to break the shackles of reality and gather allies from the Aenlong. The other tribes saw Malcorne's plans for what they were — evil and corrupt, twisted by the whisperings of demons — and the two sides could not be reconciled. Malcorne launched an attack on the other Elven tribes, determined to capture their Tears by force, and backed by ranks of savage demons and packs of Ynfernael creatures, his followers ravaged and routed the first few Elven armies sent to stop them. Soon the other tribes scattered before Malcorne and what they called the Daewyl, or "Twice Fallen" Elves, and the surviving Elves fled to remote regions, distant islands, and lonely mountaintops to protect their precious Tears from capture. Downfall In the depths of darkness, Glaciel Snowstar, son of the chieftain of the tenth tribe, the Nivalis, refused to give in to despair after witnessing Malcorne's devastation firsthand. He rescued his father's Tear and traveled to the Yrthwrights' own home to ask the dragons for guidance, gathering companions along the way: High Priestess Celeneth of the Salish, the Feredel sorcerer Keldarim, Erenil the Swift of the Latari, and others. The dragons, tasked by the First with preserving the world, at first rebuffed Glaciel's appeal, believing the Elves would need to bear this burden of their own doing — interceding, they warned, would one day force the tribes to pay a terrible price. Glaciel would not give up, and accepted the dragons' terms; he and his companions returned to rally their tribes with a flight of dragons at their back, and on the Plains of Enfreil they fought a final battle against Malcorne, in the world's most desperate hour ultimately achieving victory and striking down the dark Elven lord. The remaining Daewyl retreated from the combined Elven and draconic forces, hoping to hide themselves away, but the victors hunted down their foes to burn them from the face of the world, nearly extinguishing Malcorne's wretched tribe in the slaughter. Many worry that small enclaves of the Daewyl still lurk in the dark nooks of the world, but at least one group, now calling themselves the Deep Elves, claims to have come back to the light, seeking to atone for their sins by destroying demons in this realm and others beyond. The Shadow Tear itself — also called the Shadow War, this conflict's alternate name — went missing during the fighting; if it survived unbroken, a powerful artifact combining both Empyrean and Ynfernael magic still waits somewhere for someone to find it, akin in power to the unbound Stars of Timmorran that the original Tears of Latariana are believed to have anticipated. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), pp. 27–29 Spiritspeaking (Call to Adventure), pp. 126–127 Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 190

title: Manaan
content: Manaan Manaan is an ancient, wizened spiritspeaker who oversees the village of Selonish on the Selenic Coast, possessing a level of power seen only a few times each century. Having long since given up the active pursuit of any additional mastery, Manaan now spends her days providing counsel to the village, guiding younger spiritspeakers, and helping to ensure that the ripples caused by the Whispering Forest don't spread beyond the village's borders. [not stated in source: whether the Whispering Forest is the same place as the nearby Greywood] Sources Selenic Coast (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Manticore
content: Manticore There are many theories about how manticores came to be, most assuming an artificial origin, as no natural process can readily be imagined for how lion bodies, bat-like wings, and scorpion tails could come to exist in a single entity. Such theories tend to involve drunken mages and spells gone horribly wrong. Unfortunately, the fierce nature of these creatures means there are very few opportunities to study them. Manticores appear to be not only perpetually hungry but vicious as well, especially those that fly across the western islands of The Torue Albes. They take delight in each raking claw that draws blood and each stinging stab of their insectoid tail. Many foes learn far too late that the creatures can also hurl volleys of spikes from their tails, which can puncture armor to deliver deadly venoms; some alchemists who have studied the venoms claim they have traces of magical properties, but proof of this has not yet been established, and no reliable antivenom has been developed either. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 227–228

title: Margath
content: Margath Margath the Unkind was the dragonlord who led the invasion of Terrinoth during the Third Darkness, ultimately slain by Lord Roland of Kell at the war's culmination. History In 1024, Margath was one of six dragonlords — alongside Levirax, Baalesh, Zir the Black, Avox, and Gehennor — who each led a band of lesser drakes against a different part of the world, motivated by greed for the Stars of Timmorran; the attacks were nearly simultaneous but uncoordinated between the rival dragonlords, none of whom were acting with the sanction of the Great Dragon Rex Shaarina. Margath knew from the outset what he wanted and where to get it: a great cache of Stars held in the treasury of King Trevnor Soulstone in Tamalir. His host flew to the Free City and faced little opposition, his dragon hybrids descending on its towers and artillery while his drakes incinerated the infantry sent against them; Margath himself is said to have broken into the royal palace and burned the king to charred meat along with his family and retainers, leaving Terrinoth without a ruler once more and gathering up the palace's riches, including a sizable cache of Stars. As the war dragged on and the dragonlords turned Stars into weaponized runebound shards, Margath's host became nigh unbeatable, so confident in its new power that he ceased managing it as a coherent force, instead letting each dragonlord raid independently. In 1029, in the war's final days, Lord Roland of Kell led the defense of the city of Kell using a ruse — false rumors of Stars hidden there — to lure Margath's forces into a hail of ballista fire from the city's defensive redoubts. As the dragons retreated to the cold skies above the Mountains of Despair, Roland took to the air on his winged Yeron and summoned freezing rain onto Margath's position with an ice storm runebound shard, leaving the dragonlord dazed and weakened from the cold; Roland then drove his lance through the great drake's neck, killing him. In his death throes, Margath broke the wings of Roland's mount, and both riders tumbled from the sky to their deaths — their remains were never recovered from the snow-shrouded peaks. [not stated in source: a separate account, tied to the cult of Aris, instead holds that Margath's body fell to earth at the Weeping Basin and was slain by a "Baron Rolan." The two accounts are not reconciled in the sources and are recorded here as each source states them.] Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 45–48 Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 123 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Marnn
content: Marnn Marnn is the great nimbus giant among the Stormlords, said to smash ships to smithereens with his great hammer from within the dark storm that churns on the western horizon of the Great Sea. Sailors make signs to ward away his wrath as they placate the Stormlords with offerings. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 124

title: Marshals of the Citadel
content: Marshals of the Citadel The Marshals of the Citadel are foremost among the few knightly orders that swear fealty to Terrinoth as a whole rather than any single baron, each Marshal both a skilled warrior and an expert scholar well versed in the laws of Terrinoth. Marshals deliver justice across Terrinoth, dealing with threats ranging from traitorous nobles and highwaymen to goblin warbands and practitioners of forbidden magic; they are empowered to serve as judge, jury, and executioner, and their loyalty is beyond dispute. In these times, even the Marshals are scarcely sufficient for the many threats emerging across Terrinoth, leading Warden Gravia Kein to increasingly employ itinerant adventurers and mercenaries alongside them. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 142

title: Masons' Guild
content: Masons' Guild The Masons' Guild is one of the Dunwarr Guilds, responsible for constructing new buildings and maintaining venerated structures within the Dunwarr Mountains, working in tandem with the Miners' Guild, which excavates the tunnels and chambers the Masons then build within. In the Age of Courage, Ingunn Vergsbold, then head of the Masons' Guild in Thelgrim, set out to rebuild the city's long-destroyed districts after the devastation of the Third Darkness. Her decades-long reconstruction effort — including having the Miners' Guild cut the great chasm linking Thelgrim to the Hearth Road — grew into the movement that cemented the political dominance of the Dunwarr Guilds, and she herself rose to become First Speaker of Dunwarr. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 50–51

title: Melinesh the Cruel and Terrible
content: Melinesh the Cruel and Terrible Melinesh the Cruel and Terrible was one of Llovar's most feared lieutenants, commanding a contingent of the Host of Thorns during the First Darkness, one of the names that became bywords for wickedness and treachery among the allies of Terrinoth. At The Ashen Field in 487, a blow from King Falladir Penacor's sword nearly cleaved Melinesh's head from his shoulders, but Llovar's numbers, magic, and malice ultimately proved too great, and the three Penacors on the field died before the day's end. Melinesh's ultimate fate is not recorded. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 36–37

title: Mennara's Teeth
content: Mennara's Teeth Mennara's Teeth is an unusual mountain range across the plains from Otrin — small in area but piercing sharp and narrow into the sky, like the fangs of a great beast. Dragons are said to come to these mountains when they feel their life's end drawing close, and most people avoid the foothills for fear of encountering one. Stories persist of the Cave of Wonders said to lie somewhere amid its dagger-like slopes. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Mennara
content: Mennara Mennara is the Yrthwright who architected the great glade that would become The Aymhelin, and the being for whom some dare name the mortal world itself. History The Yrthwrights, winged serpents who set about creating the Firma Dracem — the mortal realm — through incantations reminiscent of the Lays of The First, adorned it with spinning bodies, planets, and suns. When Emorial led the Elves in mutiny against the First and marched his host through The Gate of Years, they found themselves not in the halls of the First as they had hoped, but lost in the Aenlong; after countless days, they emerged into a great green glade bathed in golden sunlight and spied its architect, the majestic winged serpent Mennara. Mennara held Emorial's cold gaze with its own implacable one and passed the judgments of the First down upon the rebellious Elves: they were exiled from the Empyrean, Light and Air no longer theirs to command, and they were now imprisoned upon the mortal plane — bound, Emorial realized, to the very object that was both their destination and their damnation, a crowning realm of light, air, life, and dreams. This world. When Latariana agreed to Mennara's terrible bargain — that a window to the Empyrean might one day reopen for the Elves, at the cost of her entering the Void herself — it was upon Mennara's back that she climbed before the dragon spread its vast wings and flew her up into the darkening skies to become the first star. Sources Tales of Darkness, p. 24 The Elves (Tales of Darkness), pp. 26–27

title: Merchants' Guild
content: Merchants' Guild The Merchants' Guild is one of the Dunwarr Guilds, overseeing the selling of Dunwarr's goods both to communities within the mountains and to the outside world. In the Age of Courage, the Merchants' Guild partnered with the Miners' Guild and Explorers' Guild to reestablish ties with the other Dunwarr holds once the Hearth Road linking Thelgrim to the outside world had been reopened; as trade and travel increased along the road, so did the power of the Guilds. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 51

title: Merciful Tower
content: Merciful Tower The Merciful Tower is the oldest of all the Caliph's hospitals, one of the glorious places in Al-Madena where A'tar's radiance can be seen. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Merriod
content: Merriod Among Mennara's aquatic beasts, few elicit as much terror and dread as the merriod. Sailors and pirates in Shellport taverns swear it is the last vengeance of a dead sea god, one who cursed the world with an avatar borne of its own unfathomable malice, combining the jaws of the shark, the grasping tentacles of the kraken, and the cleverness of the octopus. Thankfully, these amphibious beasts are relatively rare, slow to reproduce, and often simply slumber in their dark, damp lairs. When stirred by hunger or some darker motivation, however, merriods become one of the most dangerous predators adventurers can face, especially adept at luring or driving their targets to places where they can entrap or encircle them, such as a dank cavern or flooded dungeon. Merriods often use their mawed tentacles to stealthily grasp an adventurer and pull them down to a watery grave, but the creatures are also formidable when confronted in open battle — they move with a speed that belies their bulk, their great jaws allow them to bite clean through armor, and their thick hide can ward off the mightiest blows. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 228–229

title: Methras
content: Methras Methras is a hidden Elven township within The Bloodwood, its core an eclectic collection of dwellings fashioned high in the trees and joined by suspension bridges and shared platforms. In the center of the interconnected sprawl sits Ledish Schall, the ancestral seat of the Etharyon champion Dareine, the governing magistrate of all Elves who choose to set foot within the Bloodwood. Given its remote, often secretive nature, Methras is a home for Elves who seek refuge from the traditional caste and political structures of Latari society, and a destination for those restless Elves who seek more adventure than Elven life typically offers. Living wild among the Bloodwood, they are free to indulge in more ignoble pursuits, and within isolated huts, one can find Elves engaged in a host of scandalous ventures. Sources The Bloodwood (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Miners' Guild
content: Miners' Guild The Miners' Guild is one of the Dunwarr Guilds, digging ores and precious gems and excavating new tunnels and chambers for the Masons' Guild to build within. It was a team from the Miners' Guild, led by Master Miner Deurg, whose fateful decision to follow an unusual seam of ore led to the discovery of the Labyrinth of Deurg. In the Age of Courage, the Miners' Guild worked with First Speaker Ingunn Vergsbold of the Masons' Guild to cut the great chasm linking Thelgrim to the Hearth Road, and later partnered with the Merchants' Guild and Explorers' Guild to reestablish ties with the other Dunwarr holds. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 Labyrinth of Deurg (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 51

title: Minor Elemental
content: Minor Elemental Elemental magic, a legacy of the Djinni, runs through the bedrock of Al-Kalim. These vestiges of trapped sorcery tend to draw together to manifest as living things, gathering together like droplets of water might form a shimmering pool or lake. The elemental beings thus created may roam as lone predators, but they are just as likely to group together to form entire regions where the laws of nature no longer apply. Either way, they exist to feed upon mortals, whether drinking the water from their flesh, burning their blood for fuel, or devouring the breath from their lungs. There are many kinds of minor elementals in Al-Kalim: quicksand elementals lie in wait upon trade routes and near wells to trap the unwary, moving across the wastes of the Endless Desert's salt swamps in the night to surround caravans; flame elementals drift on the wind like flickering embers, drawn to the heat of the living, bursting into blazing life to burn away the flesh of their victims when they find their prey; and spring elementals pose as pools, lakes, or streams of tempting water in the desert wastes, though it is the fluids of their quarry they seek — should a creature be foolish enough to try to drink from one, the elemental sucks them dry, leaving only a desiccated husk behind. Sources Life in the Sands (Al-Kalim), pp. 248–249

title: Mirror Hammer
content: Mirror Hammer The Mirror Hammer is a Dwarven masterwork forged by the outcast smith Gildspar, who charged its metal with the energies of a thousand lightning bolts drawn from a storm said to be created by a floating runebound shard. In accordance with its name, when swung, the Mirror Hammer could reflect any magic and repel any blow. It held another power, too, one that revealed its true nature: when the Mirror Hammer struck the surface of a lake, the water would freeze into a silver pane, and anyone who looked into it could see visions of the distant past, the reflection of the ages. Sources Dwarves (Character Species), p. 65

title: Mirror Lake
content: Mirror Lake Mirror Lake is a wonder of the Onoit people, marked by a rune-carved way stone, where it is said one might see one's future in the sky's reflection upon its surface. Sources An Uncharted Wilderness (Isheim), p. 235

title: Misty Plains
content: Misty Plains The Misty Plains lie south of Dawnsmoor, home to settlements like Brightvale founded by folk who relocated from the Free City. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 146

title: Moakileki
content: Moakileki Moakileki, the lizard god, is an ancient figure of legend believed to have caused the downfall of the great lizardman empire of Zanaga. A beast of entropic glory, Moakileki is worshipped only by hateful and evil beings who seek the death of the world. Some say the last act of the lizardmen's potent spellcasters, the Crystal Seers, was to cage Moakileki, giving up their lives in the last days of their empire to entomb the god somewhere beneath the jungles of Zanaga. Heroes seeking out the fabled bejeweled skulls of the Crystal Council may find themselves on the path to Moakileki — and, if they are very unfortunate, perhaps even to the giant lizard's final resting place. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Mogro the Swift
content: Mogro the Swift Chieftain Mogro the Swift leads Lok Urak, the Bow Tribe, overseeing the lifelong weapons training every member undergoes with the tribe's U'Rek bows. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Mok'Thul Urak
content: Mok'Thul Urak The Mok'Thul Urak, roughly "Grey Moon Tribe," are less a clan and more a religious movement — a wandering band of spiritspeakers and bone-reading mystics based at The Mok Plateau. Considered under Pillar of Gharmuth law to be composed entirely of neutral Phantom Walkers, the Grey Moon Tribe is a universally welcoming source of counsel and aid for any sentient beings who seek their guidance. On the rare occasions that something has dared approach the Mok'Thul Urak with ill intent, those creatures — be they Orcs or otherwise — quickly discover that the spirits also believe that the Grey Moon Tribe should be protected from harm. Typically, the most difficult challenges for the Mok'Thul Urak are simple logistical ones: providing enough food for themselves and the pilgrims who seek their wisdom, ensuring that each soul is heard and helped, and resolving any disputes that arise among them. Governing these mortal concerns is a wise council led by Spiritspeaker Anka and Elder Jutta, supernaturally ancient sisters who have seen several normal Orc lifetimes come and go. Almost certainly sustained by the phantasms they commune with, the sisters are a benevolent force who offer kindness and clarity to all they touch. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Monkey God
content: Monkey God The Monkey God, cousin to Gor-Bor-Gor, is the mysterious master of the blood apes of Zanaga. Little is known of the Monkey God. For a long time, explorers believed the crude idols the apes erected represented an alpha among their kind, some great creature who ruled over their brutal tribes. It became evident, however, that they worship the Monkey God as a divine being and bring it sacrifices and meat from their kills. The Monkey God's motivations and desires remain a troubling mystery. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 254

title: Morath az Moran
content: Morath az Moran Morath az Moran was the great capital of The Karok Doum, the lost Dwarven kingdom of The Molten Heath, its fallen walls and crumbling towers shattered and seared by dragon fire. Sources The Karok Doum (The Molten Heath), p. 194

title: Mount Valborne
content: Mount Valborne Mount Valborne is the towering mountain in the Dunwarr Mountains into which Hadranhold is built, first as a lonely watchpost and, over the centuries, as a fortress and then a city. Sources Hadranhold (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188

title: Mountains of Despair
content: Mountains of Despair The Mountains of Despair are a great mountain chain marking Southern Terrinoth, off which storms roll in roiling waves, often accompanied by creatures awoken during the turmoil — dangers that have harried the region's residents for generations, molding a vigilant and resilient people. The Smokeblue Hills and the range itself have long served as a gathering place for sorcerous cults, dragon-worshippers, and other servants of darkness, and in recent years scouts have reported dragon hybrids lurking among its ruins in numbers unseen since the end of the Dragon Wars, while villages in its foothills suffer strange maladies and disappearances. The barony of Otrin abuts the range and lives in its shadow; some knowledgeable folk dismiss tales of an ancient and powerful sorcerer who dwells within and commands the elements as mere stories. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 137–138

title: Mounts Arrik and Orrik
content: Mounts Arrik and Orrik Mounts Arrik and Orrik are two peaks set on either side of the River of Sighs, not far from Orris in Lorimor, with small watchtowers along each where sharp eyes look for signs of invasion and monitor whether the powerful river is cresting to once again spill into the Queldan floodlands. Few remember the initial reports from when Arrik and Orrik were first explored, and fewer still have followed up on them, particularly the indications in the mountains of winding tunnels that appear artificial. Tales have spread from Orris and into The Torue Albes of vaulted caverns, crumbling but still intact, dug far into the mountainsides, with dungeons and catacombs said to lie deeper underground; some tales even claim that passages connect the two mountains, twisting deep under the rushing river and out across the Narrows of Gracor, and that some of the caves contain inhumanly tall stone figures reaching out in terror and rage. The scholars of Lorim have refrained from any comment, as official history states these lands were entirely unoccupied when the empire was birthed. Secretly, through magical inspections, scholars have gathered some evidence that Arrik and Orrik were one gigantic mountain many thousands of years ago, but were sundered atwain through agencies unimaginable — what could have done this, and what sins the mountains' former denizens could have committed to deserve it, are things the empire's scholars believe are better left undiscussed. Sources Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 221

title: Naga Priestess
content: Naga Priestess Naga priestesses are the leaders of the naga serpent cults of Zanaga and blessed with the power of their Primal God, Set. The coils of their long, snakelike lower bodies constantly shift in pattern and color, while their slit eyes bore into the minds of any being foolish enough to meet their gaze. Even the sternest warrior might become hypnotized by a priestess and powerless as she moves to sink her venomous fangs into their throat. If the priestess chooses, she can even turn her enemies against each other, the weak-minded so enraptured by the naga that they throw themselves at anyone who might bring her harm. Sources Life in the Jungle (Zanaga), pp. 258–259

title: Nagas
content: Nagas Ancient enemies of the Lizardmen, nagas spent centuries hiding in the shadows from their hated cousins. On the day the old empire fell, they rose up, giving thanks to their snake god Set and seeking to claim what was theirs. Since that time, the half-snake, half-humanoid nagas have grown strong in Zanaga. Under the guidance of the Priestesses of Set, they constantly fight the remnants of the lizardmen, hoping to exterminate them once and for all. Even though the nagas are opposed by the Mahkim, many former lizardman temples are now nests of naga power, among them Omaga the Obsidian Sunrise and Jatok, the Water Temple. Treacherous and cunning, nagas often manipulate explorers into finding ancient lizardman artifacts for them, or wiping out Mahkim villages that stand in their way; some such pawns might be lucky enough to escape with their lives, but many others are coaxed into the jungle depths to fill the belly of the serpent god. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Nashaia King's Bane
content: Nashaia King's Bane Nashaia King's Bane was one of Llovar's most feared lieutenants, commanding a contingent of the Host of Thorns during the First Darkness, one of the names that became bywords for wickedness and treachery among the allies of Terrinoth. History In 478, as Llovar's Uthuk Y'llan first scattered the forces of King Falladir Penacor, Nashaia struck the king from his steed and was poised to dispatch him before a desperate counterattack by Prince Parren forced the foe back long enough to rescue Falladir from the field. Nashaia met his end nine years later at The Ashen Field, where Prince Parren drove a lance through his heart even as the Host of Thorns overwhelmed the Penacor forces and slew all three Penacors upon the field. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35, 37

title: Naythen Torvic
content: Naythen Torvic Naythen Torvic was the lord of Bilehall who betrayed his fellow nobles one terrible night to swear fealty to Waiqar, becoming, along with his lesser nobles, a vampiric creature as undying as his new master when the mists claimed his lands. Sources Bilehall (The Mistlands), p. 161

title: Necromancer
content: Necromancer Necromancers are practitioners of Necromancy, the darkest of all possible magical arts, forbidden as an art that corrupts the wielder and brings ruin to those who allow it to fester. Though they may try to hide their acts, necromancers are usually found out as they are spurred on to greater acts of desecration or as their bodies become more noticeably twisted by the demands necromancy places upon living flesh. Those who survive discovery invariably find themselves in The Mistlands, wandering from crypt to crypt in search of either a patron or enough untouched dead to raise into protective retinues. Necromancers who wander long enough eventually arrive at Zorgas, their own magic drawing them to the foul power within it; there they can become servants to Waiqar and possibly go on to operate his Engines of Entropy, while those who refuse service are usually fed into the engines instead, unless they successfully flee to continue their unholy work elsewhere. Some make their way to villages across Terrinoth or even farther away, looking for corpses to awaken or simply creating new ones to ensure fresh supplies, growing networks of minions (living as well as undead) from their new lairs to further their unholy goals. Sources Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), p. 166

title: Necromancy
content: Necromancy Necromancy is the power over death itself, the most terrifying and unnatural of the myriad ways magical energies have been wielded across the millennia — to witness the dead rising as nearly unstoppable hordes of shambling monstrosities is enough to unnerve even the most seasoned of adventurers. Table of Contents History Description Sources History Such horrors have been a part of history for untold ages. Even before the Second Darkness, when an entire barony fell to corruption and sought to spread the plague of undeath across Mennara, corpses shambled out of their tombs and revenants stalked wilderness regions; tales of spectral beings such as wraiths and ghosts are among the oldest in many cultures, as are those of vampires and barghests. It took a great general and leader, though, to truly establish the necromantic arts as a powerful force that could threaten all of Mennara: when Waiqar Sumarion roared his fury and hate upon all existence and vowed to never rest until his quest was complete, something answered his cry and true necromancy was unleashed upon the world. He and his forces died only to be reborn in death, and he later discovered how to fashion new undead such as Reanimates from fallen Deathborn. Across the centuries, his followers spread his gospel of death and reanimation across Mennara, weaving new spells and adopting new ritualist techniques, though none can ever hope to match the Undying One in power and skill; some uncover ancient relics from the elder times powerful enough to perform feats none can hope to replicate or even understand. Each season sees cults who worship death itself hidden within Terrinoth sink their insidious talons further into society, and necromantic magic, practiced by both the living and the dead, spreads like a funeral shroud over the land that, if unchecked, will surely result in the end of all life. Description Necromancy is a relatively misunderstood art, despite the centuries of study its ageless practitioners conduct. Some scholars of the forbidden believe it to be of an arcane nature, its energy coming from the Turning, or Verto Magica. Though most mages hold it to be a lower form of magic, it is still quite powerful; more scholars of magical arts firmly believe it too dangerous for any study and actively work to suppress such activities, but there are always those thirsty for knowledge and power who advance its practice. Broadly speaking, the dark arts come in three major forms: raising the dead using remnants of previously raised undead, leeching life from the living to empower other beings (most notably the user themself), and twisting flesh into new forms. While most who claim knowledge of such things believe necromancers simply raise the dead, the truth is more disturbing: Waiqar discovered that the ground skeletal remains of any of his fallen creations, once properly desecrated using profane rituals of his design, could be used to animate other corpses. Only a small amount of the bone dust was needed — a single Deathborn Legionnaire could be used to raise thousands of lesser Reanimates — so his forces grew even greater even when one of his own was laid low, even though none were as powerful as his original lieutenants. It is thus an especially necessary duty for his followers to collect the remains of his creatures to fashion additional undead. Even without their undead minions, necromancers are puissant forces (see Necromancer). They can wield death magic to accelerate necrosis and decay, causing wounds to grow festering and pustules to burst forth in their enemies; as foes fall closer to death, these foul spellcasters become gorged with life and energy. Fleshwrights, also known as Flesh Moulders, affect dead tissue in even more horrific ways, altering raw tissue into twisted new shapes through their fell arts — additional limbs, insectoid eyes, and elongated fingers with venomous nails are only some of the less horrid transmutations they can achieve. Some even use their powers on themselves, constructing bizarre but deadly forms to better serve the Undying One. Sources Secrets of the Grave (The Mistlands), pp. 168–169

title: Nerekhall
content: Nerekhall Nerekhall is one of the eight Free Cities of Terrinoth, a city of paranoia — though some might say for good reason. History The region takes its name from the Tower of Nerek, a strange and forbidding ruin once used as a prison by the Lord of Nerekhall — reputedly built by Elves, who deny it, and haunted by nightmares and delusions in a Daewyl portal hidden within its attic. It was here that Prince Farrengol Penacor first bargained with an Ynfernael shade before his execution and undead return as Farrenghast. Long ago, in a titanic fall from grace, a member of Nerekhall's Council of Wizards fell to the corrupting influence of the Ynfernael and opened a portal to that blighted realm; otherworldly monsters poured forth in a massive tide, threatening the western regions of Terrinoth. Unwilling to allow the forces of darkness to gain a foothold, the Daqan Lords delivered a swift and brutal response, eradicating whole families of sorcerers in a brutal purge to force the portal closed, while those allowed to live did so under careful, unceasing watch. Haunted by the fear of once again falling to the Ynfernael's lure, the Priests of Pollux, who maintain a large cult in Nerekhall, created the Ironbound: living suits of black iron armor beyond the corruption of mortal beings, immune to magic both malign and beneficial. These constructs exceeded their artificers' expectations and soon replaced most of the city's militia, becoming common sights that safeguard the citizenry against flagrant acts of evil magic; those who claim to have witnessed a malfunction are harshly punished for spreading malicious rumors. Description Despite its dark past, Nerekhall has flourished, much to the suspicion of the inquisitors and templars of the baronies and the Church of Kellos. Its magistrates rule harshly, insisting that fear and control are the only protections against corruption, surveilling nearly every aspect of city life while promoting Nerekhall's image. Nevertheless, they take special pride in the Academy, a trusted wellspring of learning where society's elite can engage in exotic experiments and rare-tome research free of petty scrutiny owing to their exalted rank; its faculty seem even more eager than their students to explore every aspect of magic and other arts in pursuit of the city's great legacy. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), pp. 148–149 Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), pp. 32–33

title: Night Howlers
content: Night Howlers The Night Howlers hold territories close to the borderlands and are among the Uthuk Y'llan's most skilled raiders. From the depths of Nyak Sutchra'aa, the Chasm of Eternal Night, they have perfected the art of night fighting — waging war in complete darkness, their skin and weapons coated with stygian dust. The Night Howlers attack with a chorus of war cries, and for their foes, it is as though the night itself has come alive to attack them. Prisoners taken back to the Chasm of Eternal Night can look forward to taking part in the tribe's "training": let loose in lightless dungeons, they must attempt to escape while the Uthuk hunt them down. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211

title: Night of Summons
content: Night of Summons The Night of Summons was the night Llovar sprung his carefully laid scheme upon the Loth K'har, promising great rewards and using forbidden bindings to lead his tribe's greatest warriors into the T'mara T'rusheen. They emerged physically transformed, shaped by Ynfernael influence: their wiry muscles grown supernaturally powerful, and their very bones pushed through their skin to form great spikes and blades. With these warriors at his side, Llovar began to form the confederation of tribes that would become the Uthuk Y'llan. On the same night, Rala, wife of Llovar's brother Llander, gave birth to their son Timmorran, whom nightseers hailed as a man of great import to come. Sources The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), p. 34 The Rise of Timmorran (Tales of Darkness), p. 35

title: Nivalis
content: Nivalis The Nivalis were the tenth of the eleven Elven tribes among whom Emorial divided the Tears of Latariana. When Malcorne and the corrupted Daewyl devastated the Elven tribes, Glaciel Snowstar, son of the Nivalis chieftain, rescued his father's Tear and set out to seek the aid of the dragons, ultimately helping bring about Malcorne's downfall at The Battle of Enfreil. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: Nomad's Maze
content: Nomad's Maze The Nomad's Maze is a dangerous district of Al-Madena, home to the Kaliffar drug dens where decadence and vice run rampant. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Nordros
content: Nordros Nordros, Master of Cold and Death, is the icy God of Cold and Death, believed by the Weik of Isheim to be their eternal enemy, continually trying to blow them back into the sea with his icy breath — the harsh elements that seek their deaths at every turn. Table of Contents Weik Belief Kellos's Church and Nordros Sources Weik Belief Nordros's worship is banned among the Weik. Each year upon the longest day, the twelve Hearthlords of the Reaver Council come to Lagart to spit upon his broken statue and reaffirm their mastery over their land. There is even a legend that tells of a mighty warrior who will one day vanquish Nordros, a glory the Weik who train within the heroes' halls dream might be theirs. The Weik say Nordros long predates Waiqar, coming down from the north at the dawn of the world with blizzards roaring at his heels, kept at bay by the doughty warriors of Isheim, but returning each year when the sun grows weak; the Weik believe that if Nordros is not kept in check, he will finally gain dominion over the realms and see the entire world encased in ice. Kellos's Church and Nordros Some temples of Kellos teach a very different account: that Nordros is Kellos's own twin brother, whose jealousy of his sibling led him to fall to Waiqar's dark promises during the Second Darkness. When Nordros joined the Betrayer, he unlocked a terrible power within himself, a mastery over the chill of death, and the temple faithful hold that Kellos's church teaches the undead are Nordros's agents — as the twin flames of justice and hope flicker and dim, Nordros's power grows, and only when he is defeated will Kellos return and winter be forever banished from the realms. The worship of Nordros is almost unheard of in Terrinoth, with only a few pockets remaining in the Howling Giant Hills and Blind Muir Forest, where some still bring sacrifices to appease him; a few ambitious individuals in Strangehaven pledge themselves to Nordros in pursuit of dominion over cold and death, some counting on their resolve to use the magic of ice and death without succumbing to the god's will. The inhabitants of cities like Vynelvale and Dawnsmoor actively persecute any who openly follow Nordros, and the cult of Kellos continues to petition the Citadel to ban his worship outright. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 123 The Frozen North (Isheim), p. 233 Lords of the Hearth (Isheim), p. 234

title: Nornholt
content: Nornholt Nornholt is perhaps Cailn's only lifeblood in this age, a city drawing much of the barony's wealth from its position along multiple trade routes, centrally located between the Free Cities of Nerekhall, Greyhaven, and Tamalir. This trade and travel has led to a high Gnome population in the city. It has recently become evident that something greatly frightens Nornholt's Gnomes, who have largely ceased their customary, frequent celebrations, locking themselves away in the evenings, and — stranger still for a normally loquacious people — refuse to speak of the problem to others. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Northern Tribes
content: Northern Tribes The Northern Tribes gather each winter in Frostgate to perform a number of rituals meant to ensure good harvests and successful hunts, the greatest of which are the Trials of Frostgate. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), pp. 147–148

title: Noxious Glade
content: Noxious Glade In the Noxious Glade, Tarakhe's power has given rise to fungus storms in Zanaga that can induce permanent frenzy and delusion in mortals. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Nyak Sutchra'aa
content: Nyak Sutchra'aa Nyak Sutchra'aa, the Chasm of Eternal Night, is the home of the Night Howlers, from whose depths they have perfected the art of night fighting — waging war in complete darkness, their skin and weapons coated with stygian dust. Prisoners taken back to the Chasm can look forward to taking part in the tribe's "training": let loose in lightless dungeons, they must attempt to escape while the Uthuk hunt them down. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211

title: Ogre
content: Ogre Ogres are found frequently in caves throughout The Broken Plains, but also pop up in abandoned fortresses and settlements — often being the cause such locations became emptied. Large, powerful, and unpleasant, they can be tremendous challenges to adventurers seeking to explore these regions. Their ability to recover from damage that would fell other creatures makes them especially tricky, for just when a group might think an ogre is defeated, it can spring back to its feet and attack again. Sources Life on the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 202

title: Old Man
content: Old Man The Old Man is a tremendous statue standing proud over the harbor city of Riverwatch, looking over a high cliff with lantern in hand — a fitting symbol for the city and its place in the greater history of Terrinoth. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149

title: Olief Hawthorne
content: Olief Hawthorne Olief Hawthorne was born in Seragart only to discover his true heritage when his uncle, Lord Hawthorne of Terrinoth, died and left the young defender his title and castle. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), p. 233

title: Omaga the Obsidian Sunrise
content: Omaga the Obsidian Sunrise Omaga the Obsidian Sunrise is a former lizardman temple now a nest of naga power in Zanaga, its gleaming corridors echoing to the screams of Set's sacrifices. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Onasan
content: Onasan Onasan is a settlement in Zanaga taken over by the touched of Tarakhe, twisted mutants only too eager to recruit new members into their family. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Onoit Shaman
content: Onoit Shaman The diminutive Onoit shamans are one of Isheim's many mysteries. Ostensibly part of the nomadic Onoit tribes, they are frequently seen moving among their people, clad in cloaks of bark and moss, healing and dispensing wisdom, yet they often travel alone in their sled-tents, drawn across the tundra by packs of trusty Ulfen. A society unto themselves, the Onoit shamans serve as guardians of the lost Salishwyrd empire. When the Elves retreated to The Green Vale, they entrusted the keeping of their abandoned cities and tombs to the Onoit shamans, granting each one a spark of elemental magic to light their way; since that time, those sparks have been passed from shaman to shaman. Onoit shamans are enemies of the Rime Storm and The White Death it brings — heroes traversing their lands might be recruited by these traveling Gnome mystics in their war against winter's soldiers: Ice Wyrms, Wendigo, and Ice-Blood Warriors. Equally, those who seek to plunder the lost realm of the Salishwyrd will find the land and sky set against them, as the shamans bend the elements to their will to make an icy tomb for any would-be looters. Sources Spiritspeaking (Call to Adventure), p. 127 Life in the Cold (Isheim), p. 239

title: Onoit
content: Onoit The Onoit are diminutive Gnome nomads who have lived in Isheim as long as history records, living in the middle lands of the frozen continent between the coastal realm of the Weik and the extremes of the far north. Description Secret trails weave their way across the ice plains and woodlands of Isheim — the paths of the Onoit and the canine Ulfen who act as their mounts. From the cursed shadows of the Witchwood in southern Isheim, across the Crystal Plains, and up into the Howling Mountains, the Onoit never stray too close to the coast, but also avoid the extremes of the far north. The Onoit can become invaluable allies to travelers delving deeper into the wilds, offering food, shelter, and guidance in a place that can seem anathema to outsiders; often the first contact adventurers have with the Onoit nomads occurs when one of the Ulfen hounds bounds out of the snow. If the newcomers are worthy, the Ulfen lead them back to the gnome camps, where kindly shamans (see Onoit Shaman) may tend to their wounds. The Onoit live at one with their surroundings, their shamans able to listen to the voice of the land and translate its wisdom for their people. Onoit settlements are constructed with the landscape in mind, the ice-hewn shelters and huts worked into the plains or forests so that they are practically invisible until one walks among them. The largest Onoit holdfast, Ukirlu, nestles in the heart of the Greenwood and is one of the few true havens in all of Isheim. Onoit shamans have a deep connection to the spirit of the land, and travelers sometimes encounter their way markers: rune-carved menhirs that stand tall among the wastes, impossibly so for a people so small, rising up as if the gnomes had called forth the stones from the ground rather than erected them with rope and muscle. Each standing stone points the way to a wonder of the Onoit people, like Mirror Lake or the Ulur Deep. The stones also act as a warning, for the Onoit do not take well to outsiders trespassing upon their sacred places — in cases of burial sites and magical cairns, shamans and Ulfen war dogs are seldom far away, ready to see off intruders. Nevertheless, heroes might seek out such markers, for they often point to the lairs of powerful ice wyrms, or to the Salishwyrd ruins. When the Elves of the Salishwyrd retreated to The Green Vale, they entrusted the keeping of their abandoned cities and tombs to the Onoit shamans, granting each one a spark of elemental magic to light their way; since that time, those sparks have been passed from shaman to shaman. Sources An Uncharted Wilderness (Isheim), pp. 234–236 Life in the Cold (Isheim), p. 238

title: Orb of the Sky
content: Orb of the Sky The Orb of the Sky was Timmorran's final and most ambitious creation, a huge crystalline sphere of pure magic meant to contain a portion of the Verto Magica's own energy, designed as a reservoir of magical power so potent that wizards who came after him would be able to use it to power countless spells with relative ease and little risk of Ynfernael corruption. History At the Tower of Meringyr, Timmorran and his acolytes strove to create the Orb, and he invested so much of his own energy into the artifact that he grew visibly infirm — his emaciation shocked those present at a memorial service for King Daqan in Archaut in 513. When Waiqar launched his assault on the Wizard's Vale during the Night of Betrayal in 515, Timmorran realized his folly in making the Orb and cast spells of unbinding, hurling the crystal sphere to the forge floor so powerfully that it shattered. Using magic, he channeled the myriad pieces into an enchanted velvet pouch and entrusted it to Lumii Tamar, having him swear to distribute the fragments throughout the world to those he deemed wise enough to use them — through a feat of high magic, Lumii slipped past Waiqar's forces with all but a single fragment. That last piece Waiqar tore from the dead hands of the wizard he had just slain, vowing to hunt down the rest. Legacy The fragments of the Orb, kept secret and safe by Lumii Tamar and the order he was granted authority to found, came to be known as the Stars of Timmorran — unstable magical artifacts capable of powering great magic in a trained caster's hands. When the dragonlords of the Third Darkness broke these Stars down into smaller, stable runebound shards, they transformed the nature of magic across Mennara. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 39–41

title: Orc Outrider
content: Orc Outrider Orc Outriders are lizard riders from Mag Ugluk Urak, the Great Beast Clan, mounted warriors who are as dangerous as any cavalry in Mennara. Nomadic Orcs who follow elk and other wild game across The Broken Plains, they tend to lead fairly simple lives as hunters and gatherers. Following their chieftain Skorn's noble example, the outriders are brutally honest and always good to their word — they will never cheat during a trade, stab an ally in the back, or abandon a pledge; if that pledge is to kill an adversary or slaughter an enemy, then one of the two is absolutely going to die. Typically armed with axes and throwing spears, and trained to make hit-and-run attacks at high speeds, outriders are at their best when mounted on their Gurak Tol steeds. These Orcs make life-bonds with their mounts, formed as an outrider personally captures one of the huge lizards; Gurak Tols are never fully tamed, though, and outriders take care to avoid getting too close to their always-hungry mouths. Outriders eventually discovered their steeds could also provide ranged support via their powerful tails — the opening minutes of any large-scale battle finds outriders dismounted next to their Gurak Tol, nudging the beasts in the proper direction, placing a skull-sized rock into brackets mounted onto those bony tails, and having the beast hurl the stone overhead. Depending on the age and strength of the Gurak Tol, these improvised projectiles can be thrown at incredible speeds up to a hundred paces, and at a rate of fire that can wreak havoc on enemy formations, often causing undisciplined units to break and flee. Then, as the battle shifts or the Orcs run out of ammunition, the outriders mount their giant lizards and execute intricately choreographed strafing runs across the enemy's front lines, carefully maintaining an ideal distance that brings their deadly throwing spears into range while keeping the duo beyond the reach of the enemy's own hurled projectiles. Sources Life on the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 202–203

title: Orc Spiritspeaker
content: Orc Spiritspeaker Orc Spiritspeakers are magic users unique to the Orcish race who use a shamanistic connection through the earth to communicate with The Unseen, the hidden, ethereal creatures of Mennara — one of the oldest forms of spiritspeaking practiced across Mennara. This not only allows them to speak as mediums for the Unseen, but also to act as conduits for the spirits to act on the mundane world. Whether attached to objects or locations, minor spirits are normally unable to summon the energy or focus it takes to act on the physical world; however, through a combination of natural ability and rigorous training, spiritspeakers can thin the barriers that surround Mennara enough to allow apparitions to manifest — letting benevolent sprites openly share their wisdom, guardian spirits physically defend their territories, and wraiths directly attack whoever holds their cursed object. That connection also gives spiritspeakers a supernatural edge in combat and adventuring, as many will have gathered a modest assortment of objects with useful entities attached which can be summoned for aid or protection. Notable spiritspeakers of The Broken Plains include Anka of Mok'Thul Urak. Sources Life on the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 202–203

title: Orcs of the Broken Plains
content: Orcs of the Broken Plains Within The Broken Plains, Orcs trade the easily gathered minerals, hunt the open ranges, ambush prey among the rocky hills, and use the deep ravines as natural protection from attacks. The Orcs are divided into large tribes, each claiming a swath of land and the landmarks and hunting grounds within for themselves — tribes such as Baruk Gro Urak, Erd'Lantir Urak, Ghur'zhun Urak, Jer'Kul Urak, Lok Urak, Mok'Thul Urak, and Mag Ugluk Urak. Yet the borders between the tribes shift frequently with inter-tribe conflicts, adding even more uncertainty and peril for adventurers traveling across the Broken Plains. Eschewing organized cities and other fixed locations, the tribes carry their villages with them as they travel their lands; once finding a suitable location, they plant stakes and settle until there is a communal urge to pack up and move again. This tradition ensures no tribe devours too much local game or vegetation, and also helps them protect their domains against predators both native and foreign. Most of Mennara's Orcs abide by the Pillars — including the Pillar of Gharmuth — and the peace treaties with the Humans, though not every tribe honors them equally. Sources The Orcs of the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 197–198

title: Orris
content: Orris Orris lies on the northern coast of Lorimor, where the turbulent River of Sighs empties into the Cerridor Sea — a thriving destination point, its docks busy day and night as heavy ships fight for space to offload their treasures from distant lands. Its success has made it feel detached from the rest of Lorimor, though, and the city has an unseemly reputation: its bars and taverns became havens for captains with a piratical bent, and many an eye is averted so long as gold and other riches continue to pour into Lorimor. The colonization of The Torue Albes was launched from Orris, and the city controlled much of the trade with the islands as the settlements prospered and grew. Many call it a city of pirates — not an entirely untrue statement, but Orris is also a city of opportunity, its ships ready for any action as long as the promise of reward is high. Sources Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 222

title: Orrush Khatak
content: Orrush Khatak Orrush Khatak, generally called the Gate of the Furnace, is a strange landmark not more than an hour's march from Castle Kellar in Kell — a great arch of blood red rock, large enough for more than four hundred soldiers to march under shoulder to shoulder. Perhaps a natural formation once seen as a good luck charm for departing armies, or perhaps carved for a part in some ancient magical ritual, no one can now say; it remains another mystery in a land already full of them. When the wind blows, one need not strain to hear anguished cries, but few would admit them to be anything more than a trick of the breeze whipping against the stone. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Oszric Cunningham
content: Oszric Cunningham Count Oszric Cunningham rules Haverford County within Allerfeldt, a house with a poor reputation despite strong, intermarriage-bolstered relationships with the other counties, each Cunningham ruler becoming notorious for a new obsession they bring to the throne. Haverford's finances grew so poor under this pattern of half-finished grand projects that Oszric was forced to marry the wealthy merchant Elene to bolster the treasury. Together the two have since reclaimed many of the county's ruins, mines, and lost regions through funded excavation and masonry work, though this has also disturbed hordes of goblins and other creatures that had taken up residence there. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Otrin
content: Otrin Otrin, the Vigilant Land, begins just northwest of Riverwatch and extends to the Blackwing Swamp in the north and as far east as Riverwatch. Its people cultivate rich farmland on the Velvet Plains and respectfully gather rare herbs from the Gardens of Tarn, where by barony law felling a tree is punishable by death. Otrin's lands abut the Mountains of Despair, which cast a long shadow over the barony; Baron Trevalyan could officially claim parts of that gloomy range and its mineral deposits, but his ancestors learned long ago that no good comes from those storm-wracked peaks. By tradition the baron protects Otrin and its neighbors from the mountains' dangers, and his ancestral home Skydown sits at the mountains' foot not as a defense against rival baronies but as a bulwark against the creatures of the foothills and heights; Trevalyan lives in constant vigilance and hosts aspiring Knights of the Citadel who hunt manticores and other monsters there to prove their worth. In recent times, foul creatures and fierce beasts have descended from the mountains more brazenly and regularly, leading Trevalyan — to the chagrin of some Knights of the Citadel — to enlist traveling adventurers for expeditions against specific beasts or preemptive strikes on the mountain denizens. Some believe the monsters flee the near-constant, worsening storms of the range, while others dismiss tales of an ancient and powerful sorcerer who dwells there and commands the elements as mere stories. Across the plains lies the unusual range called Mennara's Teeth, small in area but sharp and narrow as the fangs of a great beast; dragons are said to come there when they feel their life's end drawing close, and most avoid its foothills for fear of encountering one. Stories persist of the Cave of Wonders somewhere amid its dagger-like slopes — few who seek it return, and those who do come back strangely serene, distant from their old lives, and unwilling to speak of their experience. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Outland Scouts
content: Outland Scouts The Outland Scouts are an organization established when Riverwatch and Tamalir pushed the barons to agree to watch the wilderness of Terrinoth for nascent threats, in the aftermath of the War of Ten Brothers demonstrating that the Free Cities were not to be ignored. Two centuries later, the Outland Scouts still patrol the wilds of Terrinoth. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 53

title: Pact of Stonesense
content: Pact of Stonesense The Pact of Stonesense is the name Dwarves give to their singular affinity with the Dimora, even as they hold a seemingly innate distrust — even hatred — of the Fae. According to the history carved into the walls of the Hearth Road, this relationship began when the first Dwarves fled into the Dunwarr Mountains. As the tales tell it, as the Dwarves dug deeper and deeper to escape the predations of the dragons, they came across the Dimora in the mountains' very roots. Sources Labyrinth of Deurg (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 190

title: Path of Daggers
content: Path of Daggers The Path of Daggers is a trap-filled dungeon carved into the side of Siryasa's Shame in Siryasa, the site of a grueling competition offering prizes not just for those who complete the trial, but also for those who do so in the swiftest time, or without spilling any blood. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245

title: Path of the Stars
content: Path of the Stars The Path of the Stars is the faith of the Latari Elves, centered on Latariana and observed through a dizzying array of shrines, prayer gardens, and temples in the sacred vales of Lithelin, maintained by High Priestess Ancela. Sources Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 175

title: Path to the Stars
content: Path to the Stars The Path to the Stars is the Elven priesthood's tradition of veneration for Latariana, opened by her so that her descendants could atone for her and Emorial's ancient crime. The very first priests and priestesses were those who devoted themselves to finding and ascending Latariana's Stair through meditation, self-reflection, and prayer. Description In the intervening millennia, the priesthood has become divided as to the role of the Elves in greater Mennara, and whether involvement or seclusion is the answer. Much of the Elven priesthood are Eolam, as the priesthood is generally very old and made up of Elves who never ventured out of the city of Lithelin. The spires of the Temple to the Stars are nearly as tall as those of the Caelcira, the silver palace, and the high priestesses are common visitors to the throne in the hopes of swaying the King and his consort to their causes. The Daughters of the Empyrean and the Darnati warriors are most often drawn from the Highborn caste devoted to this path. Sources The Empyrean Arts (Elven Magic), pp. 127–128

title: Pelgate
content: Pelgate Pelgate, the Faded Barony, lies along the southern range of the Broken Crags in Terrinoth's eastern reaches, deriving most of its wealth from iron mines at the Crags' feet, its southern lands extending into the bountiful Velvet Plains. Pelgate was the site of important battles during the Dragon Wars, and its lands still bear the scars: within its bounds, the Ashen Hills — named for their condition in the war's aftermath — extend from the Broken Crags' base, useless for farming but notable for strange, rune-marked obelisks breaking forth from certain grassy mounds. The hills are also home to Fort Rodric, built after the Dragon Wars to honor its namesake hero; though never taken or even attacked, the fortress guards a route past the Broken Crags vital against invasion from the east, and after long years of peace its garrison is severely undermanned. In the centuries of peace since, Pelgate's wartime travails have been largely forgotten, its reputation eclipsed by other baronies' accomplishments. Baroness Pryor, the most aged of the Daqan Lords, is feared by some among her fellow barons and subjects to no longer possess the strength to deal with the rising threat in the east; after Kell, Pelgate lies closest of the baronies to the Ru Steppes, and its position between two mountain chains provides a natural, defensible bottleneck, though most of its subjects and peers fail to recognize the looming danger and the barony takes few steps to prepare. Dame Corinne Varr, a captain of Pelgate's army, fears her barony will soon be tested and has begun, in frustration, enlisting aid from sellswords and mercenary mages traveling through Pelgate's lands. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Penacor Kings
content: Penacor Kings The Penacor Kings were the ruling dynasty of Talindon during and after the First Darkness, descended from or including Falladir Penacor; the Free City of Riverwatch was initially founded as one of their military outposts. Description In their days, humankind finally settled down and turned its efforts to more scholastic pursuits. For the first time, magical theory was codified in parchment, and mighty wizards from the sands of Al-Kalim to the fledgling Lorimor Empire began to unlock the secrets of the Turning, the Verto Magica. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35–37 The Arcane Arts (The Magic of Mennara), p. 116

title: Phantom Walker
content: Phantom Walker A Phantom Walker is a status recognized under Orcish law granting neutrality — the Mok'Thul Urak are considered composed entirely of Phantom Walkers, and creatures who approach them with ill intent quickly discover that the spirits also believe the Grey Moon Tribe should be protected from harm. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Pilgrim's Trail
content: Pilgrim's Trail The Pilgrim's Trail runs through the Shadow Peaks mountain range not far from Greyhaven. Its natural magic is potent enough that the challenge faced by each pilgrim who walks it differs, and those who succeed are allowed to pluck a single fruit from the branches of Shika's Tree, said to bring fortune or glory to those who eat of its flesh. Those who survive the trail often travel onward to Frostgate, seeking its warmth after the ordeal. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Pillar of Gharmuth
content: Pillar of Gharmuth The Pillar of Gharmuth is one of the Pillars of Orcish law, under which the Mok'Thul Urak are considered to be composed entirely of neutral Phantom Walkers, a universally welcoming source of counsel and aid for any sentient beings who seek their guidance. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Pirate
content: Pirate Pirates have a dual identity. On one hand, they are reviled as despoilers and scourges who prowl the waterways of The Torue Albes and Lorimor, little better than thieves and murderers. On the other hand, on their voyages, they often discover new lands to be exploited and rising threats to be repelled. Despite their wicked deeds, most also operate in an honorable fashion and offer better payments and a more democratic operation than official navies. Many pirates are consummate businesspeople, inking deals to privateer or act as smugglers in exchange for amnesty; it's a difficult balancing act, and those who cannot master it rarely remain alive for long.
