In combat, pirates tend to favor flashy, quick styles learned in seaside taverns and outlaw towns rather than the formalized martial arts of mainland knights and soldiers — on a ship's deck, one tumble over the side can turn even the lightest armor into a death sentence, so most go without, and trickery is also a staple of the pirate fighting style. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 229

title: Priest of Kellos
content: Priest of Kellos In battle, the priests of Kellos most often use the power of flame, the symbol of their deity, to smite evil — conjuring mystical flame around a hand or weapon, or casting out gouts of living flame to consume their foes. Their flames can also heal, and some have claimed they can even resurrect the dead, though this must surely be myth. Encountering these priests is often a double-edged sword: they can offer aid to the sick and dying, but their presence may also indicate that the undead or other dangers lurk nearby. Sources Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 154

title: Priestesses of Set
content: Priestesses of Set The Priestesses of Set guide the Nagas of Zanaga in their constant war to exterminate the remnants of the Lizardmen. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Priests of Pollux
content: Priests of Pollux The Priests of Pollux, followers of the mysterious divine artificer Pollux, maintain a large cult in Nerekhall, and in the aftermath of a member of the city's Council of Wizards opening a portal to the Ynfernael, they created the Ironbound to protect the city from ever falling to that corruption again. Description No one knows who Pollux was, or what they did in life — there are no stories of great deeds or heroic adventures that accompany the name. Instead, Pollux comes from a series of treatises and diagrams discovered by artificers during the time of the Elder Kings, each describing some wondrous construction or artifact, or providing the formula for some alchemical creation or magical reagent. Each was written on thin sheets of steel and signed with the name "Pollux," and those artificers who followed the instructions claimed the designs must have been inspired by the divine; each treatise quickly came to be treated as a holy relic. The Artificers of Pollux do not work miracles through prayer as the disciples of Kellos do; instead they work their magic through feats of engineering, studying enchantments alongside more mundane skills such as carpentry or blacksmithing. Their holy sites are workshops and forges, and their sacred writings are treatises on natural elements and recipes for rare reagents — a prayer to Pollux is a call for inspiration and ingenuity to craft the seemingly impossible. Artificers are regarded with both affection and suspicion by the people of Terrinoth. On one hand, the followers of Pollux have produced a number of revered artifacts used in civic works and military operations, including the Ironbound that combat evil magic-users stalking the underbelly of Nerekhall. Yet the devout keep their formulae close, sharing their knowledge only with those who swear themselves to secrecy, and some of the Runemasters of Greyhaven — jealous of the artificers' achievements — have spread unsavory rumors about the true source of their wonders, rumors the Artificers of Pollux decry as unfounded slander, insisting they bear a responsibility to ensure Pollux's legacy doesn't end up in the wrong hands. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 124 The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 148

title: Prince Faolan
content: Prince Faolan Prince Faolan, son of the late King Aanir and protector of the northern borders of The Aymhelin, vehemently opposed his uncle Aenoeth's decision in the early 1600s to dispatch scouts into Terrinoth and beyond at the urging of Maegan Cyndewin. The scouts rode forth despite Faolan's objections, finding Terrinoth's lands slowly rebuilding themselves and establishing renewed ties with Elves who had long ago emigrated to the Free Cities. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 51

title: Prince Parren
content: Prince Parren Prince Parren, son of King Falladir Penacor, saved his father's life in 478 when a desperate counterattack forced back Nashaia King's Bane, who had struck the king from his steed and was poised to finish him. Nine years later, at The Ashen Field, Parren drove a lance through Nashaia's heart in turn — but Llovar's Host of Thorns proved too great, and Parren died on the field alongside his father and brothers by the day's end. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35, 37

title: Prismatic Staff
content: Prismatic Staff Prismatic Staffs were crafted by the students of Timmorran under his guidance, meant to provide the wizards with badges of office as well as a degree of personal protection. They are impressive artifacts: long shafts of silver topped with crystal orbs that display a shifting kaleidoscope of rainbow colors. A bewildering lightshow can be projected from the orbs, the intensity of which dazzles unwary opponents. Sources Magic Items, pp. 109–110

title: Pryor
content: Pryor Baroness Pryor rules Pelgate, the most aged of the Daqan Lords; some among her fellow barons and subjects fear she may no longer possess the strength to deal with the rising threat from the east. After Kell, Pelgate lies closest of the baronies to the Ru Steppes, and though its position between two mountain chains provides a natural, defensible bottleneck, most of its subjects and peers fail to recognize the looming danger, and Pryor's barony takes few steps to prepare its defenses. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Q'aro Fenn
content: Q'aro Fenn Q'aro Fenn, thought to be a title rather than a personal name — translating roughly as "demon-bone witch" — was chief of Llovar's assassins and one of his most feared lieutenants, commanding a contingent of the Host of Thorns during the First Darkness. History When a nightseer warned Llovar that his nephew Timmorran would one day strike him down, Llovar had the nightseer executed for the pessimism but secretly dispatched three killers, the feared mage-assassins known as the servants of Q'aro Fenn, to find and slay the boy in Lorimor. The assassins finally tracked Timmorran down, but Sal Meringyr fought them off at the cost of his own life, killing two and sending the third into flight. Q'aro Fenn herself later led a contingent of the Host of Thorns in the invasion of Talindon, one of the dreaded captains whose names became bywords for wickedness and treachery alongside Melinesh the Cruel and Terrible, Nashaia King's Bane, and Kul the Serpent. After Llovar's death at the Battle of the Locusts, some say Q'aro Fenn rescued his corpse from the crags and took it to a secret place far beyond The Ru — a resting place said to be found only by following the trail of her bitter tears. Her ultimate fate, like those of Llovar's other lieutenants, is not known. Sources The Rise of Timmorran (Tales of Darkness), p. 35 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 36–37

title: Quin'tar Shymaex
content: Quin'tar Shymaex The nightseer Quin'tar Shymaex dreams of larger things than mere conquest of the Land of Steel, perhaps one of the most infamous of the bloodsisters and nightseers of the Uthuk Y'llan. Shymaex seeks to take his place among the Ynfernael Lords himself and transform all Uthuk into true demons, a goal that eluded even Llovar. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 213

title: Rala
content: Rala Rala, wife of Llander, gave birth to their son Timmorran on the Night of Summons, the very night Llovar transformed his tribe's warriors into the first Uthuk Y'llan. Nightseers hailed the infant as a man of great import to come, and fearful of Llovar's increasing depravity, Rala fled with her husband and child toward Lorimor to start life anew. She died of a lingering sickness on the road before reaching the coastal empire, possibly a result of the curse Llovar called down upon the runaways in his rage at their abandonment. Sources The Rise of Timmorran (Tales of Darkness), p. 35

title: Rangers' Guild
content: Rangers' Guild The Rangers' Guild is one of the Dunwarr Guilds, patrolling the mountainsides and hunting dangerous beasts and bands of marauders across Dunwarr lands. Unlike most other Guilds, the Rangers hold that any Dwarf brave enough to live beyond the safety of rock and stone had best join their ranks and learn to protect themselves; nearly every Dwarf who lives above ground on the Northern Coast of the Frontier belongs to the Guild. Most Rangers go months or more without seeing another Dwarf, but in the depths of winter most try to make the trek to Hadranhold for Wintersmeet, the Guild's traditional week of feasting and fellowship. The Guild also maintains the original watchtower atop Mount Valborne that grew into Hadranhold, and shares kobold-extermination duty in the Dunwarr Mountains with the Warriors' Guild. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 Hadranhold (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188 The Frontier (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 190

title: Rashat
content: Rashat Rashat is the Djinn who once held the great counting houses of Ajiran, now the ruins known as the Beggar's Maze. Sources The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Rault
content: Rault Baron Rault rules Trast from Castle Artrast, a just man but quick to take offense at any perceived sleight to his honor. Trast's population is split between those who view him as too ready to acquiesce to Latari and Lorimor envoys and those who criticize his heavy-handed approach to treating with the Elves as an unnecessary provocation risking war; agitators on both sides seek to sway him, and some whisper of a conspiracy to unseat him. Rault has expressed interest in learning the truth behind rumors of a dark ceremony held twice yearly at the ancient menhirs in the foothills of Lorim's Gate, but the site's isolation prevents routine patrol. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 137–138

title: Raven Priest
content: Raven Priest In the summer of 1627, Waiqar charged a loyal follower known only as the Raven Priest with destroying the Citadel once and for all, arming him with the Carrion Fetish. With this talisman, the Raven Priest raised a massive army of skeletons and wraiths — the Raven Horde — from one of the ancient battlegrounds deep in the Tanglewood in a single night, then marched north across the Flametail River toward Archaut, burning and looting as he went. The Raven Horde was met and destroyed at the ford of Carum's Cross by the allied counties of Allerfeldt, Rostum, and Haverford; when the Raven Priest attempted to resurrect his fallen troops, Countess Cunningham of Haverford called down a bolt of lightning that burned the foul creature to cinders. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 51–52

title: Ravin
content: Ravin Ravin is a huge crocodile worshipped as a god by the Mahkim, upon whose back rides their largest village, the spiritual center of their people. Ravin bears the Mahkim throughout Zanaga across rivers and lakes, though they must constantly feed its massive appetite. When challenged or wronged, Mahkim warriors paint the god's likeness on their hides and cry out his name as they charge into battle. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Reanimate
content: Reanimate Reanimates form the backbone of most undead forces, from the smallest raiding warband of one of the lesser vampires of Bilehall to Waiqar's Deathborn Legions themselves. Reanimates feel neither pain nor fear, and when struck down, they simply pick themselves back up again and continue fighting. Perhaps most chilling is their utter silence — though they open their mouths as if to utter a war cry, the only sound from their ranks is the rattling of bone against rusted armor. Despite their terrifying presence, they are not invincible; separated from their master, for example, they lose much of their will to fight. These creatures can be found deep within the many underground catacombs in The Mistlands, patrolling against intruders to ensure that rituals are undisturbed and treasures stay intact, remaining motionless and silent seemingly forever — many an adventurer has discovered that what appeared to be a gold-laden vault strewn with assorted skeletons is in fact filled with deathless guardians eager to add to their ranks. Sources Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), pp. 166–167

title: Reaver Council
content: Reaver Council The Reaver Council is the alliance of the twelve Weik Hearthlords, meeting each year upon the longest day in Lagart to spit upon the broken statue of Nordros and reaffirm their mastery over Isheim. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), p. 233

title: Red Bridge
content: Red Bridge Red Bridge is a famous crossing within Tamalir's dominion, known for its gambling and rowdiness. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149

title: Redwater
content: Redwater Redwater is the principal port along Lorimor's western seacoast, featuring a wide bay lined with long, sturdy docks of rock cut and transported from far inland. From here, ships sail to the south through the Selenic Sea and on to Zanaga and The Broken Plains, most hugging the land for protection from pirates if they lack proper naval protection — sadly, a situation that has grown more frequent in recent years. Trading ships also sail south across the wide reach of the Great Sea, the largest body of water known to have been traversed, to distant Al-Kalim to import treasures and delicacies from the land of deserts; those who do, though, must placate or ward away the terrible gods that rule these waters, lest their ships join the countless others broken and rotting many leagues under the surface. Directly to the west of Redwater is The Endless Ocean. Sources Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 222–223

title: Revik
content: Revik Revik is an archlich who oversees the operation of The Everliving Engine on behalf of Waiqar; its true purpose is known only to the two of them. Sources Castle Dalibor (The Mistlands), p. 162

title: Rhynn
content: Rhynn Rhynn, the Envy of Terrinoth, is a largely cosmopolitan barony in the north, possessing a large city, a sophisticated castle, a rapid messenger service linking its villages and keeps, and excellent control of the River Rhynn, giving it swift movement of goods and people. Rhynn has grown wealthy from the Carthmount silver trade, and its people have a character other baronies often consider haughty. Baron Greigory, an older man with a thick white mustache who projects an air of leisurely sophistication, rules from his seat at Castle Arhynn; his close ally is the far more militant Baron Zachareth of Carthridge. Rhynn's heraldry features a tree in honor of the Grandmother Tree in the Greatwood, a sacred symbol of the barony's prosperity, and its politics are split between Greigory's inner circle and the many lesser nobles grown wealthy from their lands' proximity to the Carthmount silver mines — in many ways the baron rules as the greatest among equals, his authority more precarious than most. Centuries ago, immigrants from the Free Cities and Lorimor, as well as some from the Dunwarr Holds and Orcish Clans, came to Rhynn in large numbers, lured by pay in raw silver, and helped its citizens fight back the goblins and lesser Dragonkin plaguing the Carthmounts; they enlivened Rhynn's local culture and left it unusually open to foreigners among the baronies. In recent years, however, stories of goblins and worse plaguing the miners have grown, with the number of missing reaching frightful proportions and the mines' yield suffering, so the lords and ladies of Rhynn increasingly clamor for a solution, even hiring traveling specialists. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Rhys Soulstone
content: Rhys Soulstone King Rhys Soulstone, son of Cedrick Soulstone, shared his father's taste for pageantry and shows of wealth, planning a number of extravagant castles and holdfasts whose ruins can still be found throughout Terrinoth. Under his reign, the extravagant use of the Stars of Timmorran saw all manner of miracles performed, including feats of engineering, medicine, landscaping, and statecraft, as the ruling Soulstone line became especially adept in their use — this wondrous period of history is known as the Time of the Elder Kings, when trade and cooperation between the Dunwarr, the Latari, the Lorimor Empire, and Terrinoth peaked. Yet in accomplishing such feats, the seeds of catastrophe were planted, for overt use of the powerful and desirable Stars gained the attention of a terrible foe: the Latari Elves do not refer to this era as the Elder Kings' time at all, calling it instead "The Days before the Dragons." Sources The Rise of the Elder Kings (Tales of Darkness), pp. 43–44

title: Rime Storm
content: Rime Storm The Rime Storm is a magical maelstrom that was the doom of the Salishwyrd when, many centuries ago, it descended upon their empire, turning Isheim into a frozen nightmare. Description Isheim's weather is unpredictable and treacherous, changing between one heartbeat and the next: clear skies can suddenly fill with snow-laden clouds, winds can rise up out of nowhere, and the temperature can drop away so fast that rivers freeze solid before one's eyes. While the north's weather was never kind, it has been made all the worse by the Rime Storm. For years, the Elves sought to find and defeat the mysterious force behind it, but in the end they were driven to create a single sanctuary they could protect from its howling winds — The Green Vale. Beyond the land of the Elves, the Rime Storm runs rampant, and few among the people of Isheim can predict the weather from day to day; only Onoit shamans and Weik frost mages have any degree of success, their magical senses allowing them to read something of the storm. The White Death that plagues the far north was born of that storm, or perhaps is a result of the cursed cold itself, and the Ice Wyrms are believed by some to be the feral offspring of dragons twisted by the Rime Storm, as if they were its living embodiment. Sources An Uncharted Wilderness (Isheim), p. 236 Realm of the White Death (Isheim), p. 236

title: River Rhynn
content: River Rhynn The River Rhynn gives the barony of Rhynn excellent control over the movement of goods and people out of its lands, a key source of its wealth and cosmopolitan character. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: River of Sleep
content: River of Sleep The River of Sleep cuts through the center of the Broken Crags in Eastern Terrinoth, its banks in the valley dotted by numerous fishing villages — the most populous area of the region. The barony of Dhernas tends verdant farmland along its banks. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Riverwatch Riders
content: Riverwatch Riders The Riverwatch Riders are a special unit of Riverwatch trained at the Watch, maintaining a messenger service that reaches the far corners of Terrinoth even in times of peace, and proving the value of fast, reliable communication in ending many a threat before it becomes calamity. The entire company of Riverwatch Riders once mustered forth during the Age of Courage to relieve the fortress of Black Rock from the Usurper Geist and his ferrox during the War of Ten Brothers. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 52

title: Riverwatch
content: Riverwatch Riverwatch is one of the eight Free Cities of Terrinoth, a harbor city watched over by the tremendous statue known as the Old Man, standing on a high cliff with lantern in hand — a fitting symbol for the city's place in Terrinoth's history. Initially founded as a military outpost of the Penacor Kings, Riverwatch has since risen to become one of the most self-sufficient of the Free Cities, dedicated to the defense of the southern continent. Its arguable seat of power is the Watch, which strategically overlooks Southern Terrinoth — more than a castle or garrison, a cultural institution and sign of the city's strength and martial history, the first building constructed on the site of what became Riverwatch, whose garrison took its name as their duty. It is here that riders are trained in horsemanship and swordfighting, and a special unit acts in a vital role even in peacetime, maintaining a messenger service reaching the far corners of Terrinoth: the Riverwatch Riders, who have proven the value of fast, reliable communication in ending many a threat before it becomes calamity. To the south lies the fortress of Sundergard, which often serves as their remote base of operations against dangers from the Mountains of Despair. Riverwatch sees healthy business thanks to the intricate chain of traders and merchants needed to supply its thousands of horses and riders, and a large contingent of Orcs, originally from the Broken Plains, calls the city home, their knowledge of taming wild beasts and animal husbandry proving invaluable. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149

title: Riya Penacor
content: Riya Penacor Queen Riya Penacor, celebrated at the court of Talindon for her intelligence and charm, was banished alongside Rusticar Lorimor for their betrayal of her husband King Jerlon Penacor, and together the two founded Lorimor near the beginning of the Age of Steel, late in the third century of the Human calendar. Riya and the king's greatest friend and highest councilor Rusticar had fallen deeply for each other despite their respective vows to husband and throne; when Jerlon learned of this, he could not bring himself to condemn his queen and instead annulled his marriage, banishing the two lovers from the kingdom. A large group of the king's subjects joined them in exile, a happenstance that led some historians to wonder if there was more to the betrayal than mere love. Riya left behind two infant sons, Farrengol and Farrendon; while Rusticar and Riya went on to found an empire that rivaled anything the Penacor line produced, Farrengol's fate in Talindon after her departure would prove far darker. Sources Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), p. 32 Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 220

title: Road of Skulls
content: Road of Skulls The Road of Skulls is a winding trail through The Charg'r Wastes walked by Waiqar's lost legion during its ill-fated incursion into the Ru Darklands — for every pace marched, Waiqar left a soldier's grave in his wake. Those damned souls are said to remain here still, their grinning skulls and bleached bones marking the way to the Black Citadel, the lost stronghold of Llovar and his Ynfernael hosts. The trail hides treasures, too: following the whispers of the dead warriors can bring an adventurer to ancient artifacts from Al-Kalim and other far-off lands, or, if a spirit is spiteful, to the jaws of hungry beasts. Sources The Charg'r Wastes (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 210–211

title: Rodric
content: Rodric Rodric is a hero of the Dragon Wars honored by the naming of Fort Rodric, constructed in the Ashen Hills of Pelgate following the war's end. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Roland of Kell
content: Roland of Kell Lord Roland of Kell is said to have slain the Dragonlord Margath at the culmination of the Dragon Wars, an ancestor of Baron Fredric of Kell whose nobility many still see reflected in his descendant. History In the war's final days, Roland led the defense of the city of Kell, ringed with defensive redoubts holding ballistae of Lorimorian design, against Margath's forces — drawn there by a false rumor that a cache of Stars of Timmorran was hidden within. Roland had equipped himself with the tools needed to slay a dragonlord: an ice storm runebound shard, with which he could summon freezing rain, and a rare soulstone runebound shard from the royal vaults in Archaut, which leached the life from his enemies and filled him with stolen vigor in turn. He rode a rare Yeron, one of the winged horses of the Elves. As the dragons reeled from a hail of bolts and arrows and retreated to the cold skies above the Mountains of Despair, Roland took to the air and called forth freezing rain onto Margath's position; dazed and weakened from the cold, the dragonlord was driven through the neck by Roland's lance and slain. Roland did not live to celebrate his victory: in the dragonlord's death throes, Margath broke the wings of Roland's Yeron, and horse and rider tumbled from the sky to their deaths. In the years since, the mountainsides have been combed for the remains of Lord Roland and Margath, but no bodies have ever been recovered from the snow-shrouded peaks. [not stated in source: a separate account, tied to the cult of Aris, instead credits a "Baron Rolan" with slaying Margath at the Weeping Basin, where the dragon's body is said to have fallen to earth. The two accounts are not reconciled in the sources and are recorded here as each source states them.] Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 47–48 Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 123 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Rostum
content: Rostum Rostum is a county whose forces, led by Countess Belmont, joined those of Allerfeldt and Haverford to destroy Waiqar's Raven Horde at Carum's Cross in 1627. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 52

title: Roth's Vale
content: Roth's Vale Roth's Vale is the nebulous, borderless territory between the rest of the baronies and The Mistlands, in many ways a cursed land though it was not always so. History Before Waiqar's betrayal, Roth's Vale was a flourishing territory, protected by great magics and glorious treasures from the golden age of the Elder Kings. When the last baron of Roth's Vale died without an heir, it became a no-man's-land, and the debate over who shall become its warden has only intensified in recent years. Description Young Gaspard Bay, a rising hero ennobled for his efforts fighting with the eastern Hernfar garrison, desperately wishes to be given lordship over this territory — not just for himself, but to fulfill a promise made to his ancestors (see Gaspard Bay). Baron Zachareth of Carthridge — a capable and intense lord who, it is whispered, has fallen to the lure of sorcerous power — covets the hundreds of artifacts lost in the land's abandoned temples and castles, items that could be used to defeat the undead, or to raise and command them. Many structures here are in ruins, some dating from the defeat of Waiqar in the Second Darkness; the histories of most are lost to time. The collapsed Halls of Phetra lie in the south. One nameless citadel to the west is said to hold purifying flames deep within its mountain location, enough to painfully remove even the greatest darkness from a soul. Though the undead hungrily thrive along the vale's outskirts and in its graveyards, many beings still travel here in search of deserted keeps with forgotten vaults and underground lairs with bejeweled crypts. The largest village within Roth's Vale is Rothfeld. Sources Roth's Vale (The Mistlands), pp. 162–163

title: Rothfeld
content: Rothfeld Rothfeld is the largest village within Roth's Vale, the area most frequently plagued by the incursions of Waiqar's warbands. Years of desolation and the slow encroachment of the mists have led to a drained, depleted land, its state reflected in the poor souls who live here. Having abandoned hope of divine aid, the inhabitants have allowed their homes, fields, and temples to fall into disrepair, their will to fight utterly drained; slowly becoming brutish and destructive, Rothfelders seek succor and protection from anyone who might promise salvation from the undead threat. Some of the Daqan Lords believe that Rothfeld is where Waiqar's forces are likely to first attack in numbers. Defending this village and restoring hope to its inhabitants may mean slowing the legions of the undead long enough to rally other forces from the south to prevent the dead from overrunning the area and pouring into Terrinoth. As the village has many old temples nearby, a number of which contain the holy relics of saints or were built on sites of powerful magics, some also view Rothfeld as a natural bulwark against the undead, better fortified than forgotten and abandoned. Sources Roth's Vale (The Mistlands), p. 163

title: Rothulk Seafort
content: Rothulk Seafort The Rothulk Seafort, made from the hulls of a hundred captured ships, rides the sea just off The Thieves' Coast. From its creaking decks, both pirate fleets and the Caliphate navy set sail, later to haul their prizes home and add to the Seafort's ever-growing bulk. In Rothulk, the price of passage is often paid for with wagers, and pirates bet their vessels that they can slay the Dunnweir Kraken or find Jarl Voskol's sunken fleet. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 246

title: Ru Campaign
content: Ru Campaign The Ru Campaign was Waiqar Sumarion's war against Da'Roul Bonesplicer and the remnants of the Uthuk Y'llan, undertaken at the urging of King Daqan after Waiqar's long recuperation from his imprisonment in Llovar's Black Citadel. Once confident and brash, Waiqar had grown cold and calculating from his ordeal, but he still managed to win glory for himself, vanquishing Da'Roul and annihilating the Uthuk camps throughout the Ru and the Darklands. Daqan ordered the building of guard towers along the borders of the forbidden lands to watch for signs of resurgent Uthuk, though in the years since the watchtowers fell into disuse, so thoroughly had the Uthuk been destroyed. In the hour of his triumph, Waiqar nonetheless complained to his captains of Timmorran's complacency and arrogance, insisting that many soldiers' lives could have been saved had the wizard augmented their efforts with magic — an early sign of the resentment that would later curdle into betrayal. Sources The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 38

title: Rune Golem
content: Rune Golem Considered by many to be Terrinoth's mightiest living weapons, rune golems are hulking engines of destruction and the apex of runic magic and wizardry, impervious to all but the mightiest blows and highly resistant to the ravages of time. Unlike the Ironbound, rune golems are not automata but appear to be semi-sentient beings with memories and the potential to develop personalities. As their name implies, all rune golems are kept alive with one or more runebound shards, and it is the shard that seems to determine their attributes — shards marked with a rune of fire, it is said, make for golems quick to leap into combat and able to project flame. In the depths of several ancient keeps in the barony of Kell, magnificent rune golems await the day they are woken and called to war once more. Runemasters of Greyhaven are among the sole persons capable of awakening them. Sources The Riddles of the Runes (The Magic of Mennara), p. 117 Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 154 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Rune of Collection
content: Rune of Collection While runebound shards operate in such a simple fashion that they can be used by those without magical training, some can only be used properly by practicing wizards. Runes of collection act as fonts of magical power by slowly drawing upon the ambient magic of the Verto Magica. These shards each provide a safe and reliable well of magic, although their capacity is limited and wizards who rely on them may falter when the shard is lost. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 119

title: Rune of Fate
content: Rune of Fate Among the most subtle of runebound shards, the rune of fate directs the powerful magic held within the shard to influence the very skein of destiny. Even an untrained user who clutches the shard in their hand finds the luck of themselves and their allies improving in subtle but undeniable ways. A Runemaster can coax myriad effects forth from the shard, consigning their enemies to fumble their weapons or helping allies to fortuitously slip their blades through impossibly narrow chinks in a foe's armor. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), pp. 119–120

title: Rune of Misery
content: Rune of Misery This runebound shard imparts painful afflictions upon its target, rarely enough to seriously injure but more than enough to weaken. Elite bounty hunters in the Free Cities fight viciously for them, as such shards can allow them to bring in their quarries with less chance of bothersome bloodshed. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 120

title: Runeforge
content: Runeforge The Runeforge is the seat of the Runescribes' Guild in Thelgrim, a massive cruciform hall built partly into the cavern walls at the city's edge, housing the Dwarves' collection of known dragon runes. Its four immense wings each serve a separate purpose: the south wing, where the entrances are located, holds offices and meeting chambers; the west wing contains the forges, casting molds, and foundries where new runic items are cast and created; the north wing houses two copies of each known dragon rune, cast from an appropriate metal and hammered into rock slabs; and a further wing, buried in the stone and pointing toward the Molten Heath, protects the complete records of Dwarven history etched onto beaten copper sheets. From the Runeforge, the runescribes can gaze out over the entire city — a reminder that they, more than anyone, are responsible for preserving the soul of Dunwarr's culture. Beyond maintaining that history and etching dragon runes into arms and armor, the runescribes are also charged with discovering new runes or rediscovering those lost with the destruction of the Karok Doum; the current Master Scribe, Dorgan Hammerfist, is said to be considering hiring adventurers to explore the ruins of the Dwarves' ancestral cities on the Molten Heath in search of ancient runecraft. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 187–188

title: Runemaster
content: Runemaster Runemasters are practitioners of a form of magic that has come to dominate the esteemed halls of Greyhaven since the end of the Third Darkness, dispensing with many of the risks taken by true sorcerers since they do not tap into the Verto Magica in such a direct fashion. Description Most Runemasters are not born with the gift of sorcery and are thus unable to cast magic on their own; instead of working their own feats of magic, they activate the latent energies of runebound shards or manipulate the runes graven onto their surface to shift or focus the intended effect closer to their desires. Although anyone can activate a runebound shard, to become a Runemaster a person must learn the meanings of the runes and the manner in which the dragons originally inscribed them, a study that takes years, if not decades, to master — by tracing the runes in a subtly different pattern, or focusing on specific claw strokes, a Runemaster can direct a shard's energies, omit certain effects, or change the nature of their expression, typically increasing the duration, degree, range, or targets of an effect. In extremely rare cases, Runemasters may modify a runebound shard itself, erasing or adding certain claw strokes to change its base effect — though no matter their skill, the most fundamental elements of a rune are irrevocably branded onto the shard, meaning it cannot be erased and an unbound shard reclaimed, nor can its element or affinity be changed to a wholly different sphere: a rune of immolation might become a rune of blasting or a rune of flame, but never a rune of ice storm or of teleportation. The University of Greyhaven is the official home of the Runemasters, where tutors carefully instruct apprentices and research new methods of rune manipulation, instilling not only correct technique but also an unstinting loyalty to fellow Runemasters; senior Runemasters carefully maintain good relations with the Daqan Lords and other powerful establishments of Terrinoth, though some critics accuse them of playing a long, cynical game to oust practitioners of true sorcery in favor of their own limited but safer practices. Runemasters are among the sole persons capable of awakening the Rune Golems that protect the realms of Terrinoth in times of great need, and some are rumored to be artificing new creatures empowered by runebound shards, such as rune steeds like Baron Zachareth's Backbreaker. Other communities of Runemasters exist besides Greyhaven's, including one in the Lorimor Empire that closely follows Greyhaven's model; as the Dragon Wars were primarily confined to Terrinoth, only a handful of runebound shards are known to have crossed the great sea to Al-Kalim. Sources The Riddles of the Runes (The Magic of Mennara), p. 117

title: Runescribes' Guild
content: Runescribes' Guild The Runescribes' Guild is one of the Dunwarr Guilds, maintaining the knowledge of inscribing runes of power. The Guild's seat is the Runeforge in Thelgrim, a massive cruciform hall housing the Dwarves' collection of known dragon runes, where the Guild also preserves the complete records of Dunwarr history etched onto copper sheets. Beyond maintaining that history and etching runes into arms and armor, the runescribes — led by Master Scribe Dorgan Hammerfist — search for new runes or ones lost with the destruction of the Karok Doum. The Guild also crafted the hundreds of crystal starglobes that eternally light the cavern of Thelgrim. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 187–188

title: Rusticar Lorimor
content: Rusticar Lorimor Rusticar Lorimor, the highest councilor of King Jerlon Penacor of Talindon and his greatest friend, was banished alongside Queen Riya Penacor for their mutual betrayal of the king, and together they founded Lorimor near the beginning of the Age of Steel, late in the third century of the Human calendar. Records indicate not all of his bonded knights made it to what would become the city of Lorim, as some gave up on the trek; tavern tales in the Torue Albes speculate these figures may still wander Lorimor as Lost Knights, questing across the land in search of rights to wrong, hoping one day to be allowed to achieve a final rest. Sources Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), p. 32 Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 220 Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 227

title: Rythkin
content: Rythkin Rythkin are Hyrrinx Catfolk exiled from their villages in lean winters, cast out for being unmarried, less productive, or having run afoul of the ruling council of elders. Most Rythkin become adventurers or mercenaries and may make new lives in Human and Dwarf cities. A small few walk a different path entirely, hunting less and becoming merchants or caravan traders who roam through the far reaches of Mennara. Sources Catfolk and Half-Catfolk (Character Species), p. 68

title: Sal Meringyr
content: Sal Meringyr Sal Meringyr was a celebrated wizard of Lorimor who took the orphaned street-sorcerer Timmorran as his apprentice, exercising great power and heroism tempered by an overweening ambition to crystallize the Verto Magica's own energy — reasoning that if the Tears of Latariana were crystallized Empyrean energy, so too might raw arcane power be captured and stored. History When the servants of Q'aro Fenn, mage-assassins dispatched by Llovar to slay his nephew, finally tracked Timmorran down, Sal fought to save his apprentice, killing two of the assassins and sending the third into flight; the wizard paid dearly for his bravery, dying of the wounds he received that day. Without Sal Meringyr's sacrifice, the tale of Timmorran would have ended there. The dangerous idea he planted in his apprentice's head — that arcane power might be crystallized as the Tears once were — bore terrible fruit decades later, when Timmorran built the Tower of Meringyr in his old tutor's honor and used it to create the Orb of the Sky. Sources The Rise of Timmorran (Tales of Darkness), p. 35 The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 39

title: Salamander
content: Salamander Salamanders are Dragonkin that lack the intelligence and arcane power of true dragons, but are nonetheless fearsome creatures and the foundation for countless legends, found across The Molten Heath and within the ruins of The Karok Doum. Salamanders are creatures of magic, although they lack the requisite intelligence to consciously master this power; heat radiates from their smooth reptilian bodies, and the creatures seem particularly suited for life in the Heath, since few other environments could tolerate their inflammatory presence. Salamanders live extraordinarily long and sedentary lives — every few decades, a salamander seeks out a rift or vent in the broken terrain, rejuvenating itself in the magma below the surface. While largely peaceable, they blaze with violence if threatened, especially if any dare disturb their fiery nests. Salamander eggs (and skins) are highly desirable to mages and scholars for their magical properties, and can fetch staggering prices in Tamalir markets. Sources Life on the Heath (The Molten Heath), p. 196 The Karok Doum (The Molten Heath), p. 194

title: Salish
content: Salish The Salish were one of the eleven Elven tribes among whom Emorial divided the Tears of Latariana. High Priestess Celeneth of the Salish was among those who joined Glaciel Snowstar's quest for the dragons' aid against Malcorne and the Daewyl, helping bring about his downfall at The Battle of Enfreil. In later ages, this tribe would come to be known as the Salishwyrd, the Elves of Isheim. [not stated in source: whether the sources make this identification explicit, or whether it is inferred from the shared name] Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: Salishwyrd
content: Salishwyrd The Salishwyrd are ancient Elves who ruled Isheim before years of hunger and darkness turned their paradise into a frozen nightmare, driven from their empire by the Rime Storm. Their name recalls the Salish, one of the eleven original Elven tribes among whom the Tears of Latariana were divided. [not stated in source: whether the sources make this identification explicit, or whether it is inferred from the shared name] For years, the Elves sought to find and defeat the mysterious force behind the storm, but in the end they were driven to create a single sanctuary they could protect from its howling winds: The Green Vale, where they remain to this day. Beyond that sanctuary, only their ruins remain, still guarded by fiendish Elven traps but also filled with secrets, hunted by heroes and fought over by the ice wyrms who seek to devour the Green Vale as if they were the living embodiment of the Rime Storm. Sources Isheim (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 232 An Uncharted Wilderness (Isheim), pp. 234–236 Realm of the White Death (Isheim), p. 236

title: Sand Arenas and Scar Pits
content: Sand Arenas and Scar Pits The Sand Arenas and Scar Pits are dangerous venues within Al-Madena where people, beasts, and monsters fight for the amusement of the crowds. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Sayr-Savim
content: Sayr-Savim The Sayr-Savim are the tribes of the desert of Al-Kalim, collectively named, who were once slaves to the will of the Djinni before A'tar freed them and founded the Caliphate under the first Caliph. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), pp. 242–243

title: Scal
content: Scal The Scal were a tribe of the Ru plains many times larger than Llovar's own Loth K'har, forced to bend the knee to Llovar's growing confederation in the years before the First Darkness, becoming part of the Uthuk Y'llan. Sources The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), p. 34

title: Scarsha
content: Scarsha Scarsha the Vile, Queen of the Ice Wyrms, is perhaps the most deadly of her kind, ruling from Icegate Prison in The White Death and waging her war against the last of the Salishwyrd. The prison is a lair for her many offspring. Heroes who wander into the far north are likely to find themselves drawing her gaze, whether as potential adversaries, prey, or tools in her hunt for The Green Vale. Sources Realm of the White Death (Isheim), p. 236 Life in the Cold (Isheim), p. 237

title: Scorpion Swarm
content: Scorpion Swarm There are many dangers in the desert of Al-Kalim, but few will drive travelers to turn and run like the sight of hundreds of scorpions rising out of a dune. The entire swarm acts as a single being, each creature attacking in perfect concert like a terrible wave of death. Those who unknowingly disturb a swarm all too often end up yet another pile of bones, buried in the blowing sands and forgotten by all. Sources Life in the Sands (Al-Kalim), p. 249

title: Scurr the Huntress
content: Scurr the Huntress Scurr the Huntress is the council leader of Lok Urak, the Orc most directly responsible for keeping the tribe fed — she must not only monitor prey populations, but also oversee scouting, tracking, survival, trap construction, and ambush tactics. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Sela
content: Sela Countess Sela's stewardship of Jendra's Harbor, Telor's most prosperous city, has granted her influence throughout Terrinoth and beyond, exceeding that of her nominal ruler, Baron Echard. Sela continues to cultivate relationships with earls and barons from across Terrinoth, merchants and princes from across the sea, and even the Empress of Lorimor. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Selenic Coast
content: Selenic Coast The Selenic Coast is the southern shoreline of The Aymhelin, dashed by the fearsome Selenic Sea, whose waters are hazardous for novice crews to navigate. The sheltered port town of First Fall, southwest of Lithelin, acts as a welcome harbor and easy port for loading and unloading trade goods, almost immune to the battering winds, deep swells, and forceful riptides of the open ocean. Nearly all seaborne trade with the Elven empire comes through First Fall before being carried north and east by carts along well-maintained cobblestone roads. North of the docks lies the commune village of Selonish, and lying to the northeast, not far from where the Aymhelin empties into the Broken Plains, is The Greywood. Sources Selenic Coast (The Aymhelin), pp. 176–177

title: Selonish
content: Selonish Selonish is a commune village on the Selenic Coast, north of the docks of First Fall, a large collection of huts built on stilts above the water of the bay and overseen by Manaan. The spiritspeakers and elementalists of Selonish share resources and support each other as they seek mastery of the wind, water, and spirits of the bay. Sources Selenic Coast (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Sephone
content: Sephone The Sephone family is the noble house that has traditionally ruled the barony of Allerfeldt from Goldhall, currently headed by Baroness Katrin. The line has historically allowed the Catfolk community of Hyrrinx within Eventide Forest to govern itself independently and remain untaxed, a status quo Katrin has thus far maintained. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 142–143 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Seragart
content: Seragart Seragart is the second city of the Weik, and the heart of its shipbuilding, its shipyards spread out into a nearby bay where residents work upon the fleets night and day. It is also home to the frost mages, the weathermancers of the Weik, who imbue the vessels with magic and ensure Seragart remains sheltered from the storms and snows from the north. Many travelers from far-off lands settle here, some with powerful lineages of blood and marriage — Olief Hawthorne, for example, was born in Seragart. Seragart's Hearthlord is Baergul Rus the Betrayer. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), p. 233

title: Sern Genslyn
content: Sern Genslyn Sern Genslyn, "The Vigilant Twins," is a stoic pair of keeps standing at the edge of Blackthorn Grove on the northernmost frontier of The Aymhelin, commanded by Marshal Cennan Valareth. These two towers guard the most trafficked Elven border against bandits, raiders, and the evils that are working to corrupt the Human lands of Terrinoth, their archers, trebuchet crews, and cavalry having protected the Aymhelin from corruption and invasions for centuries. Sources Blackthorn Grove (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Serpent Dagger
content: Serpent Dagger This dagger has a sweeping blade and a hilt formed in the shape of a striking viper. Bold adventurers recovered it from the Labyrinth of Ruin, but scholars imagine that its origin was in Al-Kalim or even the Ru. Through sorcerous means, the blade constantly sweats a deadly poison, so that a mere scratch can lead to a painful death. Sources Magic Items, p. 110

title: Set
content: Set Set, the nagas' serpent god, is shrouded in lies and mystery. Legend has it that Set is the first of the Nagas, a huge snake man as tall as the highest jungle trees of Zanaga. A survivor of the catastrophe that brought down the lizardman empire, Set works from the shadows, helping his children reclaim their birthright and growing strong upon their offerings, guided by the Priestesses of Set. The nagas believe Set will one day be strong enough to slither out into the world from his hiding place and, one by one, devour the other gods of Zanaga. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Seven Sinners
content: Seven Sinners The Seven Sinners were wizards of singular and cruel power driven from Daqan by righteous citizens, slain by their own servants and buried in shallow graves in what became Haunters' Wood. Defying death, they rose up as great and evil sentient oaks that exude darkness, making the wood an ideal hunting ground for the Ru's predators; illusions of safe haven conjured by the Seven lure prey, including travelers, into the wood, where their spilled blood can feed the trees. Their wealth remains tangled about their roots, waiting for those skilled enough to traverse the midnight forest and battle its many monsters, and then the trees themselves. Sources The Ru and the Darkness (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 210

title: Shaarina
content: Shaarina Shaarina the Rex is the Great Dragon Rex who rules over the entirety of The Molten Heath from The Heart, possessor of a priceless hoard of bound and unbound shards, unbroken Stars, and other magical riches amassed from the Time of the Elder Kings. History The dragonlords Margath, Levirax, Baalesh, Zir the Black, Avox, and Gehennor invaded Terrinoth during the Third Darkness without Shaarina's sanction, each pursuing the Stars of Timmorran for personal gain rather than as a coordinated campaign. By 1029, with the dragonlords' armies greatly diminished, a great host of mighty dragons — drakes dwarfing even the dragonlords in size — flew from the Molten Heath, seemingly reinforcing Zir the Black's last known lair, only to fly back carrying the treasure looted from the Fair Realms without troubling the people of Terrinoth further. Orc scouts later found the bodies of Zir and hundreds of lesser Dragonkin, torn apart and burned; Greyhaven scholars suspect Shaarina and her court had acted to end the Third Darkness by executing those who had taken part in the invasion and claiming their plunder for her own hoard. Shaarina still lives on the Molten Heath, and periodically brave adventurers present themselves as envoys to the Dragonkin seeking both an explanation of the Third Darkness and opportunities to trade; they typically end up inside the belly of a drake, but some return telling tales of the Dragon Rex's displeasure at the wanton excesses of the Elder Kings and the abuse of power not meant for mortals. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 47–48

title: Shade
content: Shade None are sure why these spirits are so common in Tigh Higard. They can certainly be found in other lands, but on this island there are few cemeteries or other resting places from which scholars of such things would expect shades to rise. To walk about on certain nights is to watch echoes of the dead float across the grasses, ghastly blue-white forms that undulate despite the stillness of the air. Their touch is as cold as the grave, and should they find magical aid or be invigorated with sorcerous magics, they can become powerful enough to overrun settlements and fully crewed ships alike. Longtime residents of Shellport claim they are searching for the pirates who betrayed them and offer rewards in barnacle-encrusted gold coins to those who offer assistance, but if any have done so, they have not lived to speak of such deeds. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 229

title: Shadow Bracers
content: Shadow Bracers These black bracers are embossed with curved fluting and polished with an iridescent lacquer. They steadily emit a fine black mist that is odorless and safe to breathe but capable of obscuring vision. In combat, the unnatural mist given off by the bracers envelops the wearer, obscuring them and making them harder to hit; the effect is unnerving, and leaves opponents with a sense of doom. Sources Magic Items, p. 110

title: Shadow Peaks
content: Shadow Peaks The Shadow Peaks are a mountain range in Northern Terrinoth, home of the Pilgrim's Trail and Shika's Tree, not far from the Free City of Greyhaven. A gold mine once worked by the barony of Dhernas, now abandoned and rumored haunted, lies at the range's base within the Hanging Wood. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Shadowsgate Rift
content: Shadowsgate Rift The Shadowsgate Rift is reputed to be a haunt of lost souls within The Great Sand Sea, spirits cast away from the Sun God's blessed gaze. Denied the glory of A'tar, they skulk in the depths of the Rift, pining for the light, and hatefully descend upon trespassers, eagerly devouring the warmth of the sun they might still wear upon their flesh. Sources The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Sharish
content: Sharish Sun Priestess Sharish is the master of Irram and custodian of the Grand Temple of A'tar, leader of her people and one of the vizier rulers of Al-Kalim. Sharish believes that the fruits of Djinn magic are intrinsically tainted, and she would see the Caliphate's reliance upon them ended — a stance that brings her into conflict with the Collegiate Arcane and into opposition with other viziers who see only the wealth ancient Djinn artifacts can bring. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245

title: Shellport
content: Shellport In contrast to the rest of Tigh Higard, Shellport is devoted to pleasure, a port city that gives hard-worn sailors and traveling adventurers rest and fun before going off to their next destination. Taverns abound, along with plentiful distractions to separate visitors from their coins. Shellport is a place to make merry, but also a place of opportunity: the constant flux of sailors passing through means there is always word of new treasures to be found, and maps to them to be purchased. A few are accurate, while some may lead to even richer, though more perilous, rewards. New expeditions seem to form in the taverns each night, their members sailing off to unexplored lands or venturing to the north in the hope of finding new trade passages; armed groups assemble regularly here to march against the terrors in the mountains and tame their numbers, a never-ending quest that sometimes reaps benefits when they discover forgotten hoards of magical items or the frozen bodies of dragons and other valuable creatures. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 224–225

title: Shield of Coals
content: Shield of Coals The Shield of Coals is a holy artifact of Kellos kept in the vaults beneath the Eternal Flame, wielded by Lady Anastel as Justicar against Geist the Usurper during the War of Ten Brothers. After Anastel's forces were ambushed and destroyed, Geist pried the Shield from her dead hands and used its power to summon a hail of fire upon the defenders of Black Rock. When the Riverwatch Riders routed his forces at the frozen Morshan River, the Shield began to glow with searing heat in Geist's grip; he dropped it upon the ice, which melted away in the face of Kellos's wrath, drowning Geist and his ferrox in the freezing water. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 52–53

title: Shield of Light
content: Shield of Light The Shield of Light is a blessed item holy to the priesthood of Kellos: a large heater shield decorated with a bold sunburst design in red and gold. When wielded in battle, rays of golden light stream from the boss, becoming impossibly brilliant when struck. Sources Magic Items, p. 110

title: Shika's Tree
content: Shika's Tree Shika's Tree stands along the Pilgrim's Trail through the Shadow Peaks. Pilgrims who succeed in the trail's challenge are allowed to pluck a single fruit from its branches, said to bring fortune or glory to those who eat of its flesh. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Shrieker
content: Shrieker Shriekers are a horrific punishment the Uthuk Witches inflict upon berserkers who fail them: the Witch slashes open the offender's back and cruelly wrenches out their lungs, warping them into huge, overgrown mockeries of life. These so-called "shriekers" constantly scream their resulting rage and pain, and their grotesquely enlarged lungs amplify the sound so greatly as to debilitate foes. Sources A Tear in the Veil (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 213

title: Silent Chantry
content: Silent Chantry The Silent Chantry, possibly the most interesting part of Last Haven, is home to the Silent Ones, an order of exiled sorcerers who gather lost and forbidden knowledge and pay well for artifacts both ancient and deadly. Rumors persist that the Silent Ones serve an Ynfernael master, and that with the artifacts they acquire, they intend to open a tear in the veil beneath the city and coax their dark lord forth into the world. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 212

title: Singhara Hunter
content: Singhara Hunter The feline ancestry of the Singhara makes them excellent hunters. In the darkness of night, when their night sight gives them an edge over their prey, they move swiftly and silently across the plains and through the jungles of Zanaga. The favored weapon of these hunters is the lion spear, a shaft as long as a warrior is tall, tipped with a sharpened sabrecat tooth; in the hands of a Singhara hunter, such a spear can punch through toughened hide or shell and be launched into the air like a bolt of bone lightning to strike down targets hundreds of paces distant. Singhara hunters often travel in packs, all the better to herd animals to their doom, their tireless stamina carrying them on while their echoing roars coordinate the hunt — some form the pursuit, while others pick out good spots for ambush or places to corral their prey. For all their swiftness, when Singhara choose to lie in wait, often from the branches of a tree or hidden in tall grass, they become almost invisible until they burst into a blinding sprint, then enjoy the bloody victory of the kill. Sources Life in the Jungle (Zanaga), p. 259

title: Singhara Pridelord
content: Singhara Pridelord Pridelords are the largest and fiercest of the Singhara warriors, powerfully muscled, standing head and shoulders above even the tallest of Humans. Adding to their grandeur are their great manes, which hang like cloaks down their backs, the size and thickness a mark of a war chief's status among their people. Armed with spear, club, tooth, and claw, the Pridelord is always at the forefront of the hunt or where battle is at its thickest, for it is the Singhara way to lead by example; as a mark of this bravery, a Pridelord's body is often covered in scars, each one worn proudly to tell a tale of the chief's life as a warrior and veteran of war. Swift hunters, Pridelords can race across the wilds of Zanaga, their long legs and mighty muscles allowing them to run down almost any kind of prey. Despite such speed, their deafening roars precede them into battle — so great is the growl of a Pridelord that the very ground shakes with its booming, and weak-hearted creatures are set to flight, while nearby Singhara warriors are stirred to greater acts of animalistic savagery, their own roars joining those of their leader as they tear into their prey. Sources Life in the Jungle (Zanaga), p. 259

title: Singhara
content: Singhara The Singhara are an ancient and strong feline people, lions given the shape of Humans, who stride across the plains of Zanaga in mighty prides — each pride an ancient tribe holding dominance over a region, from the Road of Heroes to the Sunscathe Barrens and beyond. Among scholars who classify them alongside the Catfolk, the Singhara are noted for their full mane and rich gold and auburn fur, unlike smaller breeds such as the Hyrrinx. Table of Contents Society War Against Tarakhe Gods of the Plains Sources Society With the arrival of the water-striders (as the Singhara call those who come from across the large expanses of water to the north), some prides have learned the newcomers' languages and begun to trade with Herman's Gulch and other settlements. Merchants from the other continents are wise to be wary of Singhara customs, however: the lion people respect only martial skill and shows of strength, and many of their deals are sealed with ritual combat and the spilling of blood. A pride leader is likely to challenge a traveler to combat upon first meeting them, not out of a desire to kill or from anger, but only so the leader might best judge the stranger's worth. For every pride that has dealings with the water-striders, there are many that do not — some keep their distance and watch travelers, while others are openly hostile, seeing these newcomers as merely another evil assaulting their land. War Against Tarakhe Few foreign explorers know that the Singhara are among the most potent of Tarakhe's enemies and still fight against the influence of the dead god. Though the plague deity has been returned to his rotting tomb, much of his poison remains throughout Zanaga, corrupting and killing the land, and it is against this remnant, and the creatures it spawns, that the lion people wage a constant war. In places like the Forest of Fangs, where the jungle grows thick and twisted with Tarakhe's power, Singhara Hunter parties stalk the darkness, seeking out the god's followers. A battle against Tarakhe's servants is one of the few events that might induce a Singhara pride to ally with other races, as the lion people tolerate explorers if they choose to take up arms against the god — and if they can prove their worth in battle. They might even give an outsider the chance to be inducted into a pride, although this has happened but a very few times. Only when an adventurer has proven their worth to a pride leader, usually in battle, can they walk the Path of Bones to Singhavrem, home of the lion people; it is a long and dangerous journey, for once a person sets foot upon the path, they are an enemy of the Singhara until they can best the guardians of Singhavrem and lay a bloody palm upon the lion's temple. This, and this alone, earns them the ritual scars that mark them out as Singhara for all to see. Gods of the Plains The gods of the Singhara are, like most of the ancient deities of Zanaga, immensely powerful beasts to whom Zanagans offer their worship: Hamzah the Pridelord, the lion god of war, and his vicious brother Jararr, the panther god of the Wild Hunt. Sources A New World (Zanaga), pp. 253–254 Life in the Jungle (Zanaga), p. 259

title: Singhavrem
content: Singhavrem Singhavrem is the home of the lion people, reached only via the long and dangerous Path of Bones, and the seat of the world cave where Hamzah the Pridelord lairs beneath the vast plains of Zanaga. Once a person sets foot upon the Path of Bones, they are an enemy of the Singhara until they can best the guardians of Singhavrem and lay a bloody palm upon the lion's temple — this, and this alone, earns them the ritual scars that mark them out as Singhara for all to see. Sources A New World (Zanaga), pp. 253–254

title: Siren
content: Siren On certain remote coasts and islets of Lorimor, haunting songs draw sailors to their doom, their boats and ships dashed on the rocks. The men and women who perish in the impact or drown swiftly are the fortunate ones, for those survivors who wash ashore or climb upon the rocks become living prey for the sirens — twisted creatures combining the features of humans and birds. The hypnotic song of these creatures is unique, with qualities of both birdsong and the most beautiful human voices; few can resist the lure of the sirens' song, and those who succumb find themselves compelled to seek its source, and helpless to defend themselves against the sirens' attack. Sirens are intelligent, but are completely without mercy or culture — these cannibalistic monsters see humans and other intelligent races as nothing more than food, yet they prefer to inflict as much misery as possible on their prey. Sirens are as spiteful as they are craven, quick to flee should their victims fight back, but equally quick to return when they believe their prey to be vulnerable once more; in some rare cases, sirens have been known to pursue victims who escape back to outposts of civilization. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 230

title: Siryasa
content: Siryasa Siryasa, the City of the Warrior Women, is a vizier city-state of Al-Kalim where Kayree Sandspear, Maiden of the Wastes, commands an army in the name of the Caliph. It is from her fighting schools and training lodges that many of Al-Kalim's greatest warriors emerge. Once a year, Sandspear herself steps into the Arena of Blades at Siryasa's summit and dares any to challenge her for the right to govern the city; many have tried, but all have met their end upon her paired viper blades. Heroes often come to the city to test their skill, both in the fighting pits and in the grueling competition at the Path of Daggers, a trap-filled dungeon carved into the side of Siryasa's Shame. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245

title: Sisters of Q'aro Fenn
content: Sisters of Q'aro Fenn The Sisters of Q'aro Fenn are an Uthuk Y'llan order of assassins named for Q'aro Fenn, Llovar's own chief of assassins during the First Darkness, and who have pronounced the rediscovery of The Spire of Ruin a portent of their hoped-for revenge. Sources The Rise of Timmorran (Tales of Darkness), p. 35 A Tear in the Veil (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 212

title: Skorn
content: Skorn Skorn is the legendary rider who leads Mag Ugluk Urak, the Great Beast Tribe, coordinating their efforts both for and against the surrounding Orc tribes — a one-armed, grey-haired Orc of few words with the unnerving demeanor of an ambush predator. He is thoughtful, patient, and ruthless, though well known for believing that an Orc's word should carry the same weight as the bond with his Gurak Tol, so Skorn is considered one of the most honest and honorable mortals anyone could meet in The Broken Plains. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Skydown
content: Skydown Skydown is the ancestral home of the barons of Otrin, sited at the foot of the Mountains of Despair not as a defense against rival baronies but as a bulwark against the creatures of the range's foothills and heights. Baron Trevalyan hosts aspiring Knights of the Citadel at Skydown who hunt manticores and other monsters in the mountains to prove their worth. To the south, Riverwatch's fortress of Sundergard serves as the first line of defense against dangers from the same range. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Smiths' Guild
content: Smiths' Guild The Smiths' Guild is one of the Dunwarr Guilds, forging tools, weapons, and other useful items. Many members of the Smiths' Guild have settled in Hadranhold to take advantage of the abundant heat near the molten heart of Mennara, and it is the Smiths' Guild that tends the Firestone Furnace there, forging ores into pure ingots and the hardened, dragonfire-resistant steel used for the Gates of Thelgrim. The furnace is overseen night and day by the Greathammer Hafnir Irontamer. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 Hadranhold (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188

title: Smokeblue Hills
content: Smokeblue Hills The Smokeblue Hills, together with the Mountains of Despair, have long served as a gathering place for sorcerous cults, dragon-worshippers, and other servants of darkness in Southern Terrinoth. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 137

title: Soulbound Sword
content: Soulbound Sword Necromancers can bind the spirits of fearsome warriors within cursed blades. These soulbound swords have a sinister appearance, with morbid detailing such as skull-shaped pommels and guards made from carved bone; the black blades are slightly iridescent, and if an observer watches closely, they may discern the shifting ghost trapped within. Bearers of these swords are said to benefit from some of the skill of the warrior spirit they carry, and the blades' merest touch often proves fatal — the grim reputation and appearance of Soulbound Swords also serves to inspire dread in their bearers' foes, though a bearer who fails to master the blade's fear risks the spirit within possessing them entirely. Sources Magic Items, p. 110

title: Soulstone Rune
content: Soulstone Rune A soulstone rune is an object of dread, for it has within it the power to leech away life-energies. A bearer of such a shard soon acquires a dark reputation, though Lord Roland of Kell is still remembered for his brave use of one in the Dragon Wars. When the shard is active, the bearer can focus their will on a visible target; that foe grows increasingly weak, while any aches and injuries suffered by the bearer are assuaged. These runes work too gradually to make for effective weapons, but in time a bearer could even be brought from near death to full wellness, at the likely cost of the life of their chosen target. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 120

title: Spined Thresher
content: Spined Thresher Known to the Uthuk as the Gw'reth Chuik, or "that which feeds," these mighty demons are simply "spined threshers" to the defenders of the Land of Steel. When the enemies of the Uthuk cower behind the stone walls of their cities and keeps, the witches call out into the Ynfernael for the Gw'reth Chuik, and if their sacrifices are sufficient, a huge demon hauls its chitinous form from the beyond to do battle for the Locust Swarm. A nightmare mixture of insect and beast, the demon looms over Humans and horses, ranging from the size of a laden wagon to that of a small house. Despite their bulk, spined threshers move swiftly across the battlefield, their many legs propelling them along; they rip apart their foes with serrated mandibles or even devour them whole, while walls and other fortifications crack and crumble under their sustained assaults. The mere sight of a spined thresher is frequently enough to infect mortal minds with unreasoning fear — as the beast chitters and lifts its bulbous head above the enemy's parapet, soldiers scatter before it, dropping weapons and shields as they try desperately to flee. The demon seems to revel in the terror it causes, displaying a dark intelligence as it drives prey before it, often trapping them against their own defenses before taking its time to crush them underfoot or snip the limbs from their bodies. In great battles, a favored bloodsister might be blessed with the arrival of more than one spined thresher with which to destroy her enemies; in these instances, the great demons level everything in their path, competing to sow the most destruction until naught remains of a city or town but piles of rubble and twisted corpses. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 216

title: Spire of the Phoenix
content: Spire of the Phoenix The Spire of the Phoenix is a golden tower rising up in the Grey Wastes of The Great Sand Sea, a place where few mortals dare to tread, its shining peak warning travelers away for leagues in all directions. When A'tar's magical fires gutted the Djinn cities, one of their number transformed his palace into molten gold and chose a glittering tomb rather than banishment. The Djinn resides there still, waiting for the greed of mortals to break open his golden crypt. Sources The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Spirits
content: Spirits No one knows for certain from whence the spirits of Mennara came, or how they relate to the dragons that created the world. Some scholars theorize that spirits are the collection of magical energies from the Turning in specific locations, which eventually coalesce into intelligent beings; others postulate that spirits spilled over from the Aenlong and made their residence in the Firma Dracem; still others believe they are accidental side effects from the moment when the Yrthwright Mennara created the world. Description All that is known with certainty is that spirits dwell in beautiful and wondrous places all across Mennara, congregating most strongly in wild areas far from cities and towns — perhaps because they are most likely to inhabit ancient trees and misty caves, the very things cleared or avoided when settlements are built, or perhaps simply because spirits do not care for the mortal races. Confusion exists over the distinction between the spirits of the land and the wraiths that haunt places stained by anger, despair, or violence; the spirits found in the wilds are seen more as avatars or emissaries of the natural world, whether of a particular place or of a particular object or organism, as with tree spirits such as the one said to reside in the Tree of Tales. Spiritspeakers are believed able to commune with restless ghosts as well, but no one has tried to speak with the specters that plague the Mistlands. Those with the gift — or perhaps simply the patience — to communicate with spirits are called spiritspeakers, taught to awaken or seek the spirits' attention through chanting, drums, dance, and offerings of gifts or service. Once they have gained a spirit's ear, they may ask for boons such as healing or luck in a particular endeavor, or even ask a spirit to visit harm upon an enemy who has aggrieved it as well; spirits can also empower those who speak with them with a portion of their magic, enabling the spiritspeaker to fight with the power of flame, wind, stone, or water. Spiritspeaking is in some ways similar to dreamwalking, in that spirits can share their knowledge with those who commune with them — more reliable than dreams, but also more limited, for a spirit's answers are restricted to what it has itself learned or heard from other spirits. Spiritspeaking is one of the oldest forms of magic, arising from the need of the earliest peoples to coexist alongside the tumultuous landscape and the spirits that dwelled there. As the ages passed, the arcane arts eventually supplanted spiritspeaking in many cultures, for wizards need not cajole or appease another entity to create desired effects. In cultures that still live in close connection with the land, however, such as the Orc tribes of the Broken Plains, the Singhara prides of Zanaga, the Onoit Gnomes of Isheim, and many far-flung human settlements, spiritspeaking remains a tremendously important part of daily life and survival. Most spiritspeakers seem rather eccentric and strange, with a touch of the wild about them, whether from living in seclusion to be closer to spirits, from the spirits' own eccentric influence, or simply from a wisdom gained by learning more of the world than those who look down on them. Sources Spiritspeaking (Call to Adventure), pp. 126–127

title: Splig, King of All Goblins
content: Splig, King of All Goblins Splig, the self-styled "King of All Goblins," is a goblin leader taller than his minions by several heads and several hundred pounds heavier, embodying the two major virtues of goblin-kind: cowardice and avarice. Using his size and brutal demeanor, Splig intimidates his lackeys into running headlong into readied enemy weapons, and has even been known to grab one as a living shield when an adventurer's blade comes too close; should things go badly, he retreats quickly, all the while calling for his minions to keep fighting to the end. Like many goblins, Splig harbors grand ambitions far surpassing his worldly ability, forever wandering from county to county and cave hideout to cave hideout in pursuit of absurd schemes for gold and power. He often serves as discreet muscle for necromancers and dark wizards who do not wish to draw the attention of the holy warriors of Kellos, usually accepting such jobs hoping to steal whatever he can before quietly slipping away once adventurers inevitably show up. Sources Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), pp. 154–155

title: Staff of Light
content: Staff of Light Priests of Pollux developed Staffs of Light as an alternative to the messy business of using torches and lamps for illumination. They are short and sturdy lengths of twisted wrought iron topped with a pearlescent jewel that glows with intense white light when a word of command is spoken. Usually the staffs are simply used in place of torches, but adventurers have been known to brandish these magical staffs at foes in order to dazzle them; those with true magical skills, though, can use them for even greater tasks. Sources Magic Items, p. 110

title: Starfall Forest
content: Starfall Forest The Starfall Forest lies west of the Thelsvan Plains in Cailn, a beautiful and dangerous wood named for the haunting blue-and-black stones that litter its ground, said to have fallen from the heavens. The forest is the subject of many strange tales and legends, and many who enter in search of the valuable, allegedly mystical stones never return. The ancient castle of Caer Loc stands just beyond the forest, built of the same mysterious stones. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Stars of Timmorran
content: Stars of Timmorran The Stars of Timmorran are the shattered fragments of Timmorran's Orb of the Sky, unstable magical artifacts capable of powering great magic in the hands of a trained wizard, named and safeguarded by Lumii Tamar after the Night of Betrayal. History The Council of Barons granted Lumii Tamar the authority to found an order of wizards to protect the Stars and advise on their use, but Lumii and the Stars pass from history at that moment. As time passed and a feeling of security returned to Terrinoth, the Stars slowly began to emerge from wherever Lumii and his followers had hidden them, making their way into the treasuries of barons, the laboratories of wizards, and the workings of magical wonders — some even reached the Courts of the Latari, the Deeplord Halls of Dunwarr, and the Throne Room of the Lorimor Empire.
