Under the extravagant reign of the Soulstone Kings, the degree of secrecy that had once surrounded the Stars broke down entirely; they were traded for gold and used to engineer public works and spectacles throughout the Time of the Elder Kings, a wondrous era of trade and cooperation between the Dunwarr, the Latari, the Lorimor Empire, and Terrinoth that the Latari themselves instead call "The Days before the Dragons," for their overt use drew the attention of the dragonlords and brought about the Third Darkness. During that war, the Dragonlord Zir the Black discovered how to break the Stars down into smaller fragments inscribed with runes — runebound shards, smaller and more stable artifacts usable even by a bearer with no magical knowledge — transforming the very nature of magic across Mennara and turning Margath's host from a formidable army into one that was nigh unbeatable. Legacy Greyhaven scholars believe the Orb of the Sky was the most powerful magical artifact that ever existed, storing enough magic to have allowed later wizards to cast billions upon billions of potent spells without needing to tap into the Verto Magica, sparing Terrinoth from ever fearing invasion again — that promise died with the Orb, leaving only the Stars. [not stated in source: an explicit causal link is not drawn, but the source places the destruction of the Orb and the birth of the Undying One together as] the first horrific repercussion of Timmorran's actions, with one Star said to have been associated with the birth of the Undying One. For generations the Stars were kept secured and secret, but they grew widespread and conspicuous in the time of the Elder Kings, drawing the dragons' notice; for reasons still unknown, the dragons emerged from the Molten Heath and raged across Mennara in search of Stars, so that Timmorran's Orb brought about a second, even more devastating war on top of the first. The dragons fractured their captured Stars into runebound shards, which could only produce a single effect each but were far easier to operate than a full Star — more useful for the dragons and their hybrid minions. The use of runebound shards spread across Mennara after the war ended, even though most Stars were never found. The dragons are believed to have amassed an enormous hoard, but no one knows its eventual fate; nevertheless, so many shards were created that untold numbers remain. Some fell into the hands of the defenders during the Third Darkness, and small caches of others have been found in the wilderness in the centuries since. Powerful barons, military armories, and wealthy collectors possess most of them today, and Greyhaven University and the cult of Kellos each maintain their own private reserves. A few Stars are thought to have escaped the dragons entirely. Even the slightest hint of their existence is enough to launch legends, such as the Sunderlander's Stone, the Vault of Jade Twilight, and the Chasm of Stars. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 41 The Rise of the Elder Kings (Tales of Darkness), pp. 43–44 The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 45–46 Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), pp. 119–120

title: Stasis Rune
content: Stasis Rune A character who activates a stasis rune focuses on a single target. For a brief period, the target feels as if they are frozen in time and space. Even if left unassailed, the target finds the experience of catching up with time highly upsetting in the short term. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 120

title: Statue of Daqan
content: Statue of Daqan The Statue of Daqan is the greatest of the colossal statues lining the avenues of Archaut, an enduring monument to the lost king. More than a thousand years later, its regal likeness looks as unblemished as the day it was erected, as if the very elements defer to the lost monarch. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Stone-Dweller Orc
content: Stone-Dweller Orc Stone-Dweller Orcs have abandoned the "primitive" ancestral ways of their Broken Plains kin, having relinquished tribal philosophy as a form of "primitive superstition" to live happily alongside the other races in cities all over the world, enjoying all the comforts and advantages that city life has to offer. While there is no inherent need for Orcs to make a living using their immense size and incredible strength, most Stone-Dwellers find it too tempting a lure to resist, often finding themselves living lives of adventure as mercenaries, soldiers, constables, or crooks. Once viewed with suspicion and derision by their nomadic kin, in the past century or so it has become increasingly common for Orcs to migrate between the two ways of life, each hoping the other style of living might offer whatever they feel is missing in their own. Sources Orcs (Character Species), pp. 66–67

title: Storm Sorceress
content: Storm Sorceress Storm sorceresses are Elves of The Aymhelin with centuries of training in elemental magic and an awe-inspiring ability to take control of the air around them, calling blinding blizzards, scattering their foes with gale-force winds, and striking their enemies with brutally precise lightning. Unlike the priesthood of the Path to the Stars, who call upon the pure energy of the Empyrean, storm sorceresses instead study the arcane arts and channel the energy of the Turning much as human wizards do. Although the forms and functions of magic are as diverse as the natural world, few can truly harness and control its potential; a comparative few can meaningfully form and direct that energy, and no more than a hundred practitioners in all of Mennara can match the abilities of a storm sorceress. Primarily concerned with helping to control the environments of the Aymhelin, the storm sorceresses of Lithelin are rarely encountered by anyone other than their fellow elementalists. However, there are times when the sorceresses must journey not only into the greater Aymhelin but throughout Mennara to hunt down certain exceptionally rare minerals needed to work their magics. Sources Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 175 Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), p. 180 Elven Sorcery (Elven Magic), p. 129

title: Stormlords
content: Stormlords The Stormlords are a group of divine beings, among them Syraskil and Marnn, who cast their greedy eyes on the wonders of Mennara and would see it destroyed if they had the chance, dwelling within a dark storm that churns on the western horizon of the Great Sea. Those who would venture beyond that storm's clouds and explore the great unknown are never heard from again. Sailors who ply the seas between Al-Kalim and the Torue Albes, or along Lorimor, the Kingless Coast, and distant Zanaga, make sure to placate the Stormlords with sufficient offerings lest they incur their wrath. Legend has it that they were weakened by the legendary seven scions, but it is only a matter of time before the tempest returns to full strength; some dark clerics believe they can harness this power, calling forth the might of angry seas and violent winds to wreak havoc against their enemies, strengthening the Stormlords and bringing the day of their return ever closer. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), pp. 124–125

title: Strangehaven
content: Strangehaven Strangehaven rests in the far northern reaches of Terrinoth, within Carthridge, a den of outcasts and eccentrics outside the bounds of any barony. Far from the reach of the law, Strangehaven is a community in the loosest sense of the word, a place where just about anything can be found by those with the gold to pay and no wish to ask questions. Without the protection of the Daqan Lords or even an official militia or watch, its residents would seem vulnerable to the horrors of the Mistlands, yet despite the occasional Fog Runner tracking an undead target to the town, Strangehaven has so far gone unharmed. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 145

title: Stron
content: Stron Master Artificer Stron oversees the Duldor Deeps together with his wife, Chief Alchemist Freja Bjornhart of the Alchemists' League. They fell in love after decades of working closely together, though their relationship was taboo from the very beginning: the Artificers' Guild feared Stron's loyalty to his wife would weaken their dominant position, while the Alchemists' League saw Freja's love for her husband as fraternizing with the enemy. Both received stern admonishments to avoid the other, which they dutifully acknowledged and immediately ignored. In the years since, neither organization has been willing to admit that Stron and Freja's marriage is what has kept the Duldor Deeps running relatively smoothly; instead, the Guild and League argue over which organization the couple's eventual children will join. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189

title: Sudanya
content: Sudanya Sudanya is a village nestled near the borders of the Ru where, during a cold winter's day in 1028, representatives from Terrinoth met with those from Dunwarr, the Aymhelin, and the Lorimor Empire to discuss strategy against the dragonlords of the Third Darkness. Winter was considered an advantageous time to organize the defense, as the cold weather turned the reptilian dragons sluggish and drowsy while they consolidated their conquests. For the first time in Terrinoth's history, Orc chieftains from The Broken Plains also joined the conclave — the Orcs desperately needed help facing the dragon threat, but were widely distrusted for their part in aiding Llovar during the First Darkness and their centuries of raiding since; before being invited, the chiefs of several important Orc tribes swore powerful oaths never to raise arms against the Fair Realms again. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 47

title: Sun Blessed
content: Sun Blessed The Sun Blessed are a cult devoted to A'tar that instructs the devout to go blind staring into the Sun God's brilliance so that they might truly see. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 246

title: Sunburst Rune
content: Sunburst Rune When activated, a sunburst rune emits a powerful burst of intense light that disorients the foe and inflicts scorching-hot wounds. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 121

title: Sundergard
content: Sundergard Sundergard is a fortress south of Riverwatch, one of many such installations dotting the landscape of Southern Terrinoth; due to the sheer number of troops and riders of Riverwatch's militia and permanent rangers, it often serves as their remote base of operations, the first line of defense against dangers issuing from the Mountains of Despair to the south. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149 Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 137

title: Sunderlander's Stone
content: Sunderlander's Stone The Sunderlander's Stone is one of the Stars of Timmorran believed to have escaped capture by the dragons during the Third Darkness. Even the slightest hint of its existence is enough to launch legends among treasure-seekers and scholars alike. [not stated in source: no further detail on its appearance, powers, or current whereabouts is given] Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 120

title: Sunderlands Orc
content: Sunderlands Orc The mysterious Sunderlands Orcs eschew both the nomadic life of the Broken Plains and the city life of Stone-Dweller Orcs, instead living in small, secretive villages that dot the great deserts of Al-Kalim — so few in number that even other Orcs dismiss them as outliers. This insular way of life helps preserve Orc culture and heritage while advancing their race in step with the rest of the world. Within their villages, Sunderlands Orcs study magic and medicine with equal diligence, and their culture is highly focused on learning and experimentation rather than combat, though even their weakest scholars can be a match for any Human. Such are their skills at potion making that the alchemical contents within their signature black glass flasks are renowned throughout Mennara. Tales say it was an offshoot of the Erd'Lantir Urak tribe, along with some from the Jer'Kul Urak, that many ages ago returned with a merchant ship from Al-Kalim to become the Sunderland Orcs. Sources Orcs (Character Species), pp. 66–67 The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 198–199

title: Sword Poet
content: Sword Poet Lorimor has a long tradition of warrior-bards practicing Verse Magic, the finest of whom begin as students in one of its rare philosophic schools. They are not given a sword, though, until they have learned to also compose and sing while fighting. Sword poets are reflective and observant, seeking meaning in every duel. If two sword poets are set to duel each other, they may spend hours in combative verse until the moment is right to draw blades — lighting, ambient sounds, and mood must all be perfect, for a fight without art is one not worth having. Once their blade is drawn, however, each sword poet becomes a flurry of slashes; their techniques may seem flamboyant, but the results speak for themselves. Few actually strike to kill, though — most prefer to disarm or otherwise avoid the unseemliness of spilling blood, often likened to carelessly spilling ink upon a blank page. Only if they know the blow will be absolutely perfect will they consider striking to kill. These deadly codas are renowned and often recorded for posterity, the most famous compilation being blade-laureate Zaff Darba's masterwork Contemplations upon the Flametail. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 230–231

title: Swordsmasters
content: Swordsmasters The Swordsmasters, also known as the Darnati warriors, are a mysterious order of mystical adepts based in ancient stone temples nestled among The Darnati Highlands, who channel their spiritual energies into amazing displays of grace, speed, balance, and power. These monks are among the most feared warriors in all of Mennara, and from their modest monastery they hold perpetual vigil over the highlands. Sources The Darnati Highlands (The Aymhelin), p. 177

title: Syraskil
content: Syraskil Syraskil, the chaos serpent, is one of the Stormlords who guards the edges of the world from within the dark storm that churns on the western horizon of the Great Sea. Sailors who ply the seas between Al-Kalim and The Torue Albes, or along Lorimor, the Kingless Coast, and distant Zanaga, make sure to placate Syraskil with sufficient offerings lest they incur his wrath. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 124

title: T'mara T'rusheen
content: T'mara T'rusheen The T'mara T'rusheen is the spirit realm and the Ynfernael beyond it, reached through the rift atop The Spire of Ruin — the place where Llovar began his fateful journey into demonic power. Sources A Tear in the Veil (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 212–213

title: Tairnheath Castle
content: Tairnheath Castle Tairnheath Castle was the ancestral seat of Count Hector Ysphane, destroyed in 1701 after the count displayed three dragon eggs in a place of honor beside his great hall's hearth against his court wizard's frantic advice. A group of adventurers from Greyhaven found the castle reduced to a burned-out husk with no survivors, a dragon hatchling — already twice the size of a horse — having made its lair in the cellar and slain everyone within. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 52–53

title: Talindon
content: Talindon Talindon was the central kingdom of Terrinoth's continent, founded by Arcus Penacor and ruled by the Penacor Kings for nearly two thousand years before its destruction in the First Darkness led to its rebirth as Terrinoth. History Arcus Penacor, a noble chieftain of one of the small village fiefdoms surviving The Years of Hunger, forged a confederation with neighboring fiefs under constant attack from brutal Orcish raiders and the Bloodguard Knights, convincing them to pool resources and fighters to secure a safer land. Their united armies vanquished their enemies, and Arcus, hailed as a hero, was declared king of the new realm of Talindon. It is from this event, nearly two thousand years past, that the Human calendar is dated. King Arcus proved a capable ruler, drafting charters that codified Talindon's governance — charters whose traces can still be seen in the codes the Daqan Lords enforce today — and raising funds for temples and great works of art while keeping the people safe with fortifications, border patrols, and chivalric orders. For nearly three centuries the realm flourished under the Penacor Kings, until the betrayal of Queen Riya and Rusticar Lorimor plunged King Jerlon Penacor into grief and, generations later, Llovar's Uthuk Y'llan armies brought the First Darkness to Talindon's shores, scattering its forces and slaying three generations of Penacors together at the Ashen Field. In the war's aftermath, Baron Daqan took the throne and, with Timmorran's counsel, declared that the realm of Talindon ought to pass into history with its rulers, proposing the new name of Terrinoth, or "Land of Steel." Sources Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), pp. 31–33 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35–37 The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 38

title: Tamalir Guildmaster
content: Tamalir Guildmaster The guilds of Tamalir wield tremendous power, governed by a council of Guildmasters each tasked with overseeing some part of their guild's business, or their guild in its entirety, who jealously guard their power and make life very difficult for any who cross them. Drawing a Guildmaster's ire can make a traveler's life suddenly and inexplicably difficult — prices raised unexpectedly, porters grown unruly, meals acquiring an upsetting flavor. Bloodshed is bad for business, so nonviolent methods are the first course of action when a Guildmaster wishes to remove a troublesome opponent, ranging from a complete denial of a guild's services to outright banishment from the city. Guildmasters rarely travel or fight alone, keeping several burly apprentices around to deal with dustups, and thanks to the extensive treasuries and personal armories of their guildhalls, they are usually well equipped and fear little within their city. Sources Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 155

title: Tamalir
content: Tamalir Tamalir is the largest and wealthiest of the eight Free Cities of Terrinoth, first founded of them all and first to be granted independence, through a charter granted by King Daqan himself. History Tamalir was the seat of the Elder Kings during their reign, and its prime location along the Flametail River has long made it a locus of trade for all of Terrinoth and a destination for migrants; all roads lead to Tamalir, and its people are proud of their heritage and prominence. Today the city is still in a state of recovery, devastated in both the Second and Third Darknesses, built upon the bones, ashes, and headstones of generations past — many of its buildings are relatively new, constructed only within the last few centuries, and it has yet to fully reach its previous majesty. Description More than one legendary adventure has started in one of Tamalir's many taverns, and it is said that every inhabitant has a story to tell of seeing some warrior or mage before their name became enshrined in history — no coincidence, given the city's special place in Terrinoth's history. Its dominion extends to encompass nearly the whole of Blackwing Swamp and Red Bridge, a famous crossing known for its gambling and rowdiness. The finest inns, grandest playhouses, and most skilled artisans of nearly every craft and art call Tamalir home, and little cannot be found in its seemingly endless shops and bazaars; should its substantial militia not suffice for defense, its leaders can call upon the vast swaths of adventurers and sellswords who frequent its back alleys and guild halls to field an army in mere hours. As the largest city in Terrinoth, trade dominates nearly every aspect of life there, and rather than being led by a mayor, Tamalir is governed by a council of Guildmasters, each considered an equal to the others, ruthless and cunning but utterly dedicated to their guilds and the city's well-being, vying with each other through huge public works and extravagant fairs to sway public opinion. Despite the destruction it has suffered, Tamalir remains the preeminent location for making contacts, outfitting expeditions, and learning of events in faraway lands — for anyone claiming to be an adventurer, it is likely their home away from home. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), pp. 149–150

title: Tanngnoster's Throne
content: Tanngnoster's Throne Tanngnoster's Throne is the seat of the King or Queen of Dunwarr, located in the depths of Dunwol Kenn Karnin within Thelgrim. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Tarakhe
content: Tarakhe Tarakhe, the Plague God, has but recently been defeated and cast back into his sleep of decay beneath Zanaga — an ancient creature of entropy and corruption, a bitter enemy to the Mahkim, Lizardmen, and Singhara alike. History Long ago, Tarakhe grew from the decline and ruin of the lizardman empire, feasting upon its decay and destruction. The god's minions rampaged across all of Zanaga and its countless cities, scourging most of its peoples from history. Only through the efforts of the Mahkim and the few surviving lizardmen was Tarakhe's total victory averted; robbed of power, the plague god fell back into his slumber. Legacy Though he was cast down, Tarakhe's influence upon the land remains. In the Noxious Glade, the god's power has given rise to fungus storms that can induce permanent frenzy and delusion in mortals, while the settlement of Onasan has been taken over by the touched of Tarakhe, twisted mutants only too eager to recruit new members into their family. Creatures too have become riddled with the plague god's influence, from the scar serpents of the Darkwater to the carrion eaters of the Umbral Forest that hang the rotting carcasses of their prey until they can slurp the putrid flesh from their bones. It is through these servants and a shadowy cult of followers that Tarakhe's legacy remains and still infects the fabric of Zanaga; only the Singhara and Mahkim continue to fight against the god's threat, their greatest fear being that Tarakhe's miasma will spread to the Three Skulls Trading Company or the town of Herman's Gulch, and perhaps mark a new rise to power for the god. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 253 Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Tarianor
content: Tarianor The fabled Floating City of Tarianor is the greatest shipyard in the whole of The Torue Albes, if not the world — more akin to an island than a city, built upon a huge stretch of coral reef and able to raise anchor and drift wherever it pleases. History Tarianor was the fevered dream of Captain Eddy Bloodkelp, a Gnome pirate who never had much luck due to her greater interest in nautical engineering than combat and pillaging. After her prey escaped when her ship ran aground on the reef, she had a wild vision of a seaport built upon it: a floating island that could raise anchor and drift wherever it pleased, or to wherever the most ships happened to be going. She gathered what was left of her desperate crew and managed to inflame them with her vision; with their combined skills at shipbuilding and engineering, and perhaps a little help from magic, they started work. It took five long years — and the coffers of dozens of equally fevered investors — but finally the Floating City was open for business, and it was a runaway success. The Queen of Dallak made an offer to turn the Floating City into a proper city of the Torue Albes and declare it the royal shipyard. Description Tarianor is now the most valuable shipyard in all the world. The war galleons of Lorimor and the Albesian Royal Navy are produced here, along with vessels for other commercial interests — the Gnome crew still retain a piratical bent, and are generally open to special contracts with no questions asked. It can even act as transportation, ferrying groups with only small riverboats across dangerous open waters to destinations along the western coasts of the continent. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 224

title: Teleportation Rune
content: Teleportation Rune A user of one of these shards can teleport either themself or a small object they concentrate on a short distance. It is safest to teleport to a location within line of sight; while users may have the ability to teleport through walls, if they materialize in the same space as a solid object, it can lead to terrible injury. Teleportation runes are especially rare to find, as they are highly sought after by all manner of assassin, criminal, and adventurer. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 121

title: Telor
content: Telor Telor, the Port of Terrinoth, begins just beyond the walls of Archaut and extends to the Kingless Coast, encompassing the northern edge of Eventide Forest and the southern portion of the Greatwood. Telor's greatest feature is its coast, the largest extent of civilized coastline in Terrinoth, and it uniquely among the baronies maintains a small naval fleet against pirates and other seaborne threats. Its most prosperous city, Jendra's Harbor, sits on the southern side of Kingless Bay where the river of Korina's Tears meets the sea — one of the few reliable ports for ships arriving from across the sea, hosting travelers from Lorimor and as far as Al-Kalim, and a departure point for ships bound for the Torue Albes or, occasionally, Zanaga. Though Baron Echard officially rules Telor, Countess Sela's stewardship of Jendra's Harbor has granted her greater influence throughout Terrinoth and beyond, to Echard's frustration as he frets away his days in the crumbling halls of Grandor's Hold, while Sela cultivates relationships with earls and barons, foreign merchants and princes, and even the Empress of Lorimor. Though Telor benefits greatly from Jendra's Harbor's wealth and trade, its position on the Kingless Coast also invites cursed artifacts, mysterious priests, and wicked things concealed under long cloaks and deep hoods. While the Harbor remains busy, many of the coast's smaller ports and villages lie abandoned and half-ruined, victims of fierce storms or ravening merriods and other horrid creatures of the deep — even the lighthouse of Calem's Peak is said to be haunted by the spirits of its mad keeper and his many victims. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Temoth
content: Temoth Temoth, Keeper of the Bazaar, is the vizier who rules Trader's Fort and ostensibly controls the port lords of The Thieves' Coast, sending huge trade caravans piled with goods farther into the Caliphate. In reality, Eyrat Five Fingers and the thieves' guild have as much say as Temoth does regarding what transpires along the coastline; it is said that for every two coins that line Temoth's purse, one goes to Eyrat. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), pp. 245–246

title: Temple of Four Storms
content: Temple of Four Storms The Temple of Four Storms sits on the single island at the center of Lake Falstar in Carthridge, a seldom-visited ancient monument to a long-forgotten religion. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 145

title: Teno'tek
content: Teno'tek Teno'tek is a living ziggurat whose location changes from season to season, remaining a center for the Lizardmen of Zanaga, although they have long forgotten how to open its great sun gates and venture inside. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Terror Rune
content: Terror Rune None can fathom why the dragons crafted terror runes, given their own innate baleful nature. Some Greyhaven scholars wonder if they know more of the Ynfernael and its growing threat to Mennara, or if there are creatures beyond the Molten Heath that are to dragons as dragons are to mortal beings, and thus needed a way to ignore their fearsome effects. Adventurers fortunate enough to possess these runes find them invaluable when exploring the dark catacombs within The Mistlands or facing down the creatures of the Ru. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 121

title: The Academy
content: The Academy The Academy is Nerekhall's renowned school, a trusted wellspring of cultured learning where society's elite can engage in exotic experiments and research rare tomes free of petty scrutiny owing to their exalted rank. Its faculty seem even more eager than their students to explore every aspect of magic and other arts in their quest to establish Nerekhall's great legacy. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149

title: The Ailatar
content: The Ailatar The Ailatar, or Plain of Stars, is a clearing near Lithelin marking the place where the Elves descended to Mennara, from which her followers can see Latariana and the other glimmering lights in the night sky. Sources Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 174

title: The Ashen Field
content: The Ashen Field At the Ashen Field in 487, the Host of Thorns fell upon an army led by King Falladir Penacor and his sons. They fought valiantly — a blow from Falladir's sword nearly cleaved the head from Melinesh the Cruel and Terrible, while Prince Parren drove a lance through the heart of Nashaia King's Bane — but Llovar had numbers, magic, and malice on his side, and by the end of the day the three Penacors lay dead upon the field together with the soldiers who had pledged to follow their banner. A small group of ragged survivors, led by the noble young Baron Daqan, escaped the slaughter, saved only by the fury of a great tempest that prevented Llovar from running them down; they rode off through the pelting rain to warn Timmorran of Llovar's renewed force. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 37

title: The Aymhelin
content: The Aymhelin The Aymhelin is the ancient forest realm of the Latari Elves, a woodland region that to outsiders might look undeveloped and sparsely populated, but which in truth has been carefully harmonized between nature and civilization for millennia. When looking down from the top of the eastern Darnati mountains, it would be easy to mistake the Aymhelin for wild, uncontrolled vegetation, the kind that in Human lands would suggest an unprosperous, undeveloped people. In the case of the Elves, the reverse is true: each gleaming spire, each brilliantly sparkling stone pathway, each dense copse of stately trees, each beautifully manicured acre of prairie, and each crystal-clear pond and lake has been carefully harmonized to bring nature and civilization into near-perfect accord. It allows the Elves who dwell in the cities to commune with nature, those who live in the verdant forest townships to easily partake in the myriad benefits of a modern civilization, and the entire nation to rally together under threat of foreign or supernatural invaders. The heart of the Aymhelin is the capital Lithelin and its guardian monument Caelcira. Other notable regions include The Bloodwood and its hidden township of Methras, the frontier fortress of Blackthorn Grove, the Selenic Coast and its port of First Fall, the mineral-rich Darnati Highlands, the mysterious Deepwood, and the fertile Thalian Glades. Sources The Aymhelin (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 174

title: The Baruk Range
content: The Baruk Range The Baruk Range is the southern region of The Broken Plains, a wide spread of mountains and dormant volcanoes as well as smaller flatlands that extend to the rocky edge of Zanaga. Several rushing rivers flow from the mountains into the Zanagan jungles, nurturing the lush greenery there and proving quite favorable to mining efforts — even simple panning can produce nuggets of exceptional purity and size. Tracing them upriver, though, only ends in mystery, for they emerge from the mountains as if holes had been poked in the bare rock; some Orcs revere the waters as the Blood of the Baruk, claiming they have powerful abilities over life and death. The rivers do seem to be part of a lively battle along the southern lands, one that likely will never have a victor: the jungles and mountains themselves seem to be caught in an ongoing battle for dominance, with vegetation extending into the Plains on thick branches and vines while the rock pushes back with frequent landslides. As the war goes on, the settlements and hunting grounds of the Orcs and the varied inhabitants of Zanaga move as their lands wax and wane, and clashes between them are as ancient as their oral histories; remains of these battles, along with magical relics and other valuables, can be found everywhere along the fluid border. Even without this war, the Baruk is dangerous for other reasons — though it is as rough as any other region in the Plains, there is something that instills brutality and savagery in all who live here. Even non-Orc settlers grow bloodthirsty within a season, though this diminishes somewhat after leaving the area. Even other Orcs rarely speak of the tribe that resides here, Baruk Gro Urak, only to say its members are to be avoided and not trusted. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 198

title: The Battle of Enfreil
content: The Battle of Enfreil On the Plains of Enfreil, Glaciel Snowstar and his companions, returning with a flight of dragons at their back, fought a final battle against Malcorne and his corrupted Daewyl followers — in the world's most desperate hour, their combined forces ultimately achieved victory and struck down the dark Elven lord, ending The War of the Shadow Tear. The remaining Daewyl retreated from the combined Elven and draconic forces, hoping to hide themselves away, but the victors could not afford to let the corruption spread and hunted down their foes to burn them from the face of the world; Malcorne's wretched tribe, the Malcari, was nearly extinguished in the slaughter. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: The Bloodwood
content: The Bloodwood The Bloodwood is a forest within The Aymhelin formerly a barren, desolate plain where a horribly outnumbered army of Elves met and repelled more than ten thousand barbaric invaders. History When the Elves later returned to dispose of the legions of rotting warriors, they discovered that mysterious saplings, as red as blood, had sprouted among the dead — the origin of the Bloodwood and the source of its name. Description The Bloodwood's gruesome history has become a source of pride for all the hunters, foresters, bowyers, fletchers, scouts, and hermits who call it home. Full of densely populated trees that run for leagues in every direction, the Bloodwood is an ideal place to learn tracking and forest combat, how to lathe arrows from its unique saplings, and methods for hunting the deer and boar that help feed all of the Elves in the Aymhelin. The mystical woods are also home to a community of Elves who live in the hidden township of Methras. Sources The Bloodwood (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: The Borderlands
content: The Borderlands Bounded by the Daqan Baronies, The Aymhelin, and the Orc tribes of The Broken Plains, the Borderlands mark the edge of civilized Terrinoth, within The Ru Steppes and Beyond. Description Here, lush farmland, thick forests, and green hills give way to seemingly endless grasslands that stretch to the dark horizon in all directions. Those settlements stubborn enough to survive here are pale reflections of the towns and bulwarks to the west, and the people who inhabit them spend their days forever fearful of what might march forth from the eastern expanses. Ancient watch forts still stand sentinel along the edge of the Borderlands, their true purpose all but forgotten. Halfland Keep, the largest of Daqan's border keeps, stands at the crossroads between west and east, and it is here that many heroes gain their first taste of what the Ru has to offer, commanded by Edlund. The Borderlands is also a center for bounty hunters. Despite the presence of the watch forts, monsters stalk out of the wilds to invade the west; towns and lords are always offering up coin for their extermination. Adventurers who accept such an offer might hunt down packs of ravenous Flesh Rippers, diminutive but savage night carrion, or hulking ynferoc wyrmkin, often following the trail of slaughter such things leave in their wake. Some more enterprising individuals pay for capture rather than destruction; Calivar's Traveling Carnival of Horrors has made good business trading in the exotic creatures of the wastes. Some dangers are not so easily defined or dealt with, like the blight known only as The Tangle. Sources The Borderlands (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 209–210

title: The Broken Plains
content: The Broken Plains The Broken Plains were once a vast, rolling prairie until, many ages ago, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions shattered the flatlands of the east into a chaotic collection of razor-sharp crags jutting skyward, bottomless ravines cutting into the ground, and landslides that rain down from huge, unstable mountain ranges. Table of Contents Overview Description Sources Overview Although much of the original fertile grasslands and roaming herds of animals were spared the worst of the devastation, the cracked valleys and rockslides have exposed some of the richest, and most easily accessible, deposits of precious gemstones found anywhere in Mennara. The quakes that ripped the surface apart are rare these days, but the combination of wide flatlands and rough, torn landscapes makes the Broken Plains the perfect home for Orcs, for in it they have a land that mirrors their own tough nature. The Elves even hold that the Orcs were birthed there, themselves a product of the same primordial cataclysms that gave the land its name. Description The wealth and bounty of the Plains allowed the Orc clans to thrive, while the terrain helped them defend against the near constant siege from treasure-hunting dragons, invaders from the Ru Steppes to the north, mercenary armies of Humans, creatures emerging from the jungles of Zanaga, and other threats. The Orcs are divided into large tribes (see Orcs of the Broken Plains), each claiming a swath of land and the landmarks and hunting grounds within for themselves, in regions such as The Baruk Range, the Erd Riverlands, the Ghur Highlands, the Kul Valleys, the Lok Cliffs, the Mok Plateau, and the Ugluk Badlands. Sources The Broken Plains (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 197 The Orcs of the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 197–198

title: The Charg'r Wastes
content: The Charg'r Wastes North of the Ru, the steppe of The Ru Steppes and Beyond gives way to stony ground, shale dunes, and saw-toothed hills known as the Charg'r Wastes. Storms constantly tear at the earth, and lightning rips open the sky as the mournful keening of the wind rends the air — the Borderlands are a verdant land of plenty compared to this desolate desert of stone and storm. It is a region where few settlements have ever taken root. On the edges of the wastes, foundry cities of the Dunwarr Dwarves gnaw away at deposits of lightning quartz, the charged stone useful for weapons and tools alike, common only in the storm-lashed Charg'r. Beyond these few sparks of civilization, only the hardiest monsters and most eccentric hermits make their home, sheltering underground to protect themselves from the endless bitter weather. One of the few features to endure among the desolation is the winding trail known as the Road of Skulls. Sources The Charg'r Wastes (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 210–211

title: The Citadel
content: The Citadel The Citadel is Terrinoth's center of government and law, located in Archaut and once the castle of King Daqan. Overview After the Daqan Lords return to their baronies each year, the Warden of the Citadel executes their orders and oversees the day-to-day matters of state until the next gathering — for the last two decades this has been Gravia Kein, who has served the Daqan Lords and the people of Terrinoth with honor and passion. The servants of the Citadel proudly wear the heraldry of a gold crown on a blue field, the ancient badge of King Daqan. Description The Citadel itself is an imposing structure, the best-fortified keep in all of Terrinoth, its towering alabaster walls looming over Archaut as a constant reminder of the kingdom's power and glory. Though each baron bears responsibility for defending the realm, the Citadel also maintains its own small standing army under the Warden's leadership, the last line of defense should Archaut itself come under attack. It also hosts the few knightly orders that swear fealty to Terrinoth as a whole rather than any single baron, foremost among them the Marshals of the Citadel — each a skilled warrior and expert scholar well versed in Terrinoth's laws, empowered to serve as judge, jury, and executioner in delivering justice against traitorous nobles, highwaymen, goblin warbands, and practitioners of forbidden magic. In these times even the Marshals are scarcely sufficient for the many threats emerging across Terrinoth, and in recent years Warden Kein and her officers have employed itinerant adventurers and mercenaries against suspected dragon cults, Ferrox swarms, goblin raiders, and fugitive necromancers. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 141–142

title: The Darkwood
content: The Darkwood The roaming Darkwood is a massive and ancient woodland within the Aenlong, dense with mossy tree trunks and thick undergrowth full of ferns and fungi, one of two locations that lie within the Aenlong yet also sometimes cross into the mortal realm. The Darkwood has no fixed position in the Aenlong, but alters its position and the limit of its borders according to an unheard and random rhythm — a challenge to the non-Elven imagination, for how a physical place can exist outside the purview of reality is not easily explained; the Elves themselves obfuscate the issue, claiming that such locations are simply understood as both spiritual and physical. Sources The Myths of Creation (Tales of Darkness), p. 25

title: The Darnati Highlands
content: The Darnati Highlands The Darnati Highlands lie far to the west of The Aymhelin, close to the southernmost plains of Lorimor, where the great forest begins to thin and hills and rocky outcroppings break up the swaths of immense trees. This rough terrain makes the Elves who live in the Darnati Highlands a particularly hardy stock. Marking boulders and cliff faces like pearlescent scars, treasured moonstone is found in relative abundance here, furnishing the material for some of the Elves' most wondrous armaments; among the artisans who make their home here are miners and smiths who produce many of the Aymhelin Elves' razor-sharp weapons and intricately fitted sets of armor. These items are so extraordinary, effectual, and cherished that none dare insult or ostracize the smiths who forge them — making the Darnati the only Elves truly immune to the rigid caste politics and tangled intrigues that plague the Lithelin court. Nestled among the highlands are the ancient stone temples of the Darnati warriors, a mysterious order of mystical adepts who channel their spiritual energies into amazing displays of grace, speed, balance, and power — often referred to as the Swordsmasters, these monks are among the most feared warriors in all of Mennara, and from their modest monastery they hold perpetual vigil over the highlands. Sources The Darnati Highlands (The Aymhelin), p. 177

title: The Deepwood
content: The Deepwood The Deepwood is among the most mysterious, magical, and vital places in The Aymhelin, a miracle of both enchantment and nature at the heart of the dense forest. Table of Contents Description Sources Description The heart of the Deepwood is a collection of towering, powerful trees whose fibers are as strong as steel and bend but never seem to break; these trees grow agelessly, stretching ever taller and spreading their limbs ever wider, until the canopy of the forest obscures almost all light from its floor. Nearby lies The Fountain of Purity, near The Thalian Glades. If the trees are the heart of the forest, then its soul is the collection of gently glowing ferns and fungi that dimly light the darkness like hundreds of small candles. Despite millennia of study, the apothecaries and sorcerers of the Aymhelin are still trying to truly understand this unique flora, as beautiful as it is mysterious, that occurs nowhere else in the world. The Deepwood's magical nature also draws the attention of non-Elves: foreign forces constantly send emissaries, spies, or raiding parties, or offer lucrative contracts for samples of the life that grows uniquely here, though few survive long enough to actually catch a glimpse of its dark beauty. To spare the lives of those foolhardy enough to attempt the journey, but also to fend off greater threats, the Deepwood Archers were established to catch or repel any who dare try to infiltrate the forest. Sources The Deepwood (The Aymhelin), pp. 177–178

title: The Endless Ocean
content: The Endless Ocean The Endless Ocean lies directly to the west of Redwater, from which no ship has returned with tales of landfall. There are many tales of monstrous creatures emerging from the deeps, alluring songs heard in the black of night, spectral vessels glowing with blue fire whose sailors cry out to turn around before it becomes too late, and more. Perhaps even more terrible gods exist here, awaiting the foolish and daring to enter their domains. To look to the west is to see the great unknown, where blue waters turn dark and crimson in the setting sun, and to wonder which daring crew will discover what is on the other side. Sources Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 223

title: The Erd Riverlands
content: The Erd Riverlands The Erd Riverlands, within The Broken Plains, are uniquely covered in marshes and waterways — the relative higher ground of most of the Plains allows for hundreds of rivers to drain along here into the western sea. Orcs elsewhere say the Erd is where the Broken Plains weeps as its peoples grow more and more tame from dealing peacefully with other races; other Orcs instead say it is where the land bleeds, and that the land and its peoples are slowly dying as the old ways are lost and forgotten — though this latter saying does have something to support it. The waters here range from rushing rapids to slow, almost-sedate streams, but they are all flaked with glimmering crimson strands from sources none can detect. There are no known mineral sources upriver that could allow for this, and many assume there is something below the waterways being gradually stripped away; grains caught in thinly woven nets grow dim and grey soon after removal from the Erd, then dissolve to dust. Many Greyhaven scholars believe something magical exists — or lives — under the Erd, and that as the rivers flow, the process is eroding and removing something precious from the Broken Plains, though they cannot agree whether this is a good or bad thing for these lands. The tribe of the Erd is Erd'Lantir Urak. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 198–199

title: The Everliving Engine
content: The Everliving Engine The Everliving Engine is Waiqar's most heinous vehicle of destruction, a machine most foul housed deep below the volcanic caves under the ruins of Kelipa in The Mistlands. Its bone gears grind endlessly with a sound that reverberates across the Mistlands — so great is its mechanical noise that, on still nights, it can be heard dozens of leagues away, as far as the border of the Barony of Carthridge. Its true purpose is known only to Waiqar and the archlich Revik, who oversees its operation, but with every tick the barrier between the world of the living and the dead weakens: the undead everywhere feel themselves empowered, if only by the faintest margin, and new, unimagined horrors manifest to plague the world of the living. Those who displease Waiqar are fed to this terrible machine, and their screams mingle with each tick until they are subsumed entirely. No mortal can say exactly what it means to be consumed by the Everliving Engine, but it is a fate dire enough to strike fear into the hearts of those who serve the Undying One. Sources Castle Dalibor (The Mistlands), pp. 161–162

title: The First
content: The First The First are the entities from whom even mighty gods owe their own existence, greater than gods in potential yet lesser for lacking personality and form — neither singular nor plural, neither male nor female, existing before there was barons, wars, earth, stars, or time. Description The legends are not clear as to whether the Void came into being with the First or the First created the Void; some interpretations suggest they are one and the same, and whatever the truth, the Void is the space within which all later creation took place. Without breath, tongue, or lips, the First are said to have uttered songs or poems — the Lays of the First — that shaped the Void, defining its potential and giving birth to all things; these verses described ideal forms and natures, and Elves insist that echoes of the Lays can still be heard in the rhythms of nature, nourishing spirits like food, in the tradition that the Wealdweavers work their craft. The First conjured three distinct existences from the Void, called the Planes of Power: the highest, the Empyrean, a plane of perfection; the lowest, the Ynfernael, populated by monstrous entities that crave to visit torture and degradation upon mortals; and between them, the Aenlong, to which the plane of physical existence is connected. The First then set into motion the Verto Magica, without which everything would be fixed in place and time would stand still. According to Emorial, in his final rebellion against the First, they were tyrants, afraid of being usurped by their own children — the false hope offered to Latariana was merely a means to keep the Elves subservient and obsequious for eternity. The Latari Elves who followed Malcorne came to share this view, styling their rebellion as a war against the First's tyranny. Sources The Myths of Creation (Tales of Darkness), pp. 24–25 The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 28

title: The Fountain of Purity
content: The Fountain of Purity The Fountain of Purity is a natural spring in a rich, life-filled forest near The Thalian Glades, said by legend to be the spring the Latari used to purify The Aymhelin after the Third Darkness. It is said that while its water nourishes the pure of heart, it devours the wicked from within, rejuvenating old beauty and cleansing the forests of the shadow-touched. The cults of the Wealdweavers tend these waters and the Aymhelin saplings nourished by them. The Fountain of Purity is forbidden to all but the Elves, though nobles from lands all over Mennara have sent messengers to Caelcira begging King Aenoeth for draughts from one of the many streams that run down into the glades. Over the centuries, various desperate — and greedy — beings have attempted to take control of the mystical waters by force, only to face the combined fury of the Wealdweavers and the Forest Guardians sworn to protect nature. Sources The Deepwood (The Aymhelin), p. 178

title: The Frontier
content: The Frontier The Frontier is the name given to the north and west stretches of the Dunwarr Mountains, where the caverns of the Deeps narrow and shrink and the land begins to slope down to the frozen, ice-locked coast. Here, many Dwarves still live above ground, making their living as farmers, hunters, and foresters; though their kin describe them as foolhardy and a little odd for wanting to live on Mennara's surface, these Frontier Dwarves tend to enjoy the thin, clear light of the sun and the touch of frosty air on their cheeks. To the west, alpine valleys are warm enough in summer for the Dwarves to grow oats, wheat, barley, and other cereal crops; members of the Brewers' Guild construct terraced fields and study granaries alongside fortified manor houses built into the rocky cliffs, and the Frontier's farms would reportedly be enough to feed the whole Dunwarr nation if the Guild did not keep the best grains for beer. Further north lies The Northern Coast, where even the sparse farms and outposts of the Frontier dwindle away. Sources The Frontier (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 190

title: The Gate of Years
content: The Gate of Years The Gate of Years is the passage through which Emorial marched his host of rebellious Elves, Lady Latariana at his side, believing they would enter the halls of The First to demand dominion over the Empyrean's spheres. Instead, though they did not realize it at the time, the Elves found themselves crossing over into the Aenlong, beginning the long, hazardous march that would end in their exile to Mennara. Sources The Elves (Tales of Darkness), p. 27

title: The Ghur Highlands
content: The Ghur Highlands The Ghur Highlands are a series of tall peaks in the northern reaches of The Broken Plains. Below the heights, staggered mesas fall to lower levels in a series of sheer drops, some of which have winding trails that allow for somewhat easier passage into the Highlands. The Ghur also extends north into the Ru, but what name the Uthuk use for it in their own foul language is best left unknown. This area includes some of the coldest points of the Plains, with snow-topped mountains that often provide huge avalanches — some so powerful as to drop snow to the edges of The Kul Valleys, but also draw along chunks of rare metals torn from the cliffsides far above. Those seeking out these riches must contend with several tribes of Orcs, though many valuables lay just underneath piles of broken trees and loose soil awaiting discovery; rumors abound of other treasures in the thick runoffs, such as lost artifacts of Elven creation or ancient weapons still as sharp as the day they were forged, but none have been presented properly to verify the claims. Nearly every season new peaks here are uncovered, so maps in the Ghur are even less accurate than usual compared with the rest of the Broken Plains. Those seeking to explore this region have to rely more on examining current conditions, such as fresh trails, than on planning their journey in advance; hiring a local Orc guide is not only encouraged but mandatory, for if the Orcs of Ghur'zhun Urak do not welcome such "guests" into the mountains, the visit may wind up quite short and unpleasant. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 199

title: The Great Cataclysm
content: The Great Cataclysm No one knows what caused the Great Cataclysm, a series of quakes and upheavals of unprecedented proportion that wracked Mennara several thousand years after the Elves' arrival, washing away great swaths of land or shattering them into archipelagos. Scholars have advanced numerous theories about its origins: some say Ynfernael energies tore the land apart, or that it was the work of the Daewyl in an act of revenge; others suggest it was a terrible mishap resulting from Elven rites designed to seal the remaining Ynfernael portals shut, or simply a fact of the world's nature. In the wake of the destruction, the younger races — the ancestors of Dwarves, Orcs, and Humans — began to play a greater role in the shaping of history, ushering in The Years of Hunger. Sources The Troubled Rise of the Younger Races (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: The Great Sand Sea
content: The Great Sand Sea Beyond the walls of the city-states, the shelter of the Blessed Valley, and the windswept Thieves' Coast, the desert of Al-Kalim stretches out toward arid mountains and shadowy canyons — the parched wilderness that makes up the majority of the Caliphate, where water is more precious than gold and wasteland predators prey upon the unwary. Table of Contents Perils of the Desert Lost Cities Sources Perils of the Desert Away from the cities, Al-Kalim is a land endlessly dying of thirst; water is greedily stolen by the bone-dry air and hot sands, and travelers must guard their supplies against bandits if they are to have any hope of crossing the parched distances between settlements. The sun itself can also be an enemy, and many travelers have lost both their sight and their reason simply for lack of shade, a malady known as light blindness that affects both body and soul. Then there are the desert winds and the maelstroms they bring — sandstorms lash the deserts, cities, and mountains of Al-Kalim, so vast and terrible they can eclipse the sun for days or even months on end. All of these perils are constants that travelers must accept, but even if they survive them, a multitude of more nefarious dangers lurk in the cursed and haunted corners of the Caliphate. The Shadowsgate Rift is reputed to be a haunt of lost souls, spirits cast away from the Sun God's blessed gaze, denied the glory of A'tar and skulking in the depths of the Rift, pining for the light, hatefully descending upon trespassers to devour the warmth of the sun they might still wear upon their flesh. In the Valley of Sandstorms, the winds can flay a traveler to the bone, and in the Desert of Eternity, a maze of mirages can lead adventurers in circles until they perish. Lost Cities After the coming of A'tar, many cities ruled by the Djinni were abandoned and consumed by the desert sands. These lost places are now haunts of monsters, brigands, and worse, yet a measure of the magic of the Djinni still resides within them, and there are those who seek them out for the secrets they hold: the Beggar's Maze in the White Dunes, the golden Spire of the Phoenix in the Grey Wastes, and stranger still, cities transformed by magic into mirages or lifted up into the sky to escape the holy fires that consumed their brethren — among the greatest of these mythical places stand the City of Faith, the City of Dreams, and the City of Clouds. These gleaming bastions can appear as if from nowhere like a desert mirage, one minute little but a haze of light, the next as real as the ground beneath one's feet; Djinni still rule in these places, and to enter them is to enter a perilous realm where reality itself cannot be trusted, the Djinni being always eager for new playthings. The rewards, however, can be great, for these mythical cities offer knowledge and magical secrets lost to the world of mortals. Sources The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), pp. 246–247

title: The Green Vale
content: The Green Vale Amid the ice and snow of the far north of Isheim is a hidden realm: the Green Vale, home of the last Salishwyrd city, in stark contrast to the surrounding lands of The White Death. It is perhaps Isheim's greatest secret, and rightly so, for the Elves who built it millennia ago did so to escape the Rime Storm that had destroyed their empire and to protect themselves from all outside dangers. Few have ever managed to reach the Green Vale, for one must first brave the horrors of the Frozen Wastes and then pierce the magical blizzards that surround it. Among the conflicting tales that have reached the southern lands, it is said the Green Vale is a place of potent magic, ruled over by an immortal king — a lost exile of a forgotten age who awaits the time when the Rime Storm might be defeated and the Salishwyrd rise again from the frozen ashes of their empire. In preparation for this day, the Salishwyrd Elves have become masters of healing and life magics, hoarding artifacts of sorcery from the dawn of Mennara, and there is little they cannot mend of flesh or mind. The tales also tell of a bitter war fought between the Salishwyrd and the Ice Wyrms, creatures some believe to be the feral offspring of dragons twisted by the Rime Storm. The ice wyrms seek to devour the Green Vale, as if they were the living embodiment of the Rime Storm, and they constantly seek its location. Heroes bold enough to travel into this wilderness might find themselves caught between the cold ambitions of Scarsha the ice wyrm queen and the immortal Salishwyrd, who seek only the return of summer to their people. Sources Realm of the White Death (Isheim), p. 236

title: The Greywood
content: The Greywood The Greywood lies just to the northeast of the Selenic Sea, not far from where The Aymhelin empties into the Broken Plains — a taboo realm of unnerving legends, where realities unpredictably bleed together and the veil between Mennara and the Aenlong becomes thin enough for creatures to easily pass from one to the other. Within its shadowed trails wander creatures that were never meant to set foot upon this plane. Here, those who seek favors from the Fae may be able to bargain for whatever they seek. The Elves hold a careful, perpetual vigil around the Greywood, doing their best to stop mortals from entering the dank, lightless forest, but also to prevent anything from leaving the trees as well; much to their dismay, the Elves lack the power or ability to purge the forest of its mystical threat, so instead they greet the unnatural creatures that try to emerge from these woods with maximum aggression. Sources Selenic Coast (The Aymhelin), p. 177

title: The Heart
content: The Heart The Heart lies at the center of The Molten Heath, an isolated collection of volcanoes from whose flanks lava rivers flow, inundating the surrounding lands in a constantly changing morass of molten and cooling rock. Description A maze of lava flows and molten streams cuts through a nightmare landscape of razor-edged obsidian outcroppings and drifting dunes of rock ash. Higher up, among the volcanoes' calderas, the dragons make their roosts: younger drakes live in the cooling lava tubes and caves along the flanks of the mountains, while the elder wyrms haunt the burning craters at the very summits. The Heart and its immediate vicinity is a hellish landscape of fire and smoke that only a dragon could withstand — constant eruptions unleash vast lava flows that never truly cool, instead filling in canyons and gorges with vast lakes of searing liquid stone, across which dragons wing, hunting the Salamanders and perching upon the charred islands to rest and converse with others of their kind. Little is known of dragon society, mostly because few outsiders have managed to travel here, observe them, and survive the experience. Scholars do know that the dragons of the Molten Heath — unlike the feral beasts found in much of Terrinoth — are fiendishly intelligent, and they dominate the scattered tribes of Dragon Hybrids that roam the ash dunes and basalt slopes. The histories even tell of a Dragon Rex, the most powerful of her kind, who rules over the entirety of the Molten Heath. Millennia of eruptions have pushed the Heart above the Verdant Ring. Slopes of shattered basalt and chunks of scoria edge the Heart, punctuated by the occasional smoke-belching crevasse and bubbling hot springs. Sources The Domain of Dragons (The Molten Heath), pp. 193–194

title: The Hollow Kingdom
content: The Hollow Kingdom The Hollow Kingdom is the name given to the remains of an empire a tribe of Dwarves built in The Ru long before the rise of the Locust Horde, preceding even the First Darkness — the empire's true name is lost to history. Here and there, way markers bearing angular Dwarven runes point the way to cities that no longer exist, bridges spanning empty rivers, or forests of pillars that once supported mighty temples. Merchants and scholars pay well for artifacts from the Hollow Kingdom, for they are often wondrous in their design. The true wealth of the lost empire remains hidden, however, waiting for those who can solve the riddle of its ruins and find the Hollow Kingdom's clockwork capital, rumored to have burrowed into the earth in the last days of the Dwarves' empire. Sources The Ru and the Darkness (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 210

title: The Karok Doum
content: The Karok Doum The Karok Doum is the abandoned nation of a lost Dwarven kingdom at the far edge of The Molten Heath, where long-slumbering mountains brood over the scattered ruins of Dwarven civilization. Description Shattered and seared by dragon fire, the fallen walls and crumbling towers of Karok Zon, Dorgol Visoth, and Morath az Moran — the great capital of the lost kingdom — yet stand, their empty windows keeping watch upon their abandoned nation. Although much of the cities have been reduced to fire-scarred rubble, the dragons could not destroy Dwarven craft completely: each Dwarven settlement was encircled by a wall of obsidian, stamped with runes of fire so that it would never melt. These walls stand as ever, even if their iron gates have fallen, and are tall enough to be visible for miles across the blasted expanse of the Heath. Once inside, any would-be adventurers find broad streets radiating out from the center of the city, lined with the shattered basalt remains of the low, broad Dwarven houses, inns, smithies, and granaries — forges and smithies took advantage of the more gentle volcanic activity that lingered at the edges of the Heath. In the center of each city, the brass and gold towers have been seared down to slag-tipped stumps by dragonfire, and one can even find the hardened puddles of molten gold in the streets, a king's fortune forgotten under a coat of drifting ash. It is possible that beneath the ruined towers, a greater treasure could be found. During the Years of Fire, the Dwarves were forced to leave many wonders behind as they fled their kingdom; rumors abound of secret vaults full of gold and jewels, or weapons and armor made powerful by the earliest rune-craft. Some Dwarves even believe that one of the cities still contains the hidden workshop of Helka the Bold, mother of the Dwarves and first of the runescribes. Setting foot in the remains of the Karok Doum is not for the faint of heart, however. The ruins of its cities are infested with all manner of foul creatures: great Salamanders nest within the walls, while smaller char-worms and ripper spiders keep to the shadows, waiting for their unsuspecting prey to let down their guard before striking. Some of the smaller drakes also prefer to live among these ruins instead of the center of the Molten Heath, where they can avoid the domination of their elders. Sources The Karok Doum (The Molten Heath), p. 194

title: The Kul Valleys
content: The Kul Valleys As The Broken Plains was rent asunder in ancient upheavals, the land itself became cracked as if immense, taloned claws had gripped the surface and pulled it apart — many believe the Kul gave the Plains its name, for indeed it is a land broken apart and apparently never to be healed. Most of these cracks are hundreds of hands deep, sometimes even a league or more in rare places; some of the valleys are many leagues wide as well, enough to support the Orcs who live within as if they were flatlands. The land within the Kul is largely barren, and so game and useful vegetation is limited and must be carefully cultivated for the Orcs within to survive. Few Orcs who live within the Kul ever leave, and most live out their entire lives below the surface. There is trading with surface Orcs and other travelers, mostly through rope-drawn planks to carry goods up and down, but there are some areas where the valleys have paths allowing for easier walking to the land above. The cracks lining valley walls sometimes lead to thick veins of silver and even liquid pools of quicksilver, allowing the Kul Orcs to successfully trade for any essentials they lack. The tribe of the Kul is Jer'Kul Urak. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 200

title: The Lok Cliffs
content: The Lok Cliffs The Lok is little-known outside of Orcish society, far from the so-called "civilized" lands studied by the scholars of Terrinoth and Al-Kalim. The range emerges out of The Ugluk Badlands like a wave of jagged, cyclopean rocks, as if a gigantic castle collapsed into rubble and its remains scattered along hundreds of leagues. Few dare eke out an existence here, with most Orcs of Lok Urak living along the western edges where the land flattens and game is more plentiful. Those who do live in the peaks are solitary, as though guarding secrets they dare not reveal to the rest of Mennara. What might be found to the east of the Lok is a matter of speculation and argument: Greyhaven historians point to decaying parchments that tell of glorious kingdoms and powerful mages, but this is based on oddly dressed visitors many ages ago and their unsubstantiated claims. Some stone carvings discovered in Zanaga seem to indicate there is nothing but death and danger beyond the range, but that is a wise statement concerning much of Mennara for the foolish and unprepared. One day adventurers will travel over the Lok, perhaps with the aid of the Orcs living there, and the truth may be known. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 200

title: The Lost Keeps
content: The Lost Keeps The Lost Keeps are a series of fortresses and watchtowers a ruler of the Lorimor Empire long ago decreed be constructed in the southern regions of Lorimor, where the exiled lovers Riya Penacor and Rusticar Lorimor had traveled in search of a new home. History The task was difficult, but this was when Lorimor was at its height, and nothing seemed beyond its reach; long wagon trains transported tons of granite to the construction sites, along with soldiers, masons, and smiths. The effort took years, but finally dozens of outposts had been erected along the peninsula's thinnest width, serving the empire well for ages — such was the reputation of Lorimor's forces that none dared attack it. Some believe the hubris of the emperor in a later era was to blame for assuming the keeps were impregnable; others suspect clerical errors in the recording of messages from the keeps. All that is known is that when a fresh contingent of recruits who had traveled to a southern outpost to replace the watch arrived at their destination, the keep was empty — there were no bodies or signs of struggle, and the armories seemed complete. Every other keep proved the same. Entire armies marched south, fearing attack, but none came. Description From that day, the outposts were left empty, the empire's finest augurs and divinators having proclaimed the sites were cursed. Currently, the keeps are mostly ruins that serve as welcome resting places for travelers. Winds blow colder through them, however, and wines seem to become sour overnight; sleep is difficult and filled with terrible dreams of past ages and terrible betrayals. Few visitors stay a second night, as most sense that whatever now resides in the keeps does not desire company. Sources Lorimor (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 221–222

title: The Mistlands
content: The Mistlands The Mistlands are the cursed domain of Waiqar the Undying, the shrouded, ever-shifting lands of the thirteenth barony of Terrinoth, whose seat at Archaut has remained empty for hundreds of generations. Those who dare travel beyond Greyhaven find themselves in a landscape where warming light seldom reaches the ground, bounded by fetid marshes to the west and the Dunwarr Mountains to the north. The region is filled with volcanic crags and sprawling marshlands that bubble and boil, expelling murderous gases and trapping foolish adventurers in their black muck for eternity. Nearly impassable since Waiqar's betrayal so many hundreds of years ago, the Mistlands serve as the base from which he launches his dark campaigns to raze Terrinoth and gain control over the runebound shards. As his power has grown over the centuries, the Mistlands have spread beyond the original bounds of the Thirteenth Barony, and inexorably continue to extend ever farther into the lands of the living. Notable places within the Mistlands include Waiqar's holdfast of Zorgas, the vampiric domain of Bilehall and its subject Castle Dalibor, the haunted The Misty Hills, and the border territory of Roth's Vale. Sources The Mistlands (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 160

title: The Misty Hills
content: The Misty Hills The Misty Hills, a region within The Mistlands, have been steeped in evil since the time a sadistic Penacor Prince and his followers were executed for unspeakable crimes — death was not the end of them, for the dark oaths they had sworn the night before their hangings allowed them to rise again. History Taking the name Farrenghast, the prince moved to a towering, abandoned keep in the Misty Hills with his fellow revenants. While Mennara always had undead spirits, this was perhaps the first time such fell creatures had banded together in a mass of evil. Over time, their foul essence seeped into the earth itself and made it as vile as they; it was perhaps this darkness that called to the Mistlands, which absorbed the region into itself. Description Despite the horrific nature of the Misty Hills, some still travel here in search of ancient relics and older knowledge. Like their undead inhabitants, the Misty Hills have changed little since the time Farrenghast took the keep and the surrounding lands for his own, and opportunities there are many for the brave and clever. Within the keep, necromantic tomes of tremendous power rest on shelves of decaying wood, their leather bindings and blood-marked pages still fresh despite the centuries. Weapon stores from Farrenghast's many campaigns are said to lie inside the lesser fastnesses within the Hills, including items from across Mennara — for his foes have come from far and wide to thwart him, and after failing left their possessions along with their corpses. Rumors have spread that unbound Stars of Timmorran lie seeded away within unmarked chests, drawing the attention of mages hungry for power or eager to study such priceless rarities. Sources The Misty Hills (The Mistlands), p. 162

title: The Mok Plateau
content: The Mok Plateau Straddling the area between the Riverlands and The Kul Valleys, the Mok Plateau is perhaps the most well-known area of The Broken Plains. Orcs from almost all of the other tribes come here for spiritual guidance, and so the tribe of the Mok, Mok'Thul Urak, rarely are attacked and even gain the protection of other tribes against external threats. Travelers from Terrinoth and other lands come to visit the Orcs here for guidance as well, and pass along tales of the area to others as if the Mok Plateau represented the entirety of the Broken Plains, not knowing the true nature of this many-faceted land. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: The Molten Heath
content: The Molten Heath The Molten Heath lies far to the northeast of the Daqan Baronies, where the sturdy rock that shields Mennara's raging heart grows thin and great gouts of tempestuous fire and molten stone erupt from the ground. Sharp-toothed obsidian crags, black rock ridges, and smoldering rivers of lava radiate out from the center of the heath, but surrounding it is some of the most picturesque lands in all of Mennara: crystal-clear streams, wildflower-dotted plains, and mighty evergreens shelter this primordial landscape, where rich volcanic soil and mountain snowmelt combine to foster a lush and verdant paradise. This impossible land of life and death is known to mortals as the Molten Heath, home to The Heart where the dragons make their roost, the ruined Dwarven cities of The Karok Doum, and the scarred cleft of Black Ember Gorge. Sources The Molten Heath (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 193

title: The Northern Coast
content: The Northern Coast The Northern Coast is the northernmost stretch of The Frontier in the Dunwarr Mountains, where even the sparse Dwarven farms and outposts of the Frontier dwindle away. Its rare inhabitants are most often herders or hunters, making their living tending flocks of bighorn sheep or herds of mountain goats, or bringing down deer, mountain Leonx, and burlback bears in the high crags. Nearly every Dwarf who lives here belongs to the Rangers' Guild, which holds that anyone brave enough to live beyond the safety of rock and stone had best learn to protect themselves; most go months or more without seeing another Dwarf, but in the depths of winter most make the trek to Hadranhold for Wintersmeet. Sources The Frontier (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 190

title: The Raider's Coast
content: The Raider's Coast The broken coast of Isheim, known as the Raider's Coast, is the first great barrier between the land and outsiders, home of the Weik peoples — hardy raiders and pirates. The coast is also the gateway to the continent's interior and its many secrets and treasures. The coasts of Isheim are ruled by the Hearthlords, jarls of the Weik; each lord controls a city or town and has a fleet to prowl the waters beyond the cliff tops and sheltered bays. Adventurers and merchants wishing to make landfall on Isheim must strike a deal with a Hearthlord, for only the Weik and their longships can navigate the coast of Isheim with any degree of certainty. Even with the help of a Weik storm guide, travelers face many dangers that can send a vessel to the icy depths, such as labyrinths of gigantic icebergs, undersea volcanoes that vent geysers of burning steam, and enormous riftwhales that can tear a hole in the hull of a ship to devour those within. Despite the dangers of the frozen sea, the cities and towns of the Weik dot the cliffs and coves of the Raider's Coast. Largest of these is Lagart; second is Seragart, the heart of Weik shipbuilding. Beyond Lagart and Seragart, there are dozens of smaller towns and cities, like the trapper settlement of Weikgart upon the Cracked Lake, or Holmgart and its pirate markets that occupy the Berserker Fjords. Some of these places are inhabited by but a single raider clan, which might comprise a longship and a dozen families, while the larger ones are ruled by a Hearthlord. All are fiercely proud and independent, often fighting with their neighbors, and outsiders can easily become embroiled in these conflicts if they wish to win the support of a Hearthlord. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), pp. 232–233

title: The River Taare
content: The River Taare The River Taare appears in the myths of many races, said to form a border between the Empyrean and the Aenlong, one of two locations that lie within the Aenlong yet also sometimes cross into the mortal realm. The Elves draw a poetic comparison between the waters of the river and tears shed in sorrow, claiming that sadness, like the waters of the river, is not present in the Empyrean. Timmorran himself theorized that the river was formed from the "condensation of the Void" in a moment of somewhat scholarly humor. Sources The Myths of Creation (Tales of Darkness), p. 25

title: The Ru Steppes and Beyond
content: The Ru Steppes and Beyond The wide Plains of Ru, and the dread realm that extends even farther, mark the easternmost reaches of Terrinoth — to the uninitiated they seem little more than a wasteland, the point where the outer reaches of the civilized world crumble away into nothing. Overview The howling plains and dust-cloaked badlands hide secrets as ancient as Terrinoth itself, some buried beneath the surface waiting to be uncovered, like the bones of Llovar's lost kingdom, others lurking in the shadows waiting to strike, like the teeming tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan. Some say the next great darkness to engulf the world is even now brewing out among this forsaken expanse, and each day the Ru's skies grow blacker with the coming storm.
