Of all the wilds of Terrinoth, few are as forbidding or as deadly as the Darklands, yet there are still many reasons why bold-hearted heroes might journey into them. Those in search of plunder and the wealth of ages lost might seek out the ruins of Cradle Fort, Lamenters Rest, or The Hollow Kingdom, places that tried to plant the root of law upon this land and failed. The need to defend Terrinoth's borders also draws the virtuous and brave to the Darklands; adventurers may find themselves throwing in with Daqan patrols, hunting Uthuk raiders deep into their own territories, or even seeking out the source of the ever-spreading Tangle. For the greatest of heroes, the Ru Darklands offer a chance to uncover and perhaps even stem the coming darkness by taking the fight to the gathering Uthuk tribes, seeking out the Black Citadel and Llovar's lost power, or facing the Ynfernael Lords themselves and trying to close the gateways they use to cross the veil. The region encompasses The Borderlands, The Ru proper and its Darklands, and The Charg'r Wastes to the north. Sources The Ru Steppes and Beyond (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 208

title: The Ru
content: The Ru Beyond the reach of the watch forts, where the steppes become broken and scoured by constant winds, the true Ru begins — jagged ridges and gullies, desert plateaus, and dry lake beds baking under a blood-red sky. Table of Contents Overview Description Sources Overview These are the hunting grounds of the Uthuk Y'llan, where their tribes come to shed blood and await a great leader to unite them for their long-awaited revenge. Though the savage Uthuk raiders and their merciless witches and warlocks are a constant peril, the Ru has seen wars and death more than most lands, and many secrets hide beneath its soil. Description Long before the rise of the Locust Horde, a tribe of Dwarves built an empire in the Ru: the remains of their realm, which preceded the First Darkness, are known only as The Hollow Kingdom, the empire's true name lost to history. The Dwarves are not the only ones to have left their mark upon the Ru. It has been the refuge of cabals of sorcerers and dens of criminals. Haunters' Wood, a petrified forest cloaked in eternal shadow, marks the resting place of the Seven Sinners. Countless caves and warrens hold beasts and horrors that have been driven out of other lands; the Caves of Shiverfang, perhaps the most well-known of these caverns, have a fell reputation that even the Uthuk have learned to respect. Sources The Ru and the Darkness (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 210

title: The Spire (Zanaga)
content: The Spire (Zanaga) The Spire is an Orc ruin in Zanaga that stares down upon the Sunscathe Barrens and surrounding lands, a peak that looks like a great slumbering ape when the sun sets upon its slopes — legend holds that Gor-Bor-Gor resides within, waiting for a champion to break the stone chains that hold him. It is the seat of the brigand lord Urgash the Pitiless and his bloodthirsty army of followers. For the most part, Urgash and his people do not leave the Spire, preying upon those foolish enough to enter their lair, though they occasionally venture forth in search of fresh meat. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 254 The Lost Expedition (Zanaga), p. 255

title: The Spire of Ruin
content: The Spire of Ruin The Spire of Ruin was raised by early Uthuk Y'llan warlocks near the place where Llovar began his fateful journey into the T'mara T'rusheen, to commemorate the birth of Uthuk demonic powers. Table of Contents History Description Sources History The Spire was said to bless visions of greatness upon those who flayed themselves with its sharp stones. It was never found or destroyed during the scourging of the wastes, and its location is now a mystery. As the Uthuk reclaim their home, they search for the Spire, for the Sisters of Q'aro Fenn have pronounced its rediscovery a portent of their hoped-for revenge. Also seeking this gateway between worlds are powerful groups and individuals including warlock covens from the shadows of Daqan, necromancers searching for the secrets of true undeath, and even Djinni and dragons who see it as a way to restore their kind to glory. Description Though many covet the power that this rift offers, reaching the Spire is an almost impossible task. Even the Uthuk tread with care, relying on the guidance of their strongest witches and warlocks when they travel in search of the cursed place. Demon winds bellow forth from the hole in reality, gusting out across the Darklands, and as travelers get closer, the land itself becomes tormented and twisted by its power: valleys with teeth that tear at the earth, clouds that scream their hatred at the ground, and rivers that swerve from their beds to drown those on their banks are all possible. Monsters this close to the Spire are almost always possessed by demons, their bestial minds overwhelmed and consumed, leaving only the drive to hunt and kill. The Spire of Ruin rises up from the ground like a spear thrust into the sky. At its tip, the rift into the T'mara T'rusheen — the spirit realm and the Ynfernael beyond — glimmers like a red star, hungrily sucking the surrounding air and the earth below into its gaping maw. From the gateway, it might be possible to travel between worlds, if one can fight one's way past the hundreds of foes and horrors that nest in the Spire's warren of tunnels and then climb to the great altar just beneath the rent. Legend has it that if one can cross the threshold and find an Ynfernael Lord, one can either offer it one's oath, or kill it and gain power unimagined in return. Of course, these same legends warn that the rift is not just a door, but the first step on a path that can lead to any number of places, whether the twisting mirror worlds of the Ynfernael Lords and their burning keeps, the umbral depths where secrets forgotten by the living come to hide, or the sorcerous planes from which all magic springs and reality can be shaped with but a word. Sources A Tear in the Veil (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 212–213

title: The Tangle
content: The Tangle The Tangle is a living thorn wood, a blight that spreads out from the ruins of Athealwel, a forsaken Elven fortress deep in the steppe and rumored lair of an Elven Ynfernael cult. It has extended its briars for leagues to engulf surrounding settlements and camps like a malevolent creature, and the thickets on its fringe encroach into The Aymhelin and Kell's eastern shires. When the moon is dark, the Tangle grows fastest; in such times, defending a town from its tendrils, and from the shadow beasts that lurk within its briars, can make for a long and bloody night of battle. Edlund, among other lords, is continually on the lookout for those brave enough to venture deep into the Ru to Athealwel itself to locate and destroy the source of the Tangle — possibly a demonic tree god, if whispered tales are to be believed. So far, none have returned from such quests, and each year the Tangle pushes its thorns farther west. Sources The Borderlands (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 209–210

title: The Thalian Glades
content: The Thalian Glades The Thalian Glades lie to the west of The Deepwood, where the dense trees of The Aymhelin slowly begin to give way to patches of lush grasses — a miracle of nature, located at the perfect confluence of rain, sun, shadow, and soil. If left unattended, the glades grow wild with their own native foliage; tended by creatures with the deep, passionate respect and love of the land that Elves have, they can support a kingdom. The Elves have worked these lands for untold centuries, developing both physical and mystical connections that allow them to produce an unimaginable bounty from the relatively small open spaces between the trees, mixing golden fields of grain with long rows of vineyards and clusters of orchards with carefully placed apiaries — enough to feed all of the Aymhelin and still have trade stock left over. To protect against raids and incursions, the Elves turned the glades into the base of operations for the Yeron Riders, a legendary flying cavalry unit overseen by Aishalan Finnan. Sources The Thalian Glades (The Aymhelin), p. 178

title: The Thieves' Coast
content: The Thieves' Coast Once, the Thieves' Coast was a shining jewel in the Caliph's crown, its ports beacons of the Caliph's law and might, their soldiers and viziers ensuring steady trade between Al-Kalim, Terrinoth, Lorimor, and a dozen other lands. Description While it remains true that trade still flows like wine and coin fills the coffers of the Caliphate, a slow rot has given the coastline a much darker reputation. These days, the many coves and harbors are as much the home of pirates and thieves as of merchants, and the direct control of the Caliph has slipped away in most of the great sea cities. From Trader's Fort, the vizier Temoth ostensibly controls the port lords of the Thieves' Coast, but in reality Eyrat Five Fingers and the thieves' guild have as much say as Temoth does regarding what transpires along the coastline. While scores of townships and villages dot the coast, there are two areas where travelers are most likely to make port: Cutpurse Bay and the Rothulk Seafort. Old sea forts can also provide their share of peril and glory, each one a jagged broken tooth guarding the entrance to one of the coast's many harbors — though many are still garrisoned, many more have fallen into ruin, becoming haunts of monsters or worse. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 246

title: The Torue Albes
content: The Torue Albes The Torue Albes are a loose association of islands not dissimilar to the Free Cities on mainland Terrinoth, consisting of four major lands and countless lesser islands, many uninhabited or used as secretive smuggling ports. As former colonies of Lorimor freed of the empire's rule, they form an ecosystem, helping one another in what ways they can and creating a system of reliance born more from necessity than family bonds or honor. While relatively independent from each other, they do recognize the authority of a single queen, whose court is held in the city of Dallak on the main island of Alben. Other notable islands include Garnet Island and its city of Gafford, the floating shipyard-city of Tarianor, and Tigh Higard with its port of Shellport and the industrial Ulthik Isle with its city of Hardell. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 223

title: The Ugluk Badlands
content: The Ugluk Badlands In a region filled with inhospitable terrain, the Ugluk Badlands are perhaps the worst of The Broken Plains. With rocky peaks and flash floods that produce new ravines, the area is rough and unforgiving; game is scarce and successful hunts are hard won, and the air is dusty with a thick, earthy odor that few find appealing, or even tolerable. The vegetation is as harsh as the land, but often can be rendered and treated to produce effective — if extremely foul-tasting and painful in application — medicines and poultices that some claim can defeat death itself with the correct preparation. Many Orcs who travel to Terrinoth claim to be from the area, if for no other reason than to impress the terrible nature of the Broken Plains onto others. Being in the interior of the Broken Plains, the Badlands see few visitors. Some travelers pass through here on their way to the narrow passage into the Ru to the north, in quests that later few speak of, as there are few survivors. Some come for the unique medicinal ingredients to be harvested, which can fetch more gold than lesser runebound shards in some cases. For those expert in the saddle, though, it is a place to find the Mag Ugluk Urak riders and their famed reptilian steeds, the Gurak Tol. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: The Unseen
content: The Unseen The Unseen are the hidden, ethereal creatures of Mennara with whom Orc Spiritspeakers communicate through a shamanistic connection to the earth, thinning the barriers that surround Mennara enough to allow apparitions to manifest. Sources Life on the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 202

title: The War of Fire
content: The War of Fire The War of Fire was fought between the Dwarves of The Karok Doum and the dragons of The Molten Heath, who grew to resent the Dwarves as thieves who had stolen the draconic knowledge of the runes Helka the Bold had won from them. Though the Dwarves fought valiantly, such a war could only have one outcome; one by one their cities burned, and the shattered remnants of their armies made a final stand at Black Ember Gorge, where old and frail, Helka led a final army against the dragons while Valnir led the remainder of their people to safety. Helka's devastating final runecraft destroyed the pass along with many dragons, but the rune magic also took the lives of Helka and the brave Dwarves who stood with her, ending the war and scattering the Dwarves into exile — some to the Jornall Clan, others to found Yrthwright's Forge, and Valnir's people north to found the Dunwarr Mountains. Sources The Early History of the Dwarves (Tales of Darkness), pp. 30–31

title: The White Death
content: The White Death Beyond the Crystal Plains, where only the Onoit dare tread, the true north of Isheim begins — the harsh weather turns deadly, and the cold descends to wrap the land in its unforgiving, icy grasp. This is the land of the White Death. Table of Contents Description The Green Vale Sources Description The tundra stretches out in all directions like a blinding white sheet of glass, broken only by twisted icy woods and, eventually, the monstrous peaks of the World's End Mountains. Monsters and dead things infest the far north, fighting among themselves and preying upon those foolish enough to enter their realm; snow falls in an almost constant curtain here, and mists roll down from the World's End Mountains like steam off a cooling corpse. In this baleful white expanse are the remains of the Salishwyrd empire, which was wiped out long ago by the Rime Storm's sorcerous weather. The White Death itself, born of that storm or perhaps a result of the cursed cold itself, thrives here — a frozen wasting that consumes anything not native to the far north, turning Humans into glistening statues or driving them delusional with rime-mania. There are many places where its power waxes strong: at the Lake of Silence, a haunt so cold that the air steals one's very breath, a visitor can't even scream as ice shades tear them asunder, while in the Thorn Vales, beings of iced blood worship wendigo as gods and drive their prey into spike-covered trees to feed their monstrous masters. Excepting the Green Vale and the scattered, ice-locked ruins of former cities, there is little left of the Salishwyrd realm. One of the few structures to remain above the snow is Icegate Prison, where the queen of the ice wyrms, Scarsha, now rules. The Green Vale Amid the ice and snow of the far north is a hidden realm: The Green Vale, home of the last Salishwyrd city. Sources Realm of the White Death (Isheim), p. 236

title: The Years of Hunger
content: The Years of Hunger The Years of Hunger followed The Great Cataclysm, appropriately named for the years in which the skies darkened and the waterlogged soil yielded meager harvests. Hard times are said to produce hard people, and a will to survive drove the Humans and the other younger races onward. A savage, nomadic culture was winning a reputation for ruthless marauding in the far northern wastes during this time; perhaps these barbarians were the ancestors of the great and terrible Uthuk Y'llan people, the oldest of the Human civilizations even as they descended deeper into savagery ever since. Humanity spread from the Ru Steppes into other lands during the Years of Hunger, perhaps fleeing as refugees from the ancestors of the Uthuk; in the lands that were to become Terrinoth, they found temperate climes, cool lakes teeming with fish, abundant woodlands, and fertile valleys, and early settlers soon gave up their roaming ways in favor of permanent residence in villages and farmsteads. The Hunger Years mark the end of history as the Elves tell it and the beginning of Humanity's own, ending with the rise of Arcus Penacor and the Age of Steel. Sources The Troubled Rise of the Younger Races (Tales of Darkness), pp. 29–30 Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), p. 31

title: Thelgrim
content: Thelgrim Thelgrim is the Dwarven capital of the Dunwarr kingdoms, a fortified city built within a vast underground cavern deep in the Dunwarr Mountains. Table of Contents Overview History Description Sources Overview Reached through the fortified Gates of Thelgrim and the seven-league Hearth Road, Thelgrim occupies a single vast cavern lit by crystal starglobes, its buildings arranged in rings around a central lake. The Dwarven king or queen rules from Dunwol Kenn Karnin on one shore, while the Guild Hall of the ten civic guilds stands on the other; the city is also home to the Runeforge, seat of the Runescribes' Guild and keeper of the Dwarves' dragon runes, and to the Hall of the Ancestors, resting place of the Dwarven dead. Founded as a refugee camp during the Years of Exile, Thelgrim was besieged twice by Llovar's Uthuk Y'llan during the First Darkness and relieved both times, before being overrun outright by the Dragonlord Gehennor's forces during the Third Darkness. Its long reconstruction in the Age of Courage, led by First Speaker Ingunn Vergsbold, cemented the political dominance of the Dunwarr Guilds that persists to this day. History Thelgrim began as a simple intersection of tunnels in one of the larger caverns of the Dunwarr Deeps, where refugees of the Years of Exile established a series of camps; over time cloth tents gave way to stone walls, and the camp grew into the fragile beginnings of the city that stands today. During the First Darkness, Llovar marched his Uthuk Y'llan north through the Dunwarr Mountains to besiege Thelgrim, considering the Dwarven capital a particular prize for the position it commanded over the region's supply routes and northern approaches; lacking siege equipment, his forces instead encircled the fortress to starve out its defenders. Falladir Penacor, fighting to hold his own lands against the Uthuk, knew that if Llovar took Thelgrim he would return to ravage Penacor territory next. An alliance of Humans and Elves under Falladir Penacor and King Triamlavar eventually relieved the fortress, though the Dunwarr Deeplords — despite promising the continued use of Thelgrim to their allies — refused to commit their own troops to the field beyond self-defense, over the objections of the Deeplord Halgir Son of Grom. Thelgrim was besieged a second time soon after, and was relieved again when Timmorran sent the Sunderland general Waiqar Sumarion to break the siege. Later in the war, Halgir Son of Grom finally persuaded the Deeplords to commit Dwarven troops, and a force from Thelgrim arrived unexpectedly to reinforce Timmorran's army as it made its stand against Llovar's Host of Thorns at the Battle of the Locusts, which ended the First Darkness with Llovar's death. Centuries later, during the Third Darkness, the dragon armies of the Dragonlord Gehennor swept along the Hearth Road and overran Thelgrim outright — unlike the Aymhelin, which the Elves managed to defend, Caelcira never falling even as the city took heavy losses. It was in the aftermath of this destruction, deep in the Age of Courage, that the reconstruction of Thelgrim began: Ingunn Vergsbold, then head of the Masons' Guild, set out to rebuild the city's long-destroyed districts. Her work continued for decades, and she did not stop at reconstruction — calling on what remained of Thelgrim's noble wealth, she had the Miners' Guild cut the great chasm linking Thelgrim to the Hearth Road that leads to the outside world, while the Merchants' Guild partnered with the Miners' and Explorers' Guilds to reestablish ties with the other Dunwarr holds. As trade and travel along the reopened Hearth Road increased, so did the power of the guilds; many of the noble families who had refused to invest in the rebuilding lost their estates in Thelgrim to the guilds' expansion, and are said to still plot in distant holds for a chance at revenge. By 1550 the Guilds ruled Dunwarr in all but name, and within two more decades had codified the laws governing the election of Dunwarr's speakers from among the Guildmasters — with Ingunn Vergsbold becoming First Speaker. Description Thelgrim is reached through the Gates of Thelgrim, banded and reinforced steel doors nearly two hundred hands high, shaped in the silhouettes of two mighty Dwarven warriors standing back to back. The doors bear the dents and scars of dozens of assaults, testament to their indestructibility, and are backed by hidden defenses: murder holes and disguised firing ports that let unseen Dwarven guardians rake attackers with crossbows, ballistae, and firebombs, hidden sally ports for counterassaults, and a diverted waterfall that can flood the entire approach valley. A light garrison holds the Gates themselves, for even a few score soldiers can hold them for weeks while Thelgrim is only a day's march away; the garrison is commanded by Bradha the Shield, a grim and experienced veteran who also inspects the caravans traveling up from Frostgate to trade with Thelgrim's merchants. Beyond the Gates lies a vast stone receiving hall, lit by shafts that bring light from the surface, from which the Hearth Road departs: an underground passage seven leagues long and wide enough for five wagons to travel abreast, its walls covered in intricate runework recording a history of the Dwarven people for those who can read it. The road is smooth and polished throughout, the work of Dunwarr Dwarves who can work stone and metal by feel as much as by sight. The Hearth Road opens into the vast cavern that houses Thelgrim itself, filled with towering stalagmites and outcroppings of living rock. Before the Third Darkness the road ran unbroken into the cavern, but since Gehennor's dragon hybrids used the Hearth Road to reach Thelgrim's heart, the Dwarves have cut a deep chasm across that side of the cavern; only a single arching bridge now links the Hearth Road to the city, guarded at its far end by further gates and battlements. Similar defenses guard the city's northern exit into the Deeps, each set of gates flanked by one of the two barracks of the Warriors' Guild — the southern barracks under Skirmisher Captain Lyssa Svensdottir, who oversees military action outside the mountains, and the northern barracks under her brother Guard Captain Einalf Svensson, who oversees the defense of the Deeps and the Palace Guard protecting King Geirmund Ragnarson. Thelgrim itself fills a single massive cavern, eternally lit by hundreds of crystal starglobes crafted by the Runescribes' Guild; from outside, their radiance makes the city look like a giant geode, while inside they give the streets a dim, gentle glow that Human visitors tend to find bothersome. Buildings are as often dug directly into the cavern walls and stalagmites as built freestanding on the cavern floor, and are arranged in rings running outward from the city center, where a towering aqueduct redirects an underground river into a Dwarf-crafted lake that also supplies the city's fresh water. At the far end of the lake stands Dunwol Kenn Karnin, "The Fortress inside the Mountain" — a fortress within the fortress-city, from whose depths King Ragnarson rules seated on Tanngnoster's Throne, the final refuge of the Dwarven people in their darkest hours. On the lake's opposite shore stands the Guild Hall, its facade bearing one ornately decorated pillar for each of the ten guilds that form the heart of Dwarven society; unlike the sober royal fortress, the Guild Hall is loud and lively, its guild heads and representatives given to spirited debate that occasionally devolves into brawls ended by dunking the combatants in the lake. Home to the Runescribes' Guild is the Runeforge, a massive cruciform hall built partly into the cavern walls at the city's edge, housing the Dwarves' collection of known dragon runes. Its four wings each serve a distinct purpose: the south wing holds offices and meeting chambers, the west wing contains the forges, casting molds, and foundries where runic items are made, the north wing houses two copies of every known dragon rune cast in metal and set into rock slabs, and a further wing pointing toward the Molten Heath preserves the complete records of Dwarven history etched onto copper sheets. Beyond preserving that history and etching runes into arms and armor, the runescribes — led by Master Scribe Dorgan Hammerfist — also search for new runes or ones lost with the destruction of the Karok Doum; Hammerfist is said to be considering hiring adventurers to explore the ruins of the Dwarves' ancestral cities on the Molten Heath for that purpose. Deeper still beneath the city's heart lies the Hall of the Ancestors, repository of the Dwarven dead: seven hundred thirty-four unsealed sarcophagi hold the newly deceased for seven hundred thirty-four days before their bones are moved into a miles-long collection of antechambers shared, in a loose sense, with their families or guilds. Only the monarchs of Dunwarr receive individual burials, interred in elaborate sealed tombs whose tableaus and engraved poetry relate the legends of their reigns. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 187–188 The Mountain Gates (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 186–187 The Dunwarr Mountains (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 186 Hadranhold (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188 Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188 Labyrinth of Deurg (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 The Early History of the Dwarves (Tales of Darkness), p. 30 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35–37 The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 46 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 50–51

title: Thelsvan Plains
content: Thelsvan Plains The Thelsvan Plains lie within the barony of Cailn, overlooked by Castle Tagis — verdant yet abandoned since the Dragon Wars, their charred farmhouse ruins uninhabited ever since. The soil is rich and fertile, said to be fertilized by the blood and ash of those who died there, and the plains are held to be haunted by the dragons' victims and the soldiers who made their final stand. All who have attempted to resettle the Thelsvan Plains in the intervening centuries have met with disaster. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Thieves' Guild (Al-Kalim)
content: Thieves' Guild (Al-Kalim) The thieves' guild holds great power in Al-Kalim, its cutpurses found everywhere within the Caliphate and enjoying a prosperous position under Eyrat Five Fingers's shadowy rule of Haruun. The guild takes a dim view of "freelancers" in its territory, so most cutpurses are accounted for; they are marked with the guild's tattoo and must tithe a measure of their take to the local den bosses. The guild also holds significant sway over the harbors of The Thieves' Coast alongside the vizier Temoth. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), pp. 245–246 Life in the Sands (Al-Kalim), p. 249

title: Thieves' Guild Cutpurse
content: Thieves' Guild Cutpurse Cutpurses of the thieves' guild are everywhere within the Caliphate, coming in many forms, from filthy street urchins and beggars feigning debilitating injuries to well-dressed merchants and offspring of the nobility, as the strength of a good thief is often the ability to get close to a target without raising suspicions. These nefarious robbers are most often found in taverns and markets where crowds are at their thickest, although daring individuals can operate wherever there is wealth for the taking. Many cutpurses work in teams, one or more distracting the mark while the others relieve them of their money; a victim who turns on a cutpurse might be in for a nasty surprise when they are led on a chase into a blind alley containing a dozen or so of the cutpurse's companions. Guild thieves are not above using clubs, blades, and fists to obtain what deception and quick fingers could not. Sources Life in the Sands (Al-Kalim), p. 249

title: Thorn Vales
content: Thorn Vales The Thorn Vales are valleys deep within the forest known as the Needles, within The White Death, where beings of iced blood worship wendigo as gods and drive their prey into spike-covered trees to feed their monstrous masters. Sources Realm of the White Death (Isheim), p. 236

title: Three Skulls Trading Company
content: Three Skulls Trading Company Of all the merchant concerns that plunder the wealth of Zanaga, none are as large and powerful as the Three Skulls Trading Company — a veritable army unto itself, controlled by the pirate lords of Orris in the Torue Albes, peopled by every race imaginable. In many ways, Three Skulls is all that passes for a non-native government in Zanaga; its distinctive triple-skull emblem can be seen on most exported goods as well as flying above settlements as far inland as Terr's Crossing. Motivated solely by a chance to make more coin, the local guild captains of Three Skulls are more than happy to help out travelers and adventurers, often funding their expeditions and even offering them guides, mercenaries, and discounts on goods — though such deals always come at a price, for canny guild captains will never strike a bargain if it is not in their best interests. Adventurers who are careless when it comes to reading the fine print may find themselves returning from an expedition owing the captain more treasure than they recovered, putting them in debt to Three Skulls, and once a person is in debt, a guild captain will do their best to keep them there. Many of the company's guild captains secretly serve the spider goddess Arachne. Sources The Lost Expedition (Zanaga), pp. 255–256 A New World (Zanaga), p. 255

title: Tigh Higard
content: Tigh Higard To the north of Garnet Island is rocky Tigh Higard, an irregularly shaped island of The Torue Albes anchored at the north and south by the Crystal Crags and the Nodan Mountains, a wide river splitting these formations and flowing eastward through Shellport, the island's largest city, before emptying into the ocean. It is a rough island with rough climates. Ice and snow cover the tall peaks to the north and south, home to terrible creatures that all too often venture downward for food; the plains below are also dangerous, with tall grasses hiding silent reptilian predators and, worse, press-gangs on the coasts ready to kidnap anyone they find into their crews. Some even whisper that on nights when the moon is blood red, the barriers between worlds begin to warp and strange things emerge from the undergrowth — long-dead sailors are said to rise from their graves in search of their lost treasure, and werewolf tribes prowl the beaches for sacrifices to their dark gods. Out beyond Tigh Higard to the west is the Sea of Smoke and deep waters, where tales in the Shellport taverns speak of gigantic aquatic creatures so large as to be mistaken for islands themselves. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 224

title: Timmorran
content: Timmorran Timmorran Lokander, son of Llander and Rala and nephew of Llovar, was one of the great heroes of the First Darkness, a wizard whose campaign against his uncle and the Uthuk Y'llan culminated in the Locust Lord's death, and who is credited with founding the Free City of Greyhaven. Table of Contents Early Life The First Darkness Later Life Legacy Sources Early Life Born to fugitive parents fleeing Llovar's wrath on the Night of Summons, Timmorran was orphaned by the age of five and struggled as a friendless beggar on the streets of Lorimor, his untrained talent for magic already apparent in street sorcery performed for astonished crowds. A conclave of local wizards inducted him into their order, and he was later apprenticed to the celebrated wizard Sal Meringyr, who planted in him a dangerous ambition to crystallize the Verto Magica's own energy. When assassins of Q'aro Fenn sent by Llovar finally tracked Timmorran down, Sal Meringyr died defending him; Timmorran then fled across the seas to the far-off continent of Ghom, making a new life for himself in Al-Kalim, also known as the Sunderlands, where he offered his services to the tribe of Ashan the Elder and grew into an ever more potent magician and adventurer, as well as a friend to one Waiqar Sumarion. The First Darkness In the year 481, Timmorran persuaded Ashan the Elder to send an army of Sundermen to the defense of Talindon against Llovar's invasion, reasoning that if the Uthuk could not be stopped there, war would eventually come to his own homeland. The plan took a year to come together; in 482 he reinforced the alliance and began clearing raiders from southeastern Talindon, and by 483 his campaign began in earnest, splitting the allied army into two contingents — one under himself, the other under the Sunderland general Waiqar Sumarion — with the consent of Falladir and Triamlavar. At the Battle of the Burning Hills, Timmorran struck down Chief Lukosh with his own magic, breaking the Orcs' loyalty to Llovar's cause. In 487, the Host of Thorns overwhelmed Falladir's forces at The Ashen Field, and Timmorran regrouped the survivors in the foothills of the Razor Crags for a final stand, reinforced unexpectedly by Dwarven troops from Thelgrim under Halgir Son of Grom. In the climactic Battle of the Locusts, Timmorran withstood Llovar's sorcerous assault behind a shield of pure force before piercing his uncle's rotten heart with a lance of arcane power, ending the First Darkness with Llovar's death. Later Life Though records of Greyhaven's founding are sketchy, most hold that it was Timmorran himself who founded the northern city, perhaps for refugees lost in the wilderness and those seeking to forget the horrors of the war he had just fought. He later journeyed with an army into the Charg'r Wastes to rescue Waiqar from the ruins of Llovar's Black Citadel, and was instrumental in persuading the Lords of Talindon to crown Baron Daqan king in Llovar's aftermath. In his final years, his obsessive quest to preserve his power for future generations led him to create the Orb of the Sky at the Tower of Meringyr — an ambition that, when Waiqar betrayed him on the Night of Betrayal, cost Timmorran his life. Legacy The Stars of Timmorran, unstable magical artifacts capable of powering great magic, are named for him; when the dragonlords of the Third Darkness broke these Stars down into smaller, stable runebound shards, they transformed the nature of magic across Mennara. Sources The Rise of Timmorran (Tales of Darkness), p. 35 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35–37 The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), pp. 38–39 The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 39–41 The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 45–46 The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 147 The Early History of the Dwarves (Tales of Darkness), p. 30

title: Torue Albes War Academy
content: Torue Albes War Academy The Torue Albes War Academy in Garnott is the premier military training school in The Torue Albes. Its graduates invariably become heroes in the Albesian or Lorimor Imperial Navy, having trained for years in every aspect of seamanship and deck fighting. Eschewing armor for the stark uniform of the officers' corps, they are a striking sight in any sea battle, and more than a match for any upstart privateer. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 223

title: Tower of Knives
content: Tower of Knives The Tower of Knives hangs like a dagger from the cavern roof of Haruun, where acrobatic killers of the Hysshari Brotherhoods master the arts of wall walking. Sources Life in the Sands (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Tower of Meringyr
content: Tower of Meringyr The Tower of Meringyr is a tall keep Timmorran had built in the remote Wizard's Vale for the purpose of magical research, named in tribute to his old tutor Sal Meringyr, whose ambition to tap the Verto Magica had become Timmorran's own. It was here that Timmorran and his acolytes strove for years to create the Orb of the Sky, and here that Waiqar and his soldiers stormed the gates on the Night of Betrayal, slaying the guards and apprentices before Waiqar himself struck down the exhausted Timmorran in his own workshop. Sources The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 39 The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 40

title: Tower of Nerek
content: Tower of Nerek The Tower of Nerek is a strange and forbidding ruin that stood upon lonely downs in the region that took its name, Nerekhall — so awful was its aspect that no farms or homesteads stood in its shadow, and a deep sense of foreboding gnawed at the sanity of anyone who spent time nearby, wracking their sleep with nightmares and their waking thoughts with delusions. It is said that Elves originally built the tower, though they refuse to confirm the rumor and stake no claim on the dismal ruin. The Lord of Nerekhall used it as a prison, and it was here that Prince Farrengol Penacor and his companions were interred to await King Jerlon Penacor's judgment; in the dark nights of their imprisonment, the group discovered the tower's ill secret — a Daewyl portal nestled in an attic nook, and within it an Ynfernael shade to whom Farrengol promised fealty in exchange for freedom, a bargain that would raise him from death as Farrenghast after his execution. Sources Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), pp. 32–33

title: Trader's Fort
content: Trader's Fort Trader's Fort is a young and vibrant vizier city-state of Al-Kalim strung out along the edges of the Vale of the Shepherds, ruled by the vizier Temoth, Keeper of the Bazaar. It is a gateway to The Thieves' Coast and the first port of call for travelers entering the Caliphate proper. Its more common name, the City of Foreigners, is well deserved — within its walls are districts dedicated to most of the world's major peoples and races. Trader's Fort is a good place to find both adventure and work, as many prominent merchants, warlords, and wizards have agents here on the lookout for recruits; some of these are more than willing to spill the blood of their rivals if it means securing the services of a talented hero. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245

title: Traitor's Wastes
content: Traitor's Wastes The Traitor's Wastes are badlands bordering the empire of Lorimor to the west of Southern Terrinoth, which together with the Lorim's Gate Mountains prevent much overland trade between the two lands. The interior is largely uninhabited, while scattered coastal communities nearby often fall prey to pirates and longboat raiders in search of slaves and supplies. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 137

title: Trast
content: Trast Trast, the Gateway to Terrinoth, lies east of the Lorim's Gate Mountains in Southern Terrinoth, its lands extending to the borders of the Tanglewood. Its proximity to the Aymhelin, and to Summersong specifically, has resulted in greater interaction between its residents and the Latari Elves than most Humans of Terrinoth experience — not all of it friendly. Trast draws its wealth from silver and iron mines in the foothills of the mountains, and its people do limited hunting and logging on the outskirts of the Tanglewood, though many claim the forest is haunted by werewolves. Latari scouting parties have grown more visible of late, and while fearful peasants blame the Elves for attacks on isolated farmsteads, belligerent nobles rail against the encroachment on Trastian lands; Baron Rault can dismiss the peasants' fears but cannot ignore the nobles' saber-rattling. Baron Rault rules from Castle Artrast, a just man but quick to take offense at any perceived sleight to his honor. Trast's population is split between those who view Rault as too ready to acquiesce to Latari and Lorimor envoys, and those who criticize his heavy-handed approach to treating with the Elves as an unnecessary provocation risking war; agitators on both sides seek to sway him, and some whisper of a conspiracy to unseat him. In the foothills of Lorim's Gate, ancient menhirs rise from a rough circle of earthen mounds, where twice a year adherents of forbidden beliefs are said to gather to commune with unknowable entities under dark and twisted priests — Rault has expressed interest in learning the truth of these rumors, but the site's isolation prevents routine patrol. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 137–138

title: Tree of Tales
content: Tree of Tales The Tree of Tales is an ancient oak within Eventide Forest, viewed as sacred by many throughout the region despite certain misgivings from the Church of Kellos — host, according to local legend, to a powerful spirit both the residents of Dragonholt and the Hyrrinx who live within Eventide regard as sacred or special. Many residents visit the tree to tell it their stories, leaving behind charms, offerings, even pages of written stories and text; the Tree of Tales is hung with many such offerings, others nailed or lacquered to the trunk or tucked into its branches. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 123 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Trelton
content: Trelton Trelton is a small coastal city to the north of Dallak and just south of Ulthik Isle, renowned even in Terrinoth for the greatness of its metalsmiths and artificers. The proximity to high-grade materials in Moonraven Heights, Stagwood Forest, and Mount Ulthik — in addition to the patronage of the queen — means that, while it is not a tremendous city in its own right, its place of honor is secured by the sheer number of its weapons that have hacked their way into legend. Trelton also contains a monastery of sorts, the Fraternity of the Mountain. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 224

title: Trevalyan
content: Trevalyan Baron Trevalyan rules Otrin from his ancestral home Skydown, sited at the foot of the Mountains of Despair not as a defense against rival baronies but as a bulwark against the creatures of the range's foothills and heights. Living in constant vigilance for threats descending from the mountains, Trevalyan hosts aspiring Knights of the Citadel who hunt manticores and other monsters there to prove their worth. In recent times he has begun — to the chagrin of some of those knights — enlisting traveling adventurers for expeditions against specific beasts or preemptive strikes on the mountain denizens more generally. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Trevnor Soulstone
content: Trevnor Soulstone King Trevnor Soulstone kept his court in the Free City of Tamalir and held a great cache of the Stars of Timmorran in his treasury during the Time of the Elder Kings. When the dragonlord Margath descended upon Tamalir at the outset of the Third Darkness, he broke into the royal palace and burned the king to charred meat along with his family and retainers, leaving Terrinoth without a ruler once more and gathering up the palace's riches, including its sizable cache of Stars. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 45

title: Trials of Frostgate
content: Trials of Frostgate The Trials of Frostgate are the greatest of the rituals performed each winter by the Northern Tribes in Frostgate, using a variety of sacred elixirs and herbs to access ancestral spirits. To prove themselves worthy, contestants enter spirit planes to face challenges of strength, cunning, and courage, often against aspects of mighty animals. Those who succeed gain the blessings of the spirits and are marked with tattoos proclaiming them Champions of Frostgate — a powerful reward in the Free City, and to travelers assembling there before venturing into the North, a sign that its bearer possesses adequate prowess for the dangers ahead. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 148

title: Triamlavar
content: Triamlavar King Triamlavar led the Latari Elves of The Aymhelin to war alongside King Falladir Penacor against Llovar's Uthuk Y'llan during the First Darkness, beginning a great tradition of alliance between Humans and Elves against Ynfernael threats. Triamlavar's forces relieved the siege of Thelgrim and later joined Timmorran's campaign against Llovar. At the climactic Battle of the Locusts, he leapt to shield Timmorran from a charging Uthuk assault led by Kul the Serpent, and was pierced through the belly by one of Kul's envenomed arrows while distracted — a sacrifice, alongside those of Halgir Son of Grom and Ashan the Elder, that was not in vain, for it allowed Timmorran to survive the onslaught and ultimately slay Llovar. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 36–37 Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 187–188

title: Truelight Lantern
content: Truelight Lantern Truelight Lanterns are wrought by the magic of the Latari Elves, looking more like large, multifaceted jewels than the glass-and-iron lanterns associated with craftspeople of the Free Cities. When activated, the lantern gives off a soft green glow that somehow illuminates the surrounding area as effectively as a flaming torch. The light cast by the lantern also pierces illusions, allowing the bearer to see things like magically concealed doors and traps. Sources Magic Items, p. 111

title: Tyrek Gorm
content: Tyrek Gorm Tyrek Gorm was a particularly zealous marshal of Dhernas, said to have hanged a thousand brigands from the boughs of the trees in the woodland that came to bear his memory: the Hanging Woods. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Ukirlu
content: Ukirlu Ukirlu is the largest Onoit holdfast, nestled in the heart of the Greenwood, one of the few true havens in all of Isheim. Sources An Uncharted Wilderness (Isheim), p. 235

title: Ulfen
content: Ulfen The Ulfen are intelligent canines that act as mounts for the Onoit, said to be able to judge a person's worth by their scent — if newcomers are worthy, the Ulfen lead them back to the gnome camps. Ulfen war dogs also guard Onoit burial sites and magical cairns alongside their shamans, ready to see off intruders. Sources An Uncharted Wilderness (Isheim), pp. 235–236

title: Ulfred Varl
content: Ulfred Varl The venerable Ulfred Varl is the Hearthlord of Lagart, and ostensibly first among equals as ruler of the Weik's largest city. In truth, however, his power has long been waning, and as though he were an old alpha wolf, his rivals — including Baergul Rus of Seragart — nip and snap around his heels, continually seeking weakness. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), p. 233

title: Ulon Heronglade
content: Ulon Heronglade Baron Ulon Heronglade held reactionary opinions regarding kingship that often led him into heated argument with King Daqan over the king's reforms. In 513, when King Daqan was ambushed and slaughtered while traveling to arbitrate a baronial border dispute, it was whispered that the Bloodguard Knights had been hired to waylay and murder the king by none other than Ulon Heronglade. Led by Waiqar, the Council of Barons took resolute action: it had Castle Heronglade razed to the ground and the baron seized. Ulon Heronglade never stopped protesting his innocence, even as he dangled from a cage from the gates of Archaut and slowly starved to death. Sources The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), pp. 38–39

title: Ulthik Isle
content: Ulthik Isle The northernmost island of The Torue Albes, Ulthik Isle is an inhospitable marshland barely above sea level, with a small volcanic mountain chain rising from the mire while the rest of the terrain is thoroughly wet and unpleasant, as though the surrounding waters were winning the battle to reclaim the land. Were it not for the purity of the many ores to be found here, it is likely it would have remained uninhabited. Those ores, from rich iron deposits to thick veins of magical minerals, have transformed the island into a hotbed of industry. Furnaces and soot-stained workshops stud the face of Hardell, its primary city, which competes with the volcanoes and their constant fumes to see which can produce more noxious gases. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 225

title: Ulur Deep
content: Ulur Deep The Ulur Deep is a wonder of the Onoit people, a cavern of weeping ice reputed to hold generations of buried shamans. Sources An Uncharted Wilderness (Isheim), p. 235

title: Urakuhl
content: Urakuhl Urakuhl is the mountain perch of Ghur'zhun Urak, the "Lightfoot Tribe," from which they have an eagle's eye view of the vast terrain surrounding The Broken Plains, acting as a kind of early warning of impending attack from outsiders. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 199

title: Urgash the Pitiless
content: Urgash the Pitiless Urgash the Pitiless is the brigand lord who rules the Spire in Zanaga with his bloodthirsty army of followers, preying upon those foolish enough to enter their lair. Legend has it that Urgash is the degenerate descendant of the Orc spiritspeaker Hrgrun, and the terrible king still wears Hrgrun's glowing magical crystal around his bloodstained neck. Sources The Lost Expedition (Zanaga), p. 255

title: Urnas the Unmarked
content: Urnas the Unmarked Urnas the Unmarked slew a thousand mortals for the A'tari Djinn Jyrrii, for the promise that no blade might ever cut his flesh again. His stone form still stands unmoving in the ruins of Jyrrii's city on the spot where the Djinn granted his wish, a cautionary tale of the risks of striking a deal with a Djinn. Sources The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Uthuk Y'llan
content: Uthuk Y'llan The Uthuk Y'llan are the corrupted, demon-worshipping raiders of The Ru, once peaceful plains-dwellers of the Loth K'har transformed into a hungry horde of locusts when Llovar fell prey to the Ynfernael. Table of Contents History Overview Tribes Sources History On the Night of Summons, Llovar led his tribe's greatest warriors into the T'mara T'rusheen with promises of great rewards and forbidden bindings; they emerged physically transformed by Ynfernael influence, wiry muscles grown supernaturally powerful and their very bones pushed through their skin to form great spikes and blades. With these warriors at his side, Llovar formed a confederation of tribes, conquering those who refused to ally willingly — even the chiefs of the Scal and L'jan tribes, many times larger than the Loth K'har, bent the knee. The campaign bloomed into full civil war between the tribes of the plains, and the Loth K'har and their allies took on the new title of Uthuk Y'llan, "locust swarm" in the language of the plains people, as they conquered more and more of the Ru — a name earned in earnest as Llovar's Host of Thorns went on to ravage Talindon during the First Darkness. Overview To traverse the Darklands is to enter the world of the Uthuk Y'llan and their Ynfernael allies. Here, the tribes rule the cursed earth beneath the baleful light cast from The Spire of Ruin — the midnight heart of the Darklands themselves. There are many Uthuk tribes, each grown from splinters of Llovar's host, yet a few stand above the rest in size and ferocity. Tribes The Gore Claws are the largest and most aggressive of the Uthuk, descendants of the prophet Golreth, who keep the legends of Llovar and the Ynfernael masters alive and strive to unite the tribes as the self-proclaimed inheritors of the Locust Swarm. The Flayed Kindred do not covet rulership of the Ru like the Gore Claws; instead they seek only to make themselves closer to the power of the Ynfernael realm, and hold many of the keys left in the wake of Llovar's demise, including those believed to open the gates to the Black Citadel. The Night Howlers hold territories close to the borderlands and are among the Uthuk's most skilled raiders, having perfected the art of night fighting from the depths of Nyak Sutchra'aa, the Chasm of Eternal Night. Beyond these three largest tribes, scores of others roam the Ru Darklands, dwelling in blighted caves, crumbling temples, and profane ruins such as the Tower of Hands, the Ynargal Cathedral, and the Spinespirit Caves. Only the barest information on the major Uthuk settlements exists, for few outsiders ever see them and live. Captives taken to the Breeding Pits of Yyrg are hurled into bone cages to be possessed by Ynfernael spirits and transformed into beasts of war. Only slightly less harrowing than the pits is the Well of Sins, deep within the Gyrar Abyss, where the Uthuk come to trade slaves and souls. The greatest Uthuk settlement is the circle of war camps around Kaylor Morbis, where the bloodsisters now hold court, settling disputes via ritual combat, gathering their forces, and planning invasions of other lands. Sources The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), pp. 33–34 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 35 Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 211–212

title: Valnir
content: Valnir Valnir was the daughter of Helka the Bold, saved as a child from a wasting sickness by her mother's dragon-bought runecraft, who grew to become a great leader of her people in The Karok Doum and led the survivors of the War of Fire to found the Dunwarr Mountains. At Helka's final stand at Black Ember Gorge, Helka charged Valnir with leading the remainder of their people to safety while she gave her life to destroy the pass and many dragons with it. Valnir led her people to the mist-shrouded peaks north of where Terrinoth would arise, and as dragons still flew out of the north, the Dwarves built their fortresses underground and eventually called the mountains the Dunwarr, or "sanctuary." Valnir's children became the first Deeplords, protecting and leading their people. Sources The Early History of the Dwarves (Tales of Darkness), pp. 30–31

title: Var Ni
content: Var Ni Var Ni is the mummified god of madness and terror, an object of horror among the people of Zanaga. Var Ni once spread his wings and blotted out the sun, or so the legend goes, before feasting upon tribes under a veil of eternal night. Only the rise of great heroes brought the mighty beast low, but they were not able to truly destroy Var Ni before his servants dragged away his corpse and embalmed it beneath the ground. In the Chasm of Despair, it was the Whispermen who unearthed Var Ni's vast remains, and it is they who pour the blood of their sacrifices into his fanged maw. Even in his inert state, the bat god sends out vile dreams and squalls of darkness across the land, causing shamans to mumble of the coming night and whole regions to suddenly plunge into darkness. Sources The Lost Expedition (Zanaga), p. 255

title: Vault of Jade Twilight
content: Vault of Jade Twilight The Vault of Jade Twilight is one of the Stars of Timmorran believed to have escaped capture by the dragons during the Third Darkness. Even the slightest hint of its existence is enough to launch legends among treasure-seekers and scholars alike. [not stated in source: no further detail on its appearance, powers, or current whereabouts is given] Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 120

title: Vel'tar Demonblood
content: Vel'tar Demonblood Vel'tar Demonblood is one of the Ynfernael Lords served by the bloodsisters and nightseers of the Uthuk Y'llan, whose greatest followers become his mortal representatives, their interests often becoming their own. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 213

title: Velvet Plains
content: Velvet Plains The Velvet Plains are a stretch of natural beauty in Southern Terrinoth, admired by the region's inhabitants and farmed by the people of Otrin; their southern extent also reaches into the barony of Pelgate. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 137 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Vengeance Seekers
content: Vengeance Seekers The Vengeance Seekers are one of several groups in Dunwarr society — alongside the Alchemists' League and Fireforgers — that strive for the power and prestige of a full Guild and constantly scheme to supplant one of the ten existing Guilds, who in turn work tirelessly to maintain their own authority. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189

title: Verdant Ring
content: Verdant Ring The Verdant Ring is the fertile band surrounding The Heart of The Molten Heath, where the hellscape of the center gives way to a plain of heather and gorse, with shrubs and even conifer trees fanning outward, and wild berries and grains sprawl across the landscape while fantastical fruits and nuts hang heavy from the branches of trees. The Dwarves have long strove to reclaim the bounty of the Verdant Ring, and now other peoples of Terrinoth look north and see a potential sanctuary from the scourges of war — if only they can keep the dragons at bay. Sources The Domain of Dragons (The Molten Heath), p. 194

title: Verdelam
content: Verdelam The Verdelam, or "green-blooded," are Elves of lower blood, often dozens of ignoble generations removed from the first Latari, who live in jarring, uncharacteristically dilapidated homes hidden far behind the borders of Lithelin's green lands. Lowborn Elves, having little chance for advancement given the Latari's incredibly long lives, tend instead to dedicate themselves to becoming masters of the vocations their tribes need for survival, forming the bulk of the Latari armies. Desperate to prove themselves worthy of social ascension, each morning these enterprising souls journey to the keep and surrounding temples to perform the mundane tasks and menial labor that keep the kingdom functioning smoothly. This allows them — at a pace that would mortify any of the world's shortlived races of Mennara — to slowly earn the respect and prestige necessary to arise to meaningful posts within Elven society. Those who fail to ascend but are unwilling or unable to return to their former lives usually take one of two paths: they embrace the life of an adventurer and seek fame and fortune in the lands beyond Lithelin, or they join the ranks of the soldiers in the Latari army under Captain Ilendar. The nomadic Leonx Riders, the wild Free Hunters of old, exemplify the primal nature more associated with the Verdelam than with the rest of Latari society. Sources Elves (Character Species), p. 62 Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), pp. 175–176 Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), p. 179

title: Verse Magic
content: Verse Magic Music has been a part of Mennara's history from its origins; many of the oldest records exist only as songs passed from one generation to the next. When the most talented or earnest pour their hearts into their music, it is as though they can truly cast a spell upon their listeners — for even mundane music echoes in its art the Lays of The First, which flow through and nourish all of creation, and some primal part of every listener remembers the songs of creation. Description Each culture has its own traditions of song and music, with different roles for music and musicians depending on their needs: Elven Loremasters sing the histories of their people, relying on tempo and key to convey what words alone cannot; the Dwarves sing ancient rhythmic work songs to keep pace at their crafts; Gnomes use music to lighten the load and lift their spirits while traveling from town to town; Catfolk use song to call the tribes together and communicate while hunting; the Orcish peoples sing to celebrate their ancestors and the spirits of the land that nourish them; and Humans use music to impress and woo one another, or simply to pass the time. Singers, musicians, dancers, and poets of sufficient skill and sincerity are able to produce magical effects from their melodies, lyrics, and movements; their rhyming structures, vocal ranges, or instrument techniques either evoke the magic of the original Lays or inspire a near-magical response in the listener. Bards need not be trained magicians to accomplish these effects, and indeed most are magically naïve — or boastful — individuals who would credit the effect of their music on their own virtuosity alone. Sorcerers and Runemasters consider bardic magic much more limited and subtle than their own arts, but the troubadour knows the potency of their craft: they can imbue themselves and their companions with improved morale, revitalizing energy, increased determination, feelings of concentration, or speed and stamina on the march, and certain performers can even produce unnerving dissonances that cause fear or resentment in their targets. The musical instruments of bards are as varied as the lands of Mennara itself. Stringed instruments such as lutes, zithers, and lyres are common in all regions, some renowned Tamalir bards using small dragon scales as picks; bowed instruments like viols and the cranked lyres of Al-Kalim offer richer sounds but require greater skill. Bards who don't rely on their voices favor pipes, flutes, and the like, or drums, chimes, and bell lyres to produce percussive martial tones before battle. Horns are also popular — the Elves employ ones made using materials gifted from sentient creatures of the Aymhelin — but most notorious are Dunwarr bagpipes made from preserved dragonskin, which fables say can turn entire armies away. Sources The Virtues of Verse (Call to Adventure), p. 125 Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), p. 125

title: Verto Magica
content: Verto Magica The Verto Magica, also called "the Turning," is the spiritual mechanism The First set into motion after conjuring the three Planes of Power, involving the rise and fall of the Empyrean and the Ynfernael planes. Without the Verto Magica, everything would be fixed in place, and time would stand still; learned beings propose that for something to occur, the energy for such an occurrence must exist, and that all such energy is due to the Turning. Timmorran's old tutor Sal Meringyr harbored an ambition to crystallize a measure of the Verto Magica's own energy, a dangerous idea he planted in his young apprentice's head — an ambition that Timmorran carried forward decades later in his creation of the Orb of the Sky. Necromancers debate whether death magic itself draws upon the Verto Magica, or upon some lower, related form of energy. True Sorcery According to texts supposedly penned by Timmorran himself, after the Empyrean and Ynfernael were created, their constant vying with one another for supremacy caused each realm's influence to rise and fall in a cyclical manner — in some ages the dark forces of the Ynfernael were ascendant and sorrow and madness reigned, in others the Empyrean's influence dominated and peace prevailed. This eternal transit between opposing forces created a spinning wheel, the motion termed the Turning; theory holds it to be the force behind the movement of the sun, moon, and stars, the turning of the seasons, and the processes behind the weather — in short, the Verto Magica is the force of all change in the world, the relentless march of time. It was rare in the days of the Steel Age for one to be born with the gift to harness the Verto Magica directly, and it is rarer still in the current age of uncertainty. This force can be touched by one with the gift, akin to dipping one's fingers in a rushing stream, allowing a "true sorcerer" to draw power from the wellspring or even redirect the flow of the energy itself. The Elves nevertheless consider this "lower magic" compared to their own Empyrean arts, tainted as it is by the influence of the Ynfernael and more destructive and chaotic in its effects; nonetheless there are more Elven true sorcerers than mortal ones, as only Elves have the long life spans necessary to dedicate themselves to mastering the Verto Magica and become powerful storm sorceresses or frost mages even without runebound or unbound shards. Sources The Myths of Creation (Tales of Darkness), p. 25 The Rise of Timmorran (Tales of Darkness), p. 35 The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 39, 41 The Source of Sorcery (The Magic of Mennara), pp. 116–117

title: Viason I
content: Viason I Emperor Viason I of Lorimor oversaw the empire's rebuilding after the Third Darkness, the only one of the so-called Elder Kings and other rulers of the age to have survived the Dragon Wars. While the dragons had ravaged the lands of the Lorimor Empire, Lorimor's great cities had largely weathered their assaults thanks to the invention of particularly powerful ballistae and the buffer that was Terrinoth separating Lorimor from the Molten Heath. In the centuries following, Lorimor not only recovered but flourished under Viason's rule: many migrants from Terrinoth moved to the peninsula, new settlements were founded to house them, and expansionist ambitions saw Lorimor establish colonies on the coastlines of The Torue Albes and beyond, with fleets reaching distant Ghom and fostering close ties with the Caliphate of Al-Kalim. Viason was a beloved monarch who took full advantage of his celebrity through self-indulgent hedonism; while he never grew fat or gouty, he was to go down in history as one of the world's most fecund monarchs, and within a generation his extended family made for a complex web of interwoven aristocracy that led to the rise of houses such as House Harthorn and House Varnii — and to generations of palace intrigue and arguments over inheritance. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), pp. 48–49

title: Viason III
content: Viason III Viason III, infant son of the assassinated Emperor Derisian IV of Lorimor, was left in the regency of his aunt Deliana until he came of age. In 1315, Viason III was seized by persons unknown; for more than a year his fate was a mystery, until it was revealed he was in the care of a distant uncle of House Varnii on one of the islands of The Torue Albes, who claimed to have rescued the boy from "a gang of pirates." Deliana's subsequent military response was averted only by her own sudden death. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), p. 49

title: Viper Legion Archer
content: Viper Legion Archer Uthuk warriors are natural raiders, and none more so than the viper legion archers. As befits the vile ways in which the Uthuk wage war, members of the viper legion make extensive use of sorcerous poisons to tip their arrows, brewed by the viper war leaders and blessed by the Blood Coven, tailored to the enemy's weaknesses. Heroes' Bane works against a foe's courage so as to kill the brave faster than the cowardly, while Nightshood is made from the powdered remains of powerful undead and can steal an enemy's sight. Perhaps the deadliest of all is the Kiss of Set, crafted from the distilled blood of a naga, which turns the target's heart into a bomb, bursting from their body and leaving a toxic cloud in their wake. For their arrows to do their work, viper legion archers train constantly amid the storm-lashed wastes of the Darklands, testing their hunting skills on vicious beasts and hapless travelers. In this manner, each legion archer becomes a master of ambush and mobile warfare, striking swiftly with surprise and then vanishing again before their foes can retaliate. For full-scale battles, the Uthuk mass their viper legion archers, favoring overwhelming force against the benefits of lone hunters; when the archers loose their arrows, the skies darken with writhing forms, and the din of battle is momentarily drowned out by the long hiss of a hundred serpentine arrows hungry for blood. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 217

title: Vision Rune
content: Vision Rune A vision rune allows a character to expand their eyesight to extraordinary lengths. They can see over the horizon and even through sealed containers or behind walls, abilities any thief or spy would pay anything to possess. Wizards can also use them to hurl spells at hidden foes or in darkness, and one is said to have allowed the sightless Jenti the Just to recover from unhealable injuries and become a famed sorcerer in the Lorimor Imperial Court. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 121

title: Vorun'thul
content: Vorun'thul Vorun'thul is one of the Lords of Bilehall, a vampiric noble of Bilehall who, like Kyndrithul, has had hundreds of years to set traps, arrange countermeasures, and prepare against almost any enemy foolish enough to venture into their domain. Sources Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), p. 165

title: Vrede
content: Vrede Vrede, City of Flame and Frost, is an ancient volcanic city of Isheim where Weik and Onoit coexist, one of the great wonders of the north. From a distance, Vrede cleaves the sky in two with the constant coiling smoke that emerges from its peak; as travelers approach, an active volcano stands out in stark relief against a backdrop of mountains, its sides free of snow as its black rocks shimmer with caged heat. The city stands at the head of a partially frozen river, which provides seasonal access to the sea but also a path deeper into the lands of the Onoit, and has become a meeting place for the races of Isheim as well as an important trade nexus. Vrede's inhabitants have built their settlements, joined by bridges and platforms, around the volcano's hissing caldera. It is never cold in Vrede, as a series of hot springs forces heat and water up from below. Adventurers stopping here might find the wonders of the north and southern goods for trade, and rub shoulders with Weik pirates, Onoit trackers, and merchants from Terrinoth to Al-Kalim. There is adventure to be had in the city of steam, for none know with any certainty how deep the hot springs go, or what may hide within their mist-shrouded depths — some believe an ancient dragon slumbers beneath the city, coiled fitfully upon a pile of plunder, while others whisper of a fire cult chanting in the dark to bring about the end of the world. Sources An Uncharted Wilderness (Isheim), pp. 234–235

title: Vynelvale
content: Vynelvale Vynelvale is one of the eight Free Cities of Terrinoth, the monastery city and holiest of them all, located southeast of Riverwatch at the juncture of the Guardian Hills and the Great Plains. History According to the current Grand Hierophants of Kellos, soon after the Second Darkness a vile necromancer near Vynelvale sought to create an undead empire for himself. A band of heroes assembled to defeat him but were struck down; the last survivor, moments from a sorcerous death, called out for aid and swore eternal service to any who would come. His eyes clouded, and his body became wreathed in flame; raising a hand that shone bright enough to make the sun seem a flickering candle, the invigorated survivor smote the necromancer with one wave and banished his undead army forever. As his sight returned he knew that a divine power had interceded. He kept the promise he had made and began preaching of the intercession and the god's power; others who remembered tales of cleansing fire from the Second Darkness, and had lit an Eternal Fire in remembrance, soon joined him, and together they established a church to the being he believed had aided him: Kellos. His followers named him the first Hierophant of Kellos, and upon his death he was canonized as the church's first saint; later hierophants added wings, halls, bastions, and other constructions, turning the Grand Cathedral of Kellos into a structure to rival the greatest castles of the Daqan Lords. Description Vynelvale is the administrative and educational center devoted to Kellos, God of Life, Flame, and Justice, a popular pilgrimage site housing the greatest library in Terrinoth outside Greyhaven University. Behind its towering walls, hundreds of initiates silently tend gardens and fields while innumerable scribes spend years copying holy texts and other rare documents. It is here that the Priests and Knights of Kellos are trained in the greatest secrets of their god, able to banish the taint of darkness with little more than a touch and beloved by the people they go out to protect with cleansing flames; pilgrims traveling to Vynelvale for healing loudly cheer them as they pass, recognizing their distinctive red and gold colors and the burning hand of Kellos each wears on their armor. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149

title: Waiqar
content: Waiqar Waiqar, later known as Waiqar the Betrayer or Waiqar the Undying, was once the famed Sunderland general Waiqar Sumarion, a trusted ally of Timmorran during the First Darkness, before his fall into undeath and treachery cost Terrinoth its thirteenth barony. Table of Contents The First Darkness The Ru Campaign The Night of Betrayal The Second Darkness Later Betrayals Sources The First Darkness In 483, during the war against Llovar, Timmorran split his allied army into two contingents, sending Waiqar Sumarion — a proficient wizard as well as a skilled military leader — to relieve the besieged fortress of Thelgrim, a task he accomplished with ease. Growing bored with the duty, Waiqar devised his own campaign against the undead forces of Farrenghast and banished the undead horde in a great success. Eager to press his advantage after the allies' subsequent victory at the Battle of the Burning Hills, Waiqar gathered a warhost and led it into the wastes of the Charg'r, directly toward Llovar's Black Citadel, and vanished from all record for the rest of the war. It was only after King Daqan's coronation that Timmorran assembled an army and journeyed nearly six months into the Charg'r Wastes to discover his fate, finding him at last in a deep oubliette among Llovar's many prisoners — a once-proud general reduced to a forlorn, emaciated figure. Little is known of the details of the rescue itself, save that Timmorran urged Daqan to forbid all further travel east and had every map of the Charg'r Wastes destroyed. The Ru Campaign Waiqar's recuperation took many months, and the signs of emaciation and neglect never left him; once confident and brash, he was now given to sullen moods. When Timmorran beseeched him to command the army once again, Waiqar accepted to the rejoicing of his troops, though his taste for recklessness had been wrung from him — he now favored a colder approach to warfare. He commenced the Ru Campaign against the Uthuk warlord Da'Roul Bonesplicer, vanquishing him and annihilating the Uthuk camps throughout the Ru so thoroughly that the threat was believed destroyed for generations. Yet in the hour of his triumph, Waiqar scorned all praise, complaining to his captains of Timmorran's complacency and arrogance — an early sign, in hindsight, of the resentment curdling within him. He was later elevated to the Council of Barons and granted the thirteenth barony in the northwest of Terrinoth, near The Misty Hills and the marshes of the Karahesh, where he ruled justly if with a militaristic bent, training a legion of veteran Sundermen who had settled his lands. The Night of Betrayal The motives behind Waiqar's betrayal are known only to himself, though it is popularly supposed that he had been turned against Timmorran and civilized people while incarcerated and tortured in Llovar's dungeons, a darkness that finally bloomed into full hatred and violence. Waiqar gathered troops to his barony, claiming that only he could be trusted with the power of Timmorran's Orb of the Sky. As twilight fell on a cool autumn day in 515, a legion led by Waiqar launched an assault on the Wizard's Vale, storming the Tower of Meringyr with an iron-bound ram, slaying the guards, and putting Timmorran's apprentices to the sword. As Waiqar's warriors neared the workshop, Timmorran — realizing his folly in creating the Orb — shattered it and had Lumii Tamar spirit its fragments away; exhausted from the effort, he could not resist when Waiqar burst in and slew his old friend, tearing the one surviving fragment from his dead hands. Waiqar vowed to hunt down the remaining fragments, swearing that anyone who denied him so much as the tiniest sliver would face his murderous wrath. Such was the dire weight of that oath, and perhaps so volatile the magical energies unleashed by the Orb's destruction, that his very vow summoned a great tempest of freezing, poisonous rain that snuffed out the lives of all who stood within sight of Meringyr — yet the dead did not rest easy. Waiqar Sumarion, now Waiqar the Undying, left the Wizard's Vale at the head of a fearful column of shambling corpses, the first of his Deathborn Legion. The Second Darkness Waiqar returned to his lands, thereafter known as the Cursed Barony, which darkened further still into the dense, dank fog that shrouds it to this day. His agent Zarihell established the first Death Cults of Waiqar in Tamalir, sparking a destructive riot that drew the barons' armies away from his own borders and let him seize the initiative; while his legions plundered towns and farmsteads for weapons and raw materials for new undead, Waiqar directed them to take specific captives back to his lands for interrogation about the Stars of Timmorran. His two chief lieutenants — Zarihell, who organized cult activity, and Ardus Ix'Erebus, who directed the Legion's movements on the field — coordinated their efforts so that every major action of the Deathborn Legion occurred in concert with riots in Terrinoth's cities, ravaging the Barony of Camford to destruction after the Battle of Ramscrossing and scourging the land for six years. Waiqar might have taken Archaut itself and the Stars kept there by the newly formed Lumii Order, but the city proved too well defended and resistant to the cults' influence; only the arrival of the mysterious holy man Kellos at the refugee camp of Dawnsmoor, and the alliance of Elves, Dwarves, and Kellos's followers he helped assemble, finally forced the Deathborn Legion to retreat to the Cursed Barony in 521. Later Betrayals His treachery cost Terrinoth its thirteenth barony, a loss so significant that the gathering of the remaining twelve Daqan Lords is still called the "Council of Thirteen" in its memory, and his black chair rests in Archaut as a constant reminder to the barons of the insidious lure of darkness. As Waiqar the Undying, he commands the Deathborn Legion and the undead of his Cursed Barony from the fortress of Zorgas, and spent years searching for the Stars of Timmorran. During the Third Darkness, he dispatched columns of undead warriors to aid the invading dragons — motives that remain disputed, whether to curry favor for a Star of Timmorran, seek revenge on the barons who once humiliated him, or, as some believe, to have engineered the dragon war himself by planting word of the Stars across the Molten Heath to draw Margath's attention. In the Age of Courage, he charged a loyal follower known as the Raven Priest with destroying the Citadel once and for all, arming him with the Carrion Fetish, a talisman infused with the bone dust of dozens of Reanimates; the resulting Raven Horde was destroyed at Carum's Cross by the allied counties of Allerfeldt, Rostum, and Haverford. Sources The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 38 The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 39–42 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 36–39 The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 47 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 51–52 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Wanderer Gnome
content: Wanderer Gnome Wanderer Gnomes rarely have a fixed home, having gotten a taste of the outside world during their year with their township's militia and set out to "scratch their itchy feet."
